These words, it says, "signify continuity and permanence" — meaning that this punishment of Hell "will materialize only when one's actions are all the time motivated by material interests only, having practically no concern for the Hereafter." It describes a settled, total direction, not a bad week.

Ayah 19 words it differently — *wa man **arāda** al-ākhirah* — and Maʿārif draws the contrast deliberately: **as soon as a true believer forms the intention of the reward of the Hereafter in whatever he proposes to do, that deed of his stands accepted** — irrespective of any corruptive element having entered into something else he was intending to do.

Maʿārif then states the principle plainly. The first condition — being all the time motivated by material interests only — "can only be that of a denier of the Hereafter, therefore none of his deeds is acceptable." The second condition is that of a true believer: a particular deed of his that issues forth with sincerity of intention, and is for the Hereafter, along with the presence of the other conditions, is acceptable. And a deed from that very same person that has no sincerity, or where the other conditions are missing, will not be acceptable.

That last line is worth sitting with. For the believer, acceptance is not a permanent label stamped on the person; Maʿārif assesses it **deed by deed**, by the sincerity and the conditions of each one.

## Striving of its own kind

Ayah 19 is unusually precise. It attaches three things to its promise, and Ibn Kathir takes them one at a time.

**First, the wanting.** *Wa man arāda al-ākhirah* — "wanting the Hereafter and its blessings and delights." The desire has to actually be for that.

**Second, the striving — done its way.** *Wa saʿā lahā saʿyahā*, "and strives for it, with the necessary effort due for it." Ibn Kathir defines this in one phrase: **"seeking it in the right way, which is following the Messenger ﷺ."** Wanting the destination does not license any road to it.

**Third, faith underneath it all.** *Wa huwa muʾmin*, "while he is a believer" — Ibn Kathir: "his heart has faith, i.e., **he believes in the reward and punishment**." That is what the faith is specified as here: belief in the reward and the punishment — the very conviction that gives striving for the Hereafter its point.

The second of those three conditions is where Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concentrates its commentary, and it builds the point on the possessive ending of *saʿyahā*, "its own striving." By adding that word, Maʿārif says, "it has been made explicit that every deed and every effort is not necessarily beneficial or acceptable with Allah. Instead, the only deed or effort credible is that which is appropriate to the essential objective (of the Hereafter)."

And how is anyone to know what is appropriate to that objective? Maʿārif answers: whether or not it is appropriate **"can only be found out from the statement of Allah Taʿālā and His Messenger ﷺ."** There is no other instrument for measuring it.

The consequence follows hard. Even *well-meaning* efforts, made "by insisting on bland personal opinion and self-invented ways" — and Maʿārif explicitly includes here the common customs of **Bidʿah**, which it glosses as "innovations in established religion" — "no matter how good and beneficial they may appear at their face," are not appropriate to the effort made for the Hereafter, and "consequently, they are neither acceptable with Allah nor are they of any use in the Hereafter." Sincerity alone does not qualify a method; the method has its own qualification, and it is revelation.

**Steadiness, too.** Maʿārif quotes Tafsir Ruh al-Maʿani on the same word: the effort should be in accordance with the Sunnah, and along with that it should also have "uprightness and firmness." In other words, the deed should be both in accordance with the Sunnah and upright and constant. "Doing it haphazardly or doing it in a cycle of doing and not doing is not good. It never yields the maximum benefit."

**And the promise.** *Fa-ulāʾika kāna saʿyuhum mashkūran* — "then such are the ones whose striving shall be appreciated, (rewarded by Allah)." Hold that beside ayah 18: there, the man himself is *madhmūm*, blamed; here, the striving is *mashkūr*, appreciated and rewarded. Two lives, two verdicts, and each verdict lands on exactly what the person invested.

## Both hands filled from one bounty

Having separated the two, ayah 20 does something that can catch you off guard: it puts them back together. *Kullan numiddu hāʾulāʾi wa hāʾulāʾ* — "On each these as well as those We bestow." Ibn Kathir: **on each of the two groups, those who desire this world and those who desire the Hereafter, We bestow what they want.** The believer is not the only one being supplied. The world-seeker's success is also something arriving from above, not a leak in the system.

*Min ʿaṭāʾi rabbik*, "from the bounties of **your** Lord" — Ibn Kathir: "He is the One Who is in control of all things, and **He is never unjust**. He gives to each what he deserves, whether it is eternal happiness or doom. His decree is unstoppable, no one can withhold what He gives or change what He wants."

Then: *wa mā kāna ʿaṭāʾu rabbika maḥẓūran* — "and the bounties of your Lord can never be forbidden," meaning, Ibn Kathir says, that no one can withhold or prevent them. He preserves two early readings of that closing word, and they sit well together:

- **Qatadah**: it means they "can never decrease."
- **Al-Hasan and others**: it means they "can never be prevented."

So no rival and no obstacle stands between Allah's giving and its recipient — and the supply does not run down by being given.

This is the ayah that answers a question people have always felt: *why do the heedless prosper?* Read with ayah 18, the answer is in front of you. They prosper because Allah gives, on His terms, to whom He wills — and ayah 18 has already told you what waits at the end of that giving for the man who wanted nothing else. Receiving is not the same as being approved of.

## The ranking you can see, and the one still being written

Ayah 21 begins with an instruction: *unẓur*, "See." And what Ibn Kathir tells us to look at is strikingly ordinary — the inequality already in plain view: **in this world "some are rich and some are poor, and others are in between; some are beautiful, some are ugly and others are in between; some die young while others live to a great age, and some die in between."** Notice how insistently he repeats "in between." Human life is not two blocks but a graded scale — and every point on it, ayah 20 has just said, comes from the bounty of your Lord, who "is never unjust."

Then the ayah lifts your eyes: *wa lal-ākhiratu akbaru darajātin wa akbaru tafḍīlā* — "and verily, the Hereafter will be greater in degrees and greater in preferment." Ibn Kathir explains: **the differences between them in the Hereafter will be greater than the differences between them in this world.** Some will be in varying levels of Hell, in chains and fetters, while others will be in the lofty degrees of Paradise, with its blessings and delights — and the people of Hell will vary in their positions and levels, just as the people of Paradise will. In Paradise, he says, there are one hundred levels, and the distance between one level and another is like the distance between heaven and earth.

To make that distance imaginable he cites a hadith recorded **in the Two Sahihs**, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "The people of the highest levels (of Paradise) will see the people of ʿIlliyīn as if they are looking at distant stars on the horizon."

(*ʿIlliyīn* is the name the report gives to a rank among the people of Paradise; Ibn Kathir brings the hadith immediately after mentioning Paradise's hundred levels, to show how vast the distance between those levels is. He does not gloss the name any further here, and neither will I.)

So even *within* the successful, the ranks stretch away like stars. That reframes the command at the start of the ayah: the inequalities you can see and resent in this life are the smaller ones. The consequential ranking has not been published yet — and, as ayah 19 has just promised, the striving that is done the Hereafter's own way is exactly what is appreciated and rewarded there.

## Living it

- **Audit the direction, not just the day.** Maʿārif ties ayah 18's threat to actions that are "all the time motivated by material interests only, having practically no concern for the Hereafter." The honest question is not "was I worldly this week?" but "when my wanting settles, where does it settle?"
- **Make the intention, deliberately.** Maʿārif's reading of ayah 19 is generous: as soon as a believer forms the intention of the reward of the Hereafter in what he proposes to do, that deed stands accepted — even if something else he was intending had a corruptive element in it.
- **Check the method against the Sunnah, not against how good it feels.** *Saʿyahā* means striving of the kind the Hereafter itself requires, and Ibn Kathir defines that as following the Messenger ﷺ. A practice that looks appealing but rests on personal opinion and self-invented ways is, in Maʿārif's words, of no use in the Hereafter.
- **Prefer small and steady to large and sporadic.** Ruh al-Maʿani's addition, as Maʿārif quotes it: uprightness and firmness alongside the Sunnah. A cycle of doing and not doing "never yields the maximum benefit."
- **Stop reading provision as a verdict.** Ayah 20 says both groups are supplied from the same bounty. Wealth is not a certificate and hardship is not a rejection; the giving proves that Allah gives.
- **Move the competition.** Ayah 21 tells you where the real degrees are. Ranks here differ by a little; there, Ibn Kathir says, the differences are greater still — and that is the ranking your striving is aimed at.

passages.title: Worship Allah alone and honour your parents
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat open the practical instructions of the sūrah: worship Allah alone, and treat the two people who raised you with honour. Tawḥīd and kindness to parents arrive in a single sentence in ayah 23, and the passage closes, in ayah 25, with mercy for the child who slips.

## Where this comes in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the sequence. The preceding verses set out conditions attached to the acceptance of deeds: no deed is accepted unless it comes with īmān (faith) and accords with the Sharīʿah (Law) and the Sunnah. Now come instructions regarding those deeds themselves, whose observance brings success in the Hereafter and whose contravention brings ruin. Since the most important of those conditions is īmān, the first injunction here is belief in the Oneness of Allah (tawḥīd); only after that come injunctions relating to the rights of the servants of Allah (ḥuqūq al-ʿibād) — and the first of those belongs to parents.

## Ayah 22: two words worth slowing down over

"Do not set up any other god with Allah." Ibn Kathīr explains that Allah is addressing those who are responsible among this Ummah: do not admit any partner into your worship of your Lord.

Ibn Kathīr renders the consequence, "or you will sit down reproved, forsaken (in the Hellfire)."

**Reproved** — because of associating others with Him.

**Forsaken** — because the Lord, may He be exalted, will not help you; He will leave you to the one whom you worshipped, and that one has no power to benefit or to harm; the Only One Who has that power is Allah alone, with no partner or associate.

Imam Aḥmad reported that ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: whoever is afflicted with poverty and goes and asks people for help will never get rid of his poverty, but if he asks Allah for help, then Allah will grant him the means of independence sooner or later. This was also recorded by Abū Dāwūd and at-Tirmidhī, who said, "Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ Gharīb."

## Ayah 23: "Your Lord has decreed"

The word is **qaḍā**, which normally means a decree. Ibn Kathīr explains that here it means "commanded." Mujāhid said it means *enjoined*, and Ibn Kathīr records that Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Ibn Masʿūd and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim recited the ayah with the word **waṣṣā**: "And your Lord has waṣṣā [enjoined] that you worship none but Him."

Ibn Kathīr observes that the idea of worshipping Allah is connected to the idea of honouring one's parents, as He says elsewhere: "give thanks to Me and to your parents. Unto Me is the final destination" (31:14).

Imam al-Qurṭubī, quoted in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, builds a ruling on this joining: in this verse Allah has made it **wājib** (necessary) to respect and treat parents well by combining it with the command to worship Him — just as the need to thank Him is combined with the need to thank one's parents (31:14). This proves that after the obligation of worshipping Allah, obeying parents is the most important thing. Qurṭubī confirms it with the hadith of Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī in which a person asked the Prophet ﷺ, "Which is the most favoured deed in the sight of Allah?" He said, "Ṣalāh at its preferred time." Asked which came after that, he said, "Treating parents well."

## Why old age in particular

Ayah 23 names a moment — "if one of them or both of them attain old age in your life." Serving parents is not restricted to any age; it is wājib under all conditions. But there are circumstances that impede fulfilment of what is obligatory, and the Qur'an's pattern, Maʿārif explains, is to address them directly while insisting that compliance is imperative anyway.

Old age is a terrible condition. Parents become helpless, depend on their children for everything, and the slightest indifference breaks their heart. Its infirmities make a person naturally irritation-prone; and in extreme old age, when reason and comprehension no longer seem to be working, some of their wishes and demands assume proportions which children find difficult to take care of.

The Qur'an takes cognizance of this and, while instructing children to comfort them, reminds them of their own childhood. There was a time when they too were far more helpless and dependent than their parents are now; their parents sacrificed their own comforts and bore their unreasonable child talk with love and affection. Reason and nobility demand that the past favour be paid back — which, says Maʿārif, is what is alluded to in the closing words of ayah 24: **"as they brought me up when I was young."**

## Maʿārif's five instructions

Across ayat 23 and 24, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out five instructions relating to the old age of parents — the first three in ayah 23, the last two in ayah 24. The fifth is the duʿāʾ, taken up below.

**1. Do not say even "uff" to them.** Ibn Kathīr: do not let them hear anything offensive from you, not even say "Uff!" which is the mildest word of disrespect. Maʿārif presses further: *uff* covers every word or expression that shows one's displeasure — even breathing out a long breath after hearing what they said is included. In a hadith narrated by Sayyidnā ʿAlī, the Prophet ﷺ said that had there been some other degree of hurting lesser than the saying of *uff*, that too would certainly have been mentioned.

**2. Do not scold them** — *wa lā tanharhumā*. Ibn Kathīr: do not do anything horrible to them. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Rabāḥ said it meant, "Do not raise your hand against them." Maʿārif notes that *nahr* means to scold or reproach. These first two instructions are the negative side — prohibiting even the least emotional pressure on parents.

**3. Address them with respectable words** — *qawlan karīman*. Ibn Kathīr notes the pattern: when Allah forbids speaking and behaving in an obnoxious manner, He commands speaking and behaving in a good manner — and glosses the phrase as speech that is gentle, kind, polite, and carries respect. Maʿārif calls this a lesson in the art of conversation with parents: talk to them softly, with love, grace and concern. The revered Tābiʿī Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib described the manner as "like a slave talking to his strict master."

**4. Submit yourself before them in humility out of compassion** — *wakhfiḍ lahumā janāḥa'dh-dhulli mina'r-raḥmah*. Ibn Kathīr: be humble towards them in your actions. Maʿārif opens the image: **janāḥ** literally means "wings" or "sides of arms," lending the sense that one should stand in a stance of submission and humility as a mark of respect for parents. The addition of *mina'r-raḥmah*, "out of compassion," warns that this stance should not be a show-off, but adopted on the foundation of genuine, heartfelt respect. Maʿārif adds that humility before parents is no disgrace — it is a prelude to real honour, for it is based on concern, compassion and kindness.

## 5. The duʿāʾ, and what it is for

The passage ends not with behaviour but with a prayer: "My Lord, be merciful to them, as they brought me up when I was young." Ibn Kathīr says: say this when they grow old, and when they die.

Maʿārif explains why a prayer is the fitting close. To provide maximum comfort for parents is humanly not possible. One should do whatever is possible and, along with it, keep praying to Allah that He, in His infinite mercy, remove all their difficulties. This last instruction is so extensive that it continues to be valid even after the death of parents; through it, one can always keep serving them.

**A ruling on this duʿāʾ.** If parents are Muslims, making a prayer for mercy in their favour is obvious. But if they are not Muslims, then — abridged from al-Qurṭubī in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān — making this prayer within their lifetime is permissible with the intention that they be delivered from worldly distress and that they be blessed with the tawfīq (granted ability) of īmān; after their death, making a prayer of mercy for them is not permissible. Ibn Kathīr moves the same way: he records that Ibn ʿAbbās said, "But then Allah revealed: (It is not (proper) for the Prophet and those who believe to ask Allah's forgiveness for the idolators...)" [9:13].

## What the Sunnah does with this ayah

Ibn Kathīr gathers many hadiths here. Narrated through a number of chains from Anas and others: the Prophet ﷺ climbed up on the minbar and said, "Āmīn, Āmīn, Āmīn." Asked why, he said that Jibrīl had come to him and named three doomed men — one who hears the Prophet ﷺ mentioned and does not send blessings upon him; one who sees Ramadan come and go and has not been forgiven; and one who grows up with both his parents or one of them still alive, and they do not cause him to enter Paradise — and after each, Jibrīl said, "Say Āmīn," and he said Āmīn.

Imam Aḥmad reported from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said three times over, "He is doomed — the man whose parents, one or both of them, reach old age while he is alive and he does not enter Paradise." Ibn Kathīr notes that this version is Ṣaḥīḥ although no one recorded it other than Muslim.

Imam Aḥmad recorded Muʿāwiyah ibn Jāhimah as-Salamī saying that Jāhimah came to the Prophet ﷺ and said he wanted to go out to fight. He asked, "Do you have a mother?" He said, "Yes." The Prophet ﷺ said, "Then stay with her, for Paradise is at her feet." Ibn Kathīr notes that this was recorded by an-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah.

Imam Aḥmad recorded that al-Miqdām ibn Maʿdīkarib said that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Allah enjoins you concerning your fathers; Allah enjoins you concerning your mothers" — the mothers repeated three times — "Allah enjoins you concerning your close relatives, then the next in closeness." This was recorded by Ibn Mājah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds reports it takes from Tafsīr Mazharī: that a father is the main gate of Jannah, and it is up to you to preserve or waste it (the Musnad of Aḥmad, Tirmidhī, Ibn Mājah and the Mustadrak of Ḥākim, from Sayyidnā Abū'd-Dardāʾ); that the pleasure of Allah is in the pleasure of a father, and the displeasure of Allah in the displeasure of a father (Jāmiʿ at-Tirmidhī and al-Mustadrak of al-Ḥākim, from Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, which Ḥākim rates as Ṣaḥīḥ); that when a person asked what rights parents have over their children, the Prophet ﷺ said, "They both are your Paradise, or Hell" (Ibn Mājah, from Sayyidnā Abū Umāmah); and that an obedient son who looks at his parents with mercy and affection receives the reward of one accepted Ḥajj against every such look cast — even a hundred times a day, for Allah is great and His treasures never run short (al-Bayhaqī, from Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās).

One more carries a sting. Al-Bayhaqī (in Shuʿab al-Īmān) and Ibn ʿAsākir report from Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās that for one who remained obedient to his parents for the sake of Allah two gates of Paradise shall remain open, and for one who disobeyed them two gates of Hell shall remain open — and one gate if he had just one of the two. Asked whether the warning held even when the parents had been unjust to him, the Prophet ﷺ said three times, *wa in ẓalamā* — "even if they were unjust." Maʿārif draws the outcome plainly: children have no right to settle scores with parents.

Al-Qurṭubī, quoted in Maʿārif, records an episode. A man came to the Prophet ﷺ complaining that his father was taking away what belonged to him. Jibrīl then came and told the Prophet ﷺ to ask the father about words he had composed in his heart which his own ears had never heard — verses recalling how he had fed the boy in infancy and nursed him through sick nights, staying awake and weeping as though the illness were his own, only to be repaid at maturity with hard-heartedness. Hearing this, the Prophet ﷺ held the son by his shirt and said that he and his property, everything, belonged to his father.

## Where obedience stops, and where it does not

**Obedience has a ceiling.** Maʿārif records that Muslim scholars and jurists unanimously hold that obedience to parents is wājib only in what is permissible — and not in what is sinful. The hadith cited: *there is no obedience to the created in the disobedience of the Creator.*

**Faith is not a condition for good treatment.** Imam al-Qurṭubī quotes from the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhārī an event concerning Sayyidah Asmāʾ, who asked the Prophet ﷺ whether she could entertain her mother, a Mushrik, who came to see her. He said, *ṣilī ummaki*: respect the bond of relationship with your mother and entertain her. And there is the statement of the Qur'an itself: if a person's parents are disbelievers and order him to become like them, it is not permissible to obey them in that matter — but while living in this world they should be treated *maʿrūfan* (31:15), in the recognised manner, which means with courtesy.

**Their permission over your projects.** As long as jihad has not become an individual obligation (farḍ al-ʿayn) but remains a collective obligation (farḍ al-kifāyah), Maʿārif states, it is not permissible for any son to participate without the consent of his parents. It is reported in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, on the authority of Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, that a person presented himself before the Prophet ﷺ for permission to participate in jihad. He asked, "Are your parents alive?" He submitted, "Yes." He said, *fa-fīhimā fa-jāhid* — "then carry out jihad in the service of those two" — the sense being that by serving them he would get the reward of being in jihad. Another report adds that the man said he had come leaving his parents crying behind, and was told, "Go. Make them laugh as you made them cry." From this, Maʿārif derives the general ruling that anything rating as a collective rather than an individual obligation may not be undertaken without the permission of parents — including travelling to acquire the knowledge of religion at the highest level, or for the daʿwah and tablīgh of dīn.

## When they are gone

Good treatment of the relatives and friends close to one's parents falls under this same injunction, Maʿārif notes, especially after the parents have died. In the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhārī it is reported from Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar that the Prophet ﷺ said the noblest regard one can show to a father after his death is to treat his friends well. And Sayyidnā Abū Usayd al-Badrī reports that he was sitting with the Prophet ﷺ when an Anṣārī asked whether any right of his parents remained due after their death. He said yes: praying and seeking forgiveness for them, fulfilling the promises they had made to someone, being kind and respectful to their friends, and showing mercy and generosity to such relatives who are linked in kinship only through them (ṣilat ar-raḥim). Maʿārif adds that it was the blessed habit of the Prophet ﷺ to send gifts to the lady friends of Umm al-Muʾminīn Sayyidah Khadījah after her demise.

## Ayah 25: the mercy that closes the passage

Maʿārif names the anxiety that warnings this heavy raise: children live with their parents all the time, and conditions vary; maybe on some occasion they utter something against the norms of due etiquette — and then they stand facing the warning of Hell.

Ayah 25 answers: **"Your Lord knows best what is in your souls."** Ibn Kathīr reports Saʿīd ibn Jubayr saying that this refers to a man who said something that he did not think would be offensive to his parents. Maʿārif draws the conclusion: should any such word be uttered out of anxiety or lack of discretion, without intentional disrespect, one must repent and resolve never to do it again — and since Allah knows the secrets of hearts and knows it was not meant to hurt, things will turn out for the better, for He is Most Merciful.

The word for those He forgives is **al-awwābīn**, rendered here as "those who turn to Him in repentance." Ibn Kathīr gathers the early views: Qatādah said, "To the obedient who pray"; Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, in a report of Shuʿbah from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, said it refers to those who commit sin then repent, and commit sin then repent; and Mujāhid narrated from ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr that it is the one who, when he remembers his sin while he is alone, seeks the forgiveness of Allah.

Ibn Jarīr said the best view is of those who said that it refers to the one who repents after committing sin, and who leaves that which Allah hates for that which He loves and is pleased with. Ibn Kathīr says this is correct, citing Allah's words, "Verily, to Us will be their return" (88:25), and adding that according to a Ṣaḥīḥ hadith the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would say when he returned from a journey, "We have returned repenting, worshipping and praising our Lord."

Maʿārif notes that *al-awwābīn* as used here carries the sense of *at-tawwābīn*, those who repent before Him, and that the Hadith calls the six rakʿahs after Maghrib and the nawāfil of al-Ishrāq *Ṣalāh al-Awwābīn* — embedded in which is the hint that the tawfīq of these prayers goes only to those who are the Awwābīn and Tawwābīn.

## Living it

Guard the smallest sounds — the sigh, the tone, the raised voice — and replace them with *qawlan karīman*. Lower the wing out of real compassion rather than performance. Do what you can for their comfort, pray for what you cannot do, and keep praying after they are gone. And when you fail — because you will — the passage ends by reminding you that your Lord knows what is in your soul, and is Ever Most Forgiving to those who keep turning back to Him.

passages.title: Kin, the needy, and balanced spending
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These five ayat lay out a believer's financial conscience in one sweep: who has a real claim on your wealth (ayah 26), what destroys wealth through excess (27), what you owe someone when you have nothing to give (28), where the balance lies between a fist and an open hand (29), and Who apportions provision in the first place (30). One movement runs through all five — give what is due, do not squander, stay in the middle, because the One deciding how much you hold is watching you.

## Where this passage sits

Ibn Kathir notes the sequence: the preceding ayat concerned honouring one's parents; Allah follows this with the command to treat one's relatives well and to maintain the ties of kinship. Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet ﷺ describing that order — "Your mother and your father, then your closest relatives and the next closest" — and his words that whoever would like to see his provision expanded and his life extended should maintain his ties of kinship. (Ibn Kathir transmits both without naming a collection.)

## "Their due" — a right, not a favour

The wording of ayah 26 is precise: give the near relative **his due** (*haqqahu*) — his right. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the implication from that one word: because what is given is their right and his duty, the giver has no reason or occasion to harp on the favour, before them or behind them. He is simply doing his duty, not showering favours on anyone.

The ayah names three claimants: **kin** (*dhu al-qurbā*), the near relative; the **Miskīn**, the poor; and the **wayfarer** (*ibn al-sabīl*).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the ayah establishes an obligation on everyone towards ordinary relatives while leaving the "what" and "how much" unspecified. The least degree in which it can be fulfilled is to share with them the graces of good social living and treat them well; and where they are needy, helping them financially in accordance with one's personal capacity is included too.

**A concrete ruling.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that Imām Abū Ḥanīfah derived from this injunction that financial help can be extended to two kinds of relative — in both cases one of near blood kinship (*dhū raḥim*) in the degree of sanguinity precluding marriage (*maḥram*):

1. A woman or child who has neither the wherewithal to eke out an existence nor the ability to earn for it.
2. A relative who is handicapped or blind, without enough money and property to eke out an existence.

Relatives who have the necessary means should help them; taking care of the essential expenses is a duty enjoined on all of them. If several relatives stand in the same degree of extended means, the expenses are divided over all of them and the subsistence allowance of the needy given in that manner. Tafsīr Maẓharī notes that this rule also has its sanction from the ayah of Sūrah al-Baqarah, "and on the heir it falls likewise" (2:233).

## Tabdhīr: the word for wasting

The second half of ayah 26 turns from giving to over-giving: "But spend not wastefully in the manner of a spendthrift" — *wa lā tubadhdhir tabdhīrā*. Ibn Kathir observes the pattern: when Allah commands spending, He forbids extravagance — and he brings the companion ayah, "And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy" (25:67).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the Qur'an expresses wasteful spending through two words: **tabdhīr**, squandering recklessly (forbidden here), and **isrāf**, extravagance (forbidden in "and do not be extravagant," 7:31). Some commentators say the two are synonymous — any spending in sin, in disobedience, or on a wrong occasion or place is both. Others refine it: *tabdhīr* is spending in sin or on some totally unsuitable occasion or place, while *isrāf* is spending beyond the level of need on an occasion where spending is itself permissible. On that reading *tabdhīr* is emphatically worse than *isrāf*, and it is the squanderers who were called brothers to Shayṭān and his cohorts.

The early authorities cited in the two commentaries sharpen this until it stops being about quantity at all:

- **Ibn Masʿūd**, as Ibn Kathir reports him: "This refers to spending extravagantly when it is not appropriate." **Ibn ʿAbbās** said likewise.
- **Ibn Masʿūd** again, in the wording Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits from Tafsīr Maẓharī: spending out of place, on what one has not been obligated with, is *tabdhīr*.
- **Mujāhid**: if a man spends all his wealth on appropriate things, he is not a spendthrift; but if he spends a little inappropriately, he is. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives his words with a figure — spending even one *mudd* (half a kilo) for what is false and non-incumbent is *tabdhīr*.
- **Qatādah**: extravagance means spending money on sin in disobeying Allah, and on wrongful and corrupt things.
- **Imām Mālik**: *tabdhīr* is that one acquires wealth and property lawfully and cleanly, exactly as he was obligated to, then spends it off in ways counter to that — and this too is given the name *isrāf*, which is unlawful.
- **Imām al-Qurṭubī**: for things unlawful and impermissible, spending even one dirham is *tabdhīr*. Spending limitlessly to fulfil permissible desires — which exposes one to the danger of becoming a needy beggar in the future — is also included under it. But if someone keeps his real capital holdings intact and spends its profit liberally on his permissible desires, that is not included under *tabdhīr*.

## "Brothers of the devils"

Ayah 27 does not merely disapprove of squanderers; it assigns them a family. Ibn Kathir explains that they share this trait: they are brothers of the *shayāṭīn* in extravagance, foolishness, failing to obey Allah and committing sin.

Then the ayah closes the loop: "and Shayṭān is ever ungrateful (*kafūr*) to his Lord." Ibn Kathir explains that he is an ingrate, because he denied the blessings of Allah and did not obey Him, turning instead to disobedience and rebellion. There is the hidden logic: wealth is a blessing from Allah, so flinging it at what He forbade is ingratitude — precisely the family resemblance.

**A whole answer in one exchange.** Ibn Kathir records that Imām Aḥmad transmitted from Anas ibn Mālik: a man of Banū Tamīm came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying he had much wealth, a family, children and the refinements of city life, and asked how he should spend and what he should do. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ told him to pay the Zakāh on his wealth if any was due, for it is a purification that will make him pure; to maintain his ties of kinship; and to pay attention to the rights of beggars, neighbours and the poor. The man asked him to make it less for him, so the Prophet ﷺ recited to him this very ayah — give the kinsman his due, and the Miskīn, and the wayfarer, and do not spend wastefully. The man said that was enough for him, and asked whether paying his Zakāh to the Prophet's ﷺ messenger would absolve him of the duty before Allah and His Messenger. He ﷺ answered yes: if you give it to my messenger, you will have fulfilled it and will have the reward for it, and the sin is on the one who changes it.

## Ayah 28: when you have nothing to give

Ibn Kathir gives the situation directly: if your relatives, and those to whom Allah has commanded you to give, ask you for something and you do not have anything, and you turn away from them because you have nothing to give — then "speak unto them a soft, kind word" (*qawlan maysūrā*). What is that soft word? Ibn Kathir says it means with a promise — the opinion of Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and others.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this an unusual piece of moral training given to the entire Muslim community through the Prophet ﷺ: if people needing help come to you and you have nothing to give, so that you are compelled to turn away, even then this turning away or excusing yourself must not be with an air of indifference, or with an attitude that could be insulting to the one asking. It should be coupled with an expression of your own inability or constraint.

**Two reports about its revelation.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits, from al-Qurṭubī, a report from Ibn Zayd that some people used to ask the Prophet ﷺ for financial help while he knew what they were given would be spent in the spreading of disorder, so he refused them — the refusal being a device to stop them from indulging in disorder — and thereupon this ayah was revealed. It also mentions that in the *Musnad* of Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr it is reported on the authority of Sabāʿ ibn Ḥakam that the Prophet ﷺ had received a supply of cloth and distributed it over those deserving; then others came when the supply was finished and he had nothing to give, and it was about the latter that this ayah was revealed. Whether the refusal is because nothing remains or because giving would do harm, it still has to be gentle.

## Ayah 29: the two hands

Now the image the passage is remembered for: "And let not your hand be tied to your neck, nor overextend it." Ibn Kathir says plainly that Allah enjoins moderation in living: He condemns miserliness and forbids extravagance.

The first half — the hand tied to the neck — means, in his words, do not be miserly and stingy, never giving anything to anyone. He then recalls that this is what the Jews said, "Allah's Hand is tied up," attributing miserliness to Him — and answers with the exclamation, "Exalted and Sanctified be the Most Generous Bestower!" In Ibn Kathir's own pairing, a clenched hand is the very posture that was slanderously attributed to Allah.

The second half — nor overextend it — means, Ibn Kathir explains, do not be extravagant in spending and giving more than you can afford, or paying more than you earn, lest you become blameworthy and find yourself in severe poverty. He then unfolds the ayah's two closing words:

- **Malūm** (blameworthy): if you are a miser, people will blame you and condemn you, and no longer rely on you.
- **Maḥsūr**: when you spend more than you can afford, you will find yourself without anything to spend, so you will be worn out — like an animal that cannot walk, so it becomes weak and incapable. Ibn Kathir notes the word is close in meaning to "exhausted," and connects it to Allah's saying that the sight returns "in a state of humiliation and worn out" (*ḥasīr*, 67:3–4).

Tafsīr Maẓharī, quoted in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, distributes the two words the same way: *malūm* relates to miserliness — if he holds back, people will reproach him — while *maḥsūrā* relates to the other condition, that one should not exaggerate in spending to the point of becoming a pauper himself, turning empty-handed, defeated and rueful. Ibn Kathir notes that Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd and others likewise understood this ayah as being about miserliness and extravagance.

**The occasion of revelation.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports this from Ibn Marduwayh on the authority of Ibn Masʿūd, and from al-Baghawī on the authority of Jābir: a boy came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, "My mother asks of you a shirt." At that time he ﷺ had no shirt except the one on his blessed body. He told the boy to come some other time, when they had enough means to respond. The boy went back home, then returned and said his mother asked that he kindly give her the very shirt on his blessed body. Hearing this, the Prophet ﷺ took the shirt off and let him have it, and his body was left bare. When the time for ṣalāh came and Bilāl called the adhān, he did not come out as usual; people were worried, and some who went in saw him sitting bare-bodied. Thereupon this ayah was revealed.

The ayah restraining over-extended giving came down about the Messenger of Allah ﷺ himself, who had just given away the only shirt he owned.

## From the Sunnah: the weight on the other side

Lest anyone read ayah 29 as licence to hold back, Ibn Kathir loads the passage with the Prophet's ﷺ warnings:

- The parable of the miser and the almsgiver, from Abū Hurayrah, reported in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs — this version recorded by al-Bukhārī in the Book of Zakāh: two men wear iron cloaks from their chests to their collarbones. When the almsgiver gives in charity, the cloak becomes spacious until it covers his whole body, to the extent that it hides his fingertips and covers his tracks. But when the miser wants to spend, every ring of it sticks fast in its place; he tries to widen it, and it does not become wide.
- Also in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah: there is no day when a person wakes up but two angels come down from heaven, one saying, "O Allah, compensate the one who gives," and the other, "O Allah, destroy the one who withholds."
- Muslim recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said wealth never decreases because of charity; Allah never increases a servant who gives in charity except in honour; and whoever is humble for the sake of Allah, Allah will raise him in status.
- Ibn Kathir also transmits the Prophet's ﷺ warning against *shuḥḥ*, greedy stinginess: beware of it, for it destroyed the people who came before you — it commanded them to be miserly and they were miserly, it commanded them to cut the ties of kinship and they cut them, it commanded them to commit immoral actions and they did so. (Narrated by Abū Kathīr from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, without a collection named.) Notice how it circles back to ayah 26: stinginess is what severs the very kinship this passage opened by commanding.

## How far does the restraint go?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful not to let ayah 29 become an excuse. On its outer view the ayah seems to prohibit the kind of spending after which the spender himself ends up poor and needy, a prey to all sorts of hardships and anxieties. Al-Qurṭubī, it reports, holds that this injunction covers the general condition of Muslims — those who would find the resulting hardships distressing and would end up contrite and grieving over what they gave. The word *maḥsūrā* itself provides a hint in this direction (as in Tafsīr Maẓharī).

As for people of high determination, who would not be emotionally disturbed by hardships that may come later and would still go on fulfilling the rights of those who hold them, this restriction does not apply. That is why it was the customary practice of the Prophet ﷺ that he would not store anything for tomorrow: what came in today was spent out today, and there were occasions when he would remain hungry to the outer limit of having to tie a piece of rock against his stomach. Many among the noble Ṣaḥābah spent their entire wealth and property in the way of Allah during his blessed lifetime, and he ﷺ neither categorically prohibited it nor blamed them for it. So the prohibition, Maʿārif concludes, is for one who cannot brave the hardships of poverty and hunger and would afterwards rue his giving — an attitude that would nullify the good he had already done.

**Poorly managed giving.** The other thing forbidden, on al-Qurṭubī's reading, is spending haphazardly: ignoring what may happen in the near future and spending on the spot, so that tomorrow, when other needy people show up or a major religious need arises, one is in no position to help out. Tafsīr Maẓharī adds the sharper case — that he may equally be rendered incapable of fulfilling the rights of his own family, which he is duty-bound to fulfil.

## Ayah 30: who is actually distributing all this

The passage closes by lifting the reader's eyes off his own wallet: "Truly, your Lord expands the provision for whom He wills and straitens it." Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is the One who provides or withholds, the Bestower running the affairs of His creation as He wills; He makes rich whomever He wills and poor whomever He wills, by the wisdom that is His. And "Verily, He is Ever All-Knower (*Khabīr*), All-Seer (*Baṣīr*) of His servants" means He knows and sees who deserves to be rich and who deserves to be poor.

Ibn Kathir adds a note that should keep anyone from envy: in some cases richness may be decreed so that a person gets carried away, leading to his own doom; in other cases poverty may be a punishment. We seek refuge with Allah from both.

Ayah 30 removes the anxiety driving both failures the passage forbids: the miser clenches because he fears running out, the reckless spender empties himself in a rush, and neither of them is the one apportioning provision. Between them sits the moderate hand, spending what is due where it is due and leaving the arithmetic of provision to the One who is All-Seer of His servants.

## Living it

- **Start with the nearest.** Parents, then the closest relative, then the next closest. Giving generously to distant causes while a needy blood relative goes unhelped has the order backwards.
- **Treat it as their right.** Never harp on the favour, before them or behind them — you are doing your duty, not showering favours on anyone.
- **Audit destination before amount.** By the standard of Mujāhid, Ibn Masʿūd and al-Qurṭubī, a small sum sent to a forbidden place is squandering; a large sum sent where it is incumbent is not.
- **When you have nothing, you still owe a word.** Not silence, not a brush-off, not a face turned away in indifference: a soft, kind word — and, as the early commentators explained it, a promise.

passages.title: Life, chastity, orphans, and honest measure
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat continue the sūrah's series of instructions about what people owe one another — the life of a child, the honour of a household, the blood of a human being, then other people's money. One moral shape runs through them: those with power in their hands are told to hold those hands back from someone who cannot defend himself.

## The running list

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts these as injunctions six through eleven in a series about human rights the previous ayat had begun. The sixth: do not kill your children (31). The seventh: do not go near zinā (32). The eighth: do not kill unjustly (33). Then three arrive together in ayat 34–35 — the orphan's property, the fulfilment of covenants, honest weights and measures. Maʿārif marks the hinge: the earlier commands concern **physical** rights, lives and bodies, while ayat 34–35 turn to **financial** rights.

## Ayah 31 — "Do not kill your children for fear of poverty"

Ibn Kathir explains the custom being uprooted: the people of Jāhiliyyah would not let their daughters inherit from them, and some would even kill their daughters lest the daughters make them poorer. Maʿārif adds that children, daughters especially, were killed at birth out of fear of the expense of maintaining them.

Ibn Kathir draws much from the placement of this command. Allah forbids killing children in the same breath in which He enjoins parents to take care of their children in matters of inheritance — which shows, he says, that **Allah is more compassionate towards His servants than a father is to his own child**.

**The word order is the sermon.** In Sūrat al-Anʿām the same prohibition reads *We provide sustenance for you and for them* (6:151). Here it is inverted: **نَّحۡنُ نَرۡزُقُهُمۡ وَإِيَّاكُمۡ** — *We shall provide for them as well as for you*. Ibn Kathir notes the children's provision is mentioned first, and Maʿārif draws it out: Allah subtly indicates that He gives to the children first and then to the parents. The child is not a drain on your rizq — the child is a **channel** of it. When Allah sees a servant supporting his family or helping others who are poor and weak, Maʿārif explains, He gives him liberally in proportion, enough to meet his own needs and to help others besides. The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that it is because of the poor and weak among you that you are helped and provided for.

**The fear, not the fact.** The wording is *khashyata imlāq* — for **fear** of poverty — which Ibn Kathir glosses as: lest they make you poor in the future. The verdict is blunt: **إِنَّ قَتۡلَهُمۡ كَانَ خِطۡـٔٗا كَبِيرٗا**, which Ibn Kathir explains as a **major sin**.

Ibn Kathir sets that verdict beside a report recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, which sin is the worst?' He said, *To appoint rivals of Allah when He has created you.* I asked, 'Then what?' He said, *To kill your child lest he should eat with you.* I asked, 'Then what?' He said, *To commit adultery with your neighbour's wife.*"

**The underlying error.** Allah admonishes them, Maʿārif says, for their ignorance in assuming the responsibility of providing sustenance — *who are you to do that?* That is the exclusive domain of Allah. On this basis Maʿārif comments on the modern panic over "population explosion" and the frantic promotion of birth control built on it: it rests on the same false assumption, that human beings are the ones responsible for sustenance. Maʿārif is careful with the ruling — this may not be a sin equal in gravity to killing children, but there is no doubt about its being blameworthy.

## Ayah 32 — "Do not go near zinā"

**وَلَا تَقۡرَبُواْ ٱلزِّنَىٰ** — *do not come near*. The prohibition is not phrased as "do not do it." Ibn Kathir reads the wording as it stands: Allah forbids His servants to commit zinā, **or to approach it, or to do anything that may lead to it**. It draws a perimeter rather than a line at the cliff edge. Then two judgments: it is a **fāḥishah**, which Ibn Kathir glosses as a major sin, and *sā'a sabīlā* — an evil way, a terrible way to behave.

**A young man who wanted permission.** Imam Ahmad recorded from Abū Umāmah that a young man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, "O Messenger of Allah! Give me permission to commit zinā." The people surrounded him and rebuked him — "Stop! Stop!" But the Prophet ﷺ said, *Come close.* He came, and the Prophet ﷺ said, *Sit down*, and he sat. Then: *Would you like it for your mother?* — "No, by Allah, may I be ransomed for you." *Neither do the people like it for their mothers.* *Would you like it for your daughter?* — "No, by Allah, may I be ransomed for you." *Neither do the people like it for their daughters.* And so through his sister, his paternal aunt, his maternal aunt; each time the same answer, each time the same reply. Then the Prophet ﷺ put his hand on him and said, *O Allah, forgive his sin, purify his heart and guard his chastity.* After that the young man never paid attention to anything of that nature.

**Why so severe?** Maʿārif gives two reasons. First, it is a shame, gross and immodest; whoever is denuded of modesty is denuded of human nobility itself and is rendered incapable of distinguishing the good from the bad. A ḥadīth puts it in a line: when your sense of shame goes — the shame that could have become a barrier against evil — then you will do what you will. This is why the Prophet ﷺ declared **ḥayā'** (a sense of shame, modesty) a division of faith: *wa'l-ḥayā'u shuʿbatun min al-īmān* (al-Bukhārī). Second, it generates limitless social disorder whose consequences sometimes destroy whole groups of people. Though this crime is not directly related to the rights of Allah's servants, Maʿārif suggests it appears among them here because it is **contagious** — it brings other crimes along with it that disturb people's rights through loss of lives and property. Hence Islam has declared this crime more serious than any other and fixed its punishment as the harshest of all: this one is a carrier of hundreds of them.

Two further reports. Al-Bazzār, on the authority of Buraidah (via Maẓharī): the heavens and the earth, the seven of them each, curse the married person who commits adultery. And from Abū Hurayrah, in al-Bukhārī and Muslim: "A fornicator when fornicating is not a believer. A thief when stealing is not a believer. And a drunkard while drinking is not a believer." Its explanation, as it appears in the report of Abū Dāwūd, is that at the time such a person is practically engaged in the crime, faith leaves his heart and comes out of him, and when he turns away from it, faith returns.

## Ayah 33 — the sanctity of blood, and the limits of revenge

**وَلَا تَقۡتُلُواْ ٱلنَّفۡسَ ٱلَّتِي حَرَّمَ ٱللَّهُ إِلَّا بِٱلۡحَقِّ** — do not kill the soul Allah has made sacred, *except by right*. Ibn Kathir: Allah forbids killing with no legitimate reason. Reported in the two Ṣaḥīḥs: *The blood of a Muslim who bears witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah is not permissible except in three cases: a soul for a soul, an adulterer who is married, and a person who leaves his religion and deserts the Jamāʿah.* Maʿārif reports the same ḥadīth from Ibn Masʿūd in al-Bukhārī and Muslim, noting the judicial punishment attached to each case — in the case of unjust killing, that the *waliyy* (legal heir) of the person killed can have him put to death under the law of qiṣāṣ, even retaliation through legal process, not private vengeance.

**How heavy is this?** The books of the Sunan record: *If the world were to be destroyed, it would be of less importance to Allah than the killing of a Muslim.* Some reports add: even if the inhabitants of Allah's seven heavens and seven earths were to join in the killing of a believer unjustly, He would put all of them into the Fire (Ibn Mājah, with a chain classified as Ḥasan, and al-Bayhaqī — from Maẓharī). Another: whoever abets the killing of a believer, assisting the killer even with one word, will be brought before Allah on the Day of Resurrection with *"Deprived of the mercy of Allah"* written on his forehead (Maẓharī, from Ibn Mājah and Iṣbahānī). And al-Bayhaqī reports on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās and Muʿāwiyah that the Prophet ﷺ said: hopefully Allah may forgive every sin except that of the person who died in a state of disbelief, or who killed a believer intentionally and unjustly.

**"We have given his heir authority."** Ibn Kathir explains that this *sulṭān* is authority **over the killer**, and that the heir has a real choice: retaliation, or forgiveness in return for the *diyah* (blood money), or forgiveness with no payment at all — as is reported in the Sunnah. Maʿārif adds that the right belongs to the *waliyy*, the legal heir; in the absence of a lineal heir it belongs to the head of the Islamic government, who is in a way the waliyy of all Muslims — the first is called the *real* waliyy, the second the *legal*.

**"But let him not exceed limits in the taking of life."** This proviso — *fa-lā yusrif fi'l-qatl* — is the moral centre of the ayah. Ibn Kathir reports the scholars saying the heir must not go to extremes in killing the killer: no mutilating the body, no taking revenge on persons other than the killer. Maʿārif supplies the background: in the days of Jāhiliyyah the Arabs would avenge a killing on whomever they could lay hands on from the killer's family or friends; when the dead man was a notable they would take two, three or many more lives for one; and some, still not satisfied after killing the killer, would go on to cut off body parts such as the nose or ears "to serve as deterrents." All of that is extra to the limits set by the law of even retaliation and is patently unlawful, and this clause is what stopped it.

**"Verily, he is helped."** Ibn Kathir: the heir is helped against the killer by the Sharīʿah and by divine decree. Maʿārif turns this over: so long as the heir upholds justice and seeks even retaliation through the legal provisions of qiṣāṣ, the law of the Sharīʿah stands in his favour and Allah is his supporter. But if he is blinded by the desire for revenge and exceeds the limits, the roles reverse — the one oppressed (*maẓlūm*) has become the oppressor (*ẓālim*). Allah and His law will no longer support him; they will support the other party. **Injustice is not answered by injustice, but by justice.**

Maʿārif adds an anecdote. Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf is the most notorious tyrant of Islamic history, who killed thousands of Companions and Successors unjustly — so people tend to feel free to say anything about him. When he was accused before certain mujtahid imams, the pious elder before whom the accusation was brought asked the accusers whether they had any authority or evidence for it. They said no. Then he said: if Allah will avenge the unjust killing of thousands of innocent people by Ḥajjāj, remember that whoever is unjust to Ḥajjāj will not escape that reckoning either. There is no partisanship in the justice of Allah.

## Ayah 34 — the orphan's wealth, and the covenant

**وَلَا تَقۡرَبُواْ مَالَ ٱلۡيَتِيمِ** — *do not go near* the orphan's property: the same perimeter-language used for zinā. Then one opening: **إِلَّا بِٱلَّتِي هِيَ أَحۡسَنُ**, except by that which is best — not "except fairly" but "except by what is *better*." Ibn Kathir: do not dispose of the orphan's wealth except in a proper manner. Maʿārif: there must be no free use of that property counter to the provisions of the Sharīʿah or to the interest and advantage of the children; those charged with managing it must spend only in the orphans' interest, and definitely not on a whim or out of lack of concern. Ibn Kathir brings the companion verse: do not consume it wastefully and hastily fearing that they should grow up; a guardian who is rich should take no wages, and one who is poor may have what is just and reasonable according to his labour (4:6). And *ḥattā yablugha ashuddah* — until he reaches his full strength — means, Maʿārif explains, until the orphaned children grow up and become capable of protecting their property themselves: the lower limit fifteen years, the higher eighteen.

**Why single out the orphan?** It is simply not permissible to spend from anyone's property through false means; the orphan is named here particularly, Maʿārif says, because orphans are themselves incapable of keeping or taking account, and no one else is expected to know about it. **A place where no one is present to demand his right is exactly the place where the demand of Allah becomes stronger and harder** — any shortfall there is more sinful than a shortfall in the rights of common people.

It is recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Abū Dharr: *O Abū Dharr, I see that you are weak, and I like for you what I like for myself. Do not let yourself be appointed as commander over two people, and do not let yourself be appointed guardian of an orphan's property.* The warning is not that guardianship is wicked; it is that it is heavy.

**"And fulfil the covenant."** Ibn Kathir: everything you promise people and the covenants you agree to, because the one who makes a covenant or a promise will be asked about it. Maʿārif maps the ground. Covenants with Allah are of two kinds: the covenant every human being made in eternity — believer and disbeliever alike — that Allah is their Lord; and the believer's covenant made by professing *lā ilāha illā Allāh*. Both necessarily result in obedience to His injunctions and the seeking of His pleasure, and fulfilling both is obligatory. Then there are covenants between human beings themselves: treaties, pacts, agreements, pledges and contracts — political, commercial or transactional.

Those too are binding, subject to the condition that they are not against Islamic law; one that *is* must be terminated, after first serving notice on the other party. If one party does not fulfil, the other has the right to go to court and compel performance. A one-sided promise is also to be fulfilled, with this difference: a contract can be enforced through the court, a unilateral promise cannot. But whoever goes back on a promise without a valid excuse permitted by the Sharīʿah commits a sin; in a ḥadīth this has been called hypocrisy in acts.

**إِنَّ ٱلۡعَهۡدَ كَانَ مَسۡـُٔولٗا** — the covenant will be asked about. On the Day of Resurrection, Maʿārif says, questions will be asked about mutual contracts just as they are asked about the fulfilment of obligatory divine injunctions. Then it notices: the ayah stops at "it will be asked about." What happens next is left untold — perhaps deliberately, signalling that the danger is great.

## Ayah 35 — the honest scale

**وَأَوۡفُواْ ٱلۡكَيۡلَ إِذَا كِلۡتُمۡ** — give full measure when you measure. Ibn Kathir: do not try to make it weigh less, and do not wrong people with their belongings. **وَزِنُواْ بِٱلۡقِسۡطَاسِ ٱلۡمُسۡتَقِيمِ** — *qisṭās* means the scales, and *mustaqīm* means that which is not distorted and will not cause confusion. Honesty here is not only in the intention; it is in the equipment.

Maʿārif relays from Abū Ḥayyān's *Tafsīr al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ* that the responsibility in this verse is placed on the **seller**: it is the seller who is responsible for weighing, measuring, and seeing that the amount is full as due. Maʿārif adds that the jurists take the ruling to its logical end — it is unlawful to give less than what is due to whoever it may be, and that includes an employee who curtails the duty entrusted to him or gives less time than should actually be given to it, and a worker who shirks and fails to deliver what is due. Short measure is short measure, whether it is grain or hours.

**ذَٰلِكَ خَيۡرٞ وَأَحۡسَنُ تَأۡوِيلٗا** — that is good, and better in the end. Ibn Kathir: *that is good* for you in your daily life and in your Hereafter, and *better in the end* concerns your ultimate end in the Hereafter. Saʿīd narrated that Qatādah said it means "better in reward and a better end." Maʿārif separates the two clauses: the rule is **intrinsically** good — no normal and decent person takes short-weighing as something nice, neither religiously, nor rationally, nor naturally — and its **outcome** is better, including the success of the Hereafter, the reward of deeds and the blessing of Paradise, as well as a happy outcome in this very life, since no business can prosper until its goodwill stands recognized in the market, and that cannot happen without commercial honesty.

Ibn Kathir closes with Ibn ʿAbbās, who used to say: **"O people, you are entrusted with two things for which the people who came before you were destroyed — these weights and measures."**

## What the passage asks of us

Look at who is being protected here — the newborn who cannot argue for his own keep, the murdered man who cannot speak at his own trial, the orphan who cannot audit his guardian, the buyer who cannot see inside your scale. Every one of them is at the mercy of someone else's honesty. And so the ayat hand the enforcement upward: the covenant *will be asked about*, and the weights and measures that destroyed earlier nations are something you are *entrusted* with.

passages.title: Knowledge, humility, and the charter's seal
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat close the long charter of commands that opened at ayah 23 with "And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him." Two final instructions are given — one governing what a person allows himself to claim and repeat (ayah 36), one governing how he carries himself among people (ayah 37) — and then the list is sealed: ayah 38 pronounces Allah's verdict over the whole of it, and ayah 39 names it revealed wisdom before returning to the worship of Allah alone, exactly where the charter began.

## Where this passage sits

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is counting as it goes. The command in ayah 36 is the twelfth injunction of this charter and the command in ayah 37 the thirteenth, and it notes that both "relate to mores of common social living" — the ordinary fabric of how people live together. The twelfth, it says, forbids doing something without having become certain about it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads these fifteen verses as, in a way, the explanation of the effort acceptable in the sight of Allah that was mentioned earlier in the sūrah in the words "and makes effort for it as due" (ayah 19). There it was said that not every effort is acceptable with Allah; the effort made in accordance with the Sunnah and teaching of the Prophet ﷺ is the only one accepted. The main divisions of that acceptable effort are what these injunctions lay out — the rights of Allah first, then the rights of His servants.

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits, from Mazhari, a remarkable saying of Ibn ʿAbbas: the commandments of the entire Torah have been reduced to fifteen verses of Sūrah Banī Isrāʼīl. What is being sealed here is not a set of tips but a condensed law.

## "Do not follow what you have no knowledge of" (36)

The verb is rendered both "follow" and "pursue" — do not go after a thing when you have no real knowledge that it is so.

The early authorities Ibn Kathir gathers each catch a different face of it:

- **Ibn ʿAbbas** (reported by ʿAli bin Abi Talhah): "Do not say anything of which you have no knowledge."
- **Al-ʿAwfi**: "Do not accuse anyone of that of which you have no knowledge."
- **Muhammad bin al-Hanafiyyah**: it means bearing false witness.
- **Qatadah**: "Do not say, 'I have seen', when you did not see anything, or 'I have heard', when you did not hear anything, or 'I know', when you do not know — for Allah will ask you about all of that."

Ibn Kathir then draws them together: what they all mean is that **Allah forbids speaking without knowledge and only on the basis of suspicion, which is mere imagination and illusions.** He brings as a parallel Allah's word, "Avoid much suspicion; indeed some suspicions are sins" (49:12).

### From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir cites four warnings here:

- "Beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the falsest of speech."
- Reported in **Sunan Abu Dawud**: "What an evil habit it is for a man to say, 'They claimed…'" — the vague, unsourced "they say", which lets a man carry a report along without ever owning it.
- "The worst of lies is for a man to claim to have seen something that he has not seen."
- And **in the Sahih**: "Whoever claims to have seen a dream (when he has not seen) will be told on the Day of Resurrection to make a knot between two barley grains, and he will not be able to do it."

A false dream is about the flimsiest lie a person could tell — no one is robbed by it, no court is misled. Yet the penalty set for it is an impossible task, performed in front of everyone. Claiming to have seen what you did not see is grave even when the claim itself seems weightless.

### How certain must you be?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a precision that saves the ayah from being read as paralysing. Certainty, it explains, has degrees. There is certainty that reaches **perfect certitude**, a state that leaves no room for even the slightest contrary doubt. Below that there is **strong likelihood** or overwhelming probability, where the probability of a contrary aspect still exists.

Divine injunctions likewise fall into two kinds:

1. **Absolutes and certainties** — the articles and principles of religion, what a Muslim believes. These require certainty of the first degree. Until that is reached, a pseudo-certainty is not trustworthy here, and acting on its dictates is not permissible.
2. **Subsidiary matters** — the injunctions relating to subsidiary deeds, the practical branches. For these, certainty of the second degree, overwhelming probability, is sufficient.

So the ayah is not demanding proof before you may do anything at all. Match the strength of your evidence to the weight of the matter: where belief itself is at stake, nothing less than real certainty will do; in the practical details of life, a well-grounded strong probability is enough to act on. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attributes this analysis to Bayān al-Qurʼān.)

## "The hearing, the sight and the heart — each will be questioned" (36)

Then the ayah does something unexpected: instead of threatening a punishment, it names three of your own faculties and says each is answerable.

Ibn Kathir's gloss is plain: "each of those ones" means these faculties — hearing, sight and the heart — and "will be questioned" means the person will be asked about them on the Day of Resurrection, and they will be asked about him and what he did with them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds it: the ear will be asked what it kept hearing throughout its life; the eye, what it kept seeing; the heart, what it kept cooking in its chambers and what it believed in throughout its life. Where the hearing was of something Shariah does not permit — such as hearing ill of someone behind his back (*ghībah*, backbiting), or unlawful music — punishment will follow the question. Where the eye looked at what it was not permitted to look at, likewise. Where the heart planted in itself a belief contrary to the Qurʼan and Sunnah, or nursed a baseless blame against someone, likewise.

This belongs to a wider truth: on that Day, questions will be asked about virtually all the blessings Allah gave — "And you shall certainly be asked on that day about all blessings" (102:8). The ear, the eye and the heart are singled out here because they are the more important and significant of those blessings.

**Why these two senses, and why in this order.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two observations. First, a person becomes aware of things through five senses, yet habitually a man finds out far more through his ears and eyes; what comes through smell, taste and touch is fairly lower in frequency by comparison. That may well be why mentioning only two of the five was considered sufficient here. Second, the ear is placed before the eye, as it is elsewhere in the Qurʼan wherever the two are mentioned together — in all likelihood because the major part of a person's information consists of things *heard*, while things seen are comparatively much less. Which is exactly the traffic this ayah is policing: what reaches you as report.

**The link between the two halves of the ayah.** Tafsir al-Qurtubi and Mazhari, as cited by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, read the two sentences as deliberately adjacent. A person who blamed someone without first ascertaining it, or did something impulsively without ascertaining it — if the matter came through his ears, the ears are questioned; if he saw it, the eyes; if he comprehended it in his heart, the heart is questioned, to determine whether he was true or false in his blame or in the belief he let take root. And these very body parts then speak up as witnesses on the Day of Resurrection. It will be a cause of disgrace for those who accuse others without being certain. As Allah says: "Today We shall set a seal on their mouths, and their hands shall speak, and their feet shall bear witness as to what they have been earning" (36:65).

There is more to it. Perhaps, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān suggests, these three have been particularized because it is through them that Allah blessed man with sense and consciousness — they are the equipment *for* verifying. The purpose is that a person first ascertains, examines and tests a thought or belief that crosses his heart: if he finds it true and sound, he puts it into practice; if it turns out false, he stays away from it. So the one who does not use these faculties and goes about following what he has no knowledge of is, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, guilty of being ungrateful for these blessings of Allah. Rumour is not merely a sin of the tongue; it is a misuse of a gift.

## "And do not walk on the earth haughtily" (37)

Having addressed what a man carries inside, the passage turns to how he carries himself. Ibn Kathir: Allah forbids His servants to strut and walk in a boastful manner — "acting proud, like those who are arrogant oppressors."

Then comes the argument: **"you can neither rend the earth nor attain the mountains in height."** On the first clause Ibn Kathir says it means you cannot penetrate the earth with your walking, and notes that this was the opinion of Ibn Jarir. On the second he comments simply that it is "with your arrogance, pride and self-admiration" that you will not attain a stature like the mountains in height.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the picture: it is as though the strutting man would like to tear the earth apart just by walking on it — something not in his power to accomplish — or, by that challenging gait, to rise much higher, when the mountains of Allah rise far higher than he could ever beat anatomically. The posture is answered not with a threat but with a fact about his size. It is, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's word, an idiotic act.

And Ibn Kathir notes that such behaviour may bring about the opposite of what the man pretends to be. As was reported in the Sahih: "While a man from the people before you was walking arrogantly in his garments, the earth swallowed him and he is still sinking down into it, until the Day of Resurrection." He wanted the earth to feel his tread; the earth took him. Allah likewise tells us of Qarun, who went to his people wearing his finery — and then Allah caused the earth to swallow him and his house.

### The disease behind the gait

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines the thing precisely: **arrogance is to take yourself superior to others and rate others to be inferior to you.** It is a major sin that can afflict the human heart mortally — and so one must guard even against the signs of arrogance shown in the way one goes about in life, for those too are impermissible. One may not be walking by exerting force on the earth, but assuming airs and posing high are impermissible under all conditions.

The hadith it gathers are severe:

- **Imam Muslim** reports on the authority of ʿIyad ibn ʿAmmar that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah Taʿala has sent this command to me through revelation: Take to humility. Let no man pride on another man, nor adopt an attitude of self-eminence and let no one be unjust to anyone." (Mazhari)
- ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud narrates that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Not to enter Paradise is he who has arrogance in his heart even to the measure of a particle" (Mazhari, with reference to the **Sahih of Muslim**).
- Reported in a *hadith qudsi* — a saying in which the Prophet ﷺ conveys words from his Lord — on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah Taʿala says that grandeur is My mantle and greatness is My breech. Whoever tries to snatch these from Me, him I shall put in Jahannam." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note of creed here: the words *ridāʼ* and *izār* signify dress, and Allah has no mass or body that would need a dress; therefore at this place it means the attribute of divine glory. So whoever betrays the wish to become associated with Allah in this attribute belongs to Hell.
- And in another hadith the Prophet ﷺ has been reported to have said: "On the day of Qiyamah, arrogant people will be raised as humans scaled down to the size of tiny ants under the shadow of disgrace descending from all sides. They will be driven to a prison of Hell called Bulas. It will be surrounded with blazing fire, the highest around, and they will be drinking pus and blood excreted by the inmates of Hell to quench their thirst." (**Tirmidhi**, on the authority of ʿAmr ibn Shuʿaib, from his father, from his grandfather — Mazhari)

The reversal is exact. They magnified themselves in the world; they are shrunk in the Hereafter.

Finally, speaking from the pulpit, ʿUmar said: "I have heard from the Holy Prophet ﷺ that a person who takes to humility, Allah Taʿala elevates him to higher ranks following which he is, though, insignificant in his own sight, but he is great in the sight of everybody else. And whoever waxes proud, him Allah Taʿala puts to disgrace following which he is, though, great in his own sight but he is, in the sight of people, worse than a dog and pig." (Mazhari) Humility is not self-erasure. It is the road to being genuinely honoured.

## The seal on the whole list (38)

**"That which is evil, of all these, is detestable in the sight of your Lord."** One short sentence gathers everything that has come before.

Ibn Kathir notes that the recitation of the key word affects how far back the sentence reaches:

- Read as *Sayyiʼatan* — "evil deeds" — the sense is that everything mentioned is forbidden, running from "And kill not your children for fear of poverty" (17:31) up to this ayah. So everything mentioned there is an evil deed for which a person is to be blamed before Allah, who does not like or accept such deeds.
- Read as *Sayyiʼuhu* — a genitive construction, "the bad aspects of these" — the reach is longer, from "And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him" (17:23) up to this ayah, meaning that the worst of the things mentioned are disliked by Allah. This was the view of Ibn Jarir, may Allah have mercy on him.

Why the wording is "that which is *evil* of all these" rather than simply "all these" is explained by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān. Where things were forbidden in these injunctions, their repugnance is obvious. But some items in the charter are commandments rather than prohibitions — the rights of parents and relatives, the fulfilment of promises. There too the purpose is to avoid doing the opposite: hurting parents, breaking off from relatives, going back on solemn promises. The phrasing lets one verdict cover both kinds of item at once.

And a note on the word *makrūh*, "detestable". In settled legal usage *makrūh* means merely disliked, less than forbidden — but here, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out (citing Bayān al-Qurʼān), since all these things are *harām* (forbidden) or reprehensible, the word is used in its general sense of "detestable", which includes the *harām* and the *makrūh* both. Do not read this ayah as softening anything.

## Revealed wisdom — and the frame that closes (39)

**"This is part of the wisdom which your Lord has revealed to you."** Ibn Kathir puts the sense in Allah's voice: what We have commanded you to do is part of good manners, and what We have forbidden you are evil qualities; We have revealed this to you, O Muhammad, so that you may command the people likewise.

Everything just laid down — parents, kin, honest dealing, not following what you do not know, not strutting — is called *al-hikmah*, wisdom, and it is *revealed*: it did not arise from social convention or a survey of what works. And it is given to the Prophet ﷺ not merely to hold but to pass on.

Then the charter closes exactly where it opened. It began, "And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him" (17:23); it ends, **"And set not up with Allah any other god lest you should be thrown into Hell, blameworthy and rejected."** Everything in between sits inside that frame. The ethics are not free-standing; they are the shape a life takes when it worships One alone.

Ibn Kathir on the two closing words:

- **"Blameworthy"** — your own self will blame you, as will Allah and His creation.
- **"Rejected"** — far removed from everything good. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah said it means *cast out*.

One more thing Ibn Kathir notes, and it matters for how you hear the whole passage: this is an address to the Ummah via the Messenger ﷺ, for he is infallible. The warning is aimed past him, at us.

## Living it

- **Trace what you repeat, and never upgrade a suspicion into a fact.** "They claimed…" is named in the Sunnah as an evil habit because it moves a claim along without anyone owning it. A thought that crossed your heart is not evidence; Qatadah's test is whether you really saw it, really heard it, really knew it.
- **Match certainty to weight.** In what you believe, settle for nothing short of perfect certitude; in the subsidiary matters of practice, act on overwhelming probability without scruple.
- **Guard the two gates.** The ear and the eye will be questioned about what they took in over a lifetime, and the heart about what it nursed. Choose the intake.
- **Watch your bearing, not only your words.** Arrogance is rating yourself above others, and even its outward signs are impermissible. The cure offered is not shrinking but humility — which, as ʿUmar reported from the Prophet ﷺ, Allah answers by raising a person's rank.

passages.title: No daughters for Allah, no partners beside Him
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These five ayat answer a specific slander of the Makkan idolaters — that the angels are Allah's daughters — and then widen into a general argument against any partner beside Allah. The false claim is named (ayah 40), the response of the wrongdoers to clear explanation is described (41), the claim is dismantled by argument (42), Allah is declared far above it (43), and the whole of creation is shown testifying against it (44) — closing on Allah's forbearance and forgiveness.

## Where we are in the surah

Just before this, Sūrah Banī Isrāʾīl has laid down a long run of commands.
