Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes that these injunctions take up the rights of Allah first and then the rights of the servants of Allah, and that they spell out the kind of effort that is acceptable in Allah's sight — effort made in accordance with the Sunnah and teaching of the Prophet ﷺ. Maʿārif also records that Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) said the commandments of the entire Torah have been reduced to fifteen verses of Sūrah Banī Isrāʾīl (cited from Mazharī).

Ayah 38 sealed that list with one verdict — all that is evil among these is "detestable in the sight of your Lord." Maʿārif explains why *makrūh* is used there in a general sense covering both the ḥarām and the merely disliked: some of these commands are positive duties, such as the rights of parents and relatives and the fulfilment of promises, where what is being warned against is the opposite — hurting parents, cutting off relatives, going back on solemn promises. Having taught a servant how to live, the surah now returns to the foundation under all of it: who your Lord actually is.

## Ayah 40 — three errors folded into one sentence

Ibn Kathir sets out what the idolaters had done. The angels are the servants of ar-Raḥmān, the Most Beneficent. The Makkans (1) made them female, (2) called them daughters of Allah, and (3) then worshipped them. As Ibn Kathir puts it, they were gravely wrong on all three counts.

The ayah does not argue at first — it holds the claim up as a question. *A-fa-aṣfākum rabbukum bi'l-banīn* — "Has then your Lord preferred for you sons?" Ibn Kathir glosses it: has He given only you sons? — and taken for Himself from among the angels daughters, meaning, has He chosen for Himself, as you claim, daughters?

Then, says Ibn Kathir, Allah denounces them even more severely: "Verily, you indeed utter an awful saying." The awfulness is twofold: the claim that Allah has children at all, and then that His children are female — "which you do not like for yourselves and may even kill them by burying them alive." They assign to their Lord the very thing they refuse for themselves. In Ibn Kathir's words: "That is indeed a division most unfair!"

Ibn Kathir then brings in the parallel from Sūrah Maryam, where Allah says of this same claim that it is "a terrible evil thing," whereby "the heavens are almost torn, and the earth split asunder, and the mountains fall in ruins" — because they ascribe a child to the Most Beneficent (19:88–95). That passage also supplies the true relationship: "There is none in the heavens and the earth but comes unto the Most Beneficent as a servant. Verily, He knows each one of them, and has counted them a full counting. And every one of them will come to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection." Not offspring — servants, counted one by one.

## Ayah 41 — the Qurʾān explained, and the response to it

*Wa laqad ṣarrafnā fī hādha'l-Qurʾān* — "And surely, We have explained in this Qurʾān that they may take heed." Ibn Kathir reads it as: We have explained Our warnings so that they may remember the proof, the evidence and the exhortations contained in it, and be prevented from shirk, from wrongdoing and from scandal.

Then the ayah says what came of it: *wa mā yazīduhum illā nufūrā* — "but it increases them in naught save aversion." Ibn Kathir specifies who is meant by "them": the wrongdoers among them. And he glosses *nufūr* — aversion, a shying away — as aversion towards the truth: they go further away from it.

It is worth sitting with as a question rather than a theory: when a passage presses on something we would rather keep, does it draw us nearer, or do we quietly find a reason to put it down?

## Ayah 42 — the argument that ends the matter

Now comes the proof, and the Prophet ﷺ is told to deliver it: "Say: If there had been other gods along with Him as they assert, then they would certainly have sought out a way to the Lord of the Throne."

**Ibn Kathir's reading — your own logic destroys your practice.** Ibn Kathir describes what these idolaters claimed: that Allah has a partner among His creation, and they worship others besides Him so that those others may bring them nearer to Him and intercede for them with Him. He answers on exactly those terms: if the matter is as you say, and there is another god besides Him whom you worship in order to draw closer to Him, "then those whom you worship would themselves worship Him and seek means to draw closer to Him." The thing you are leaning on is itself leaning on Him. So, says Ibn Kathir, worship Him alone, just as those on whom you call besides Him worship Him. Then the decisive line: you have no need of a deity to be an intermediary between you and Him, "for He does not like or accept that, rather He hates it and rejects it, and has forbidden that through all of His Messengers and Prophets."

**Maʿārif ul Qurʾān's reading — a divided godhead is an impossible universe.** Taking the same phrase, "then they would have found out a way to the Lord of the Throne," Maʿārif draws out the proof of tawḥīd (the Oneness of Allah) contained in it: Allah alone is the Creator, Owner and Master of the entire universe. Were it otherwise, and He had partners in this godhead, differences would necessarily have emerged among them; and in the eventuality of a difference, the whole universal system would have gone to ruin — because, as Maʿārif puts it, "ever abiding peace among them is habitually impossible." Maʿārif notes that the argument is stated here in brief, while the books of ʿilm al-kalām (scholastic theology) set out the logical rationale behind it in great detail.

Note the title the ayah uses for Allah: *dhi'l-ʿArsh*, the Lord of the Throne — the One towards whom, on Ibn Kathir's reading, any supposed partner would itself be seeking a way.

## Ayah 43 — far above what they say

*Subḥānahu wa taʿālā ʿammā yaqūlūna ʿuluwwan kabīrā.* Ibn Kathir explains that Allah here glorifies and sanctifies Himself far above all of that — above what these idolaters say when they transgress and do wrong by claiming that there are other gods besides Him — and that *ʿuluwwan kabīrā* means far above.

Ibn Kathir states plainly who is being wronged by that speech: "He is Allah, the One, the Self-Sufficient Master, Whom all creatures need. He begets not, nor was He begotten, and there is none comparable or coequal unto Him."

Read that against ayah 40 and every part of it lands. *He begets not, nor was He begotten* — so there are no daughters and no sons. *There is none comparable or coequal unto Him* — so there is no partner. *The Self-Sufficient Master, Whom all creatures need* — so there is no one who could be an intermediary, because everyone who might be proposed for the role is himself among those who need Him.

## Ayah 44 — everything in existence glorifies Him

"The seven heavens and the earth and all that is therein glorify Him, and there is not a thing but glorifies His praise."

Ibn Kathir draws out the force of this: the seven heavens and the earth and the creatures that dwell in them sanctify Him, exalt Him, venerate Him, glorify Him and magnify Him far above what these idolaters say, and they bear witness that He is One in His Lordship and His divinity. In everything there is a sign of Allah indicating that He is One. And of the phrase "there is not a thing but glorifies His praise," Ibn Kathir says: there is no created being that does not celebrate the praises of Allah.

So the idolater is not merely wrong — he is alone in it. This is why Ibn Kathir recalls again the ayat about the heavens nearly tearing, the earth splitting and the mountains falling in ruins because a child is ascribed to the Most Beneficent (19:90–91): creation is not neutral about this speech.

**"But you understand not their glorification."** Ibn Kathir explains: you do not understand them, O mankind, because it is not like your languages. And he states that this applies to all creatures generally — animal, inanimate and botanical — which is the better known of the two opinions, and the more reliable.

### Is this real speech, or the testimony of their existence?

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān lays the discussion out. The tasbīḥ (glorification of Allah) offered by the angels, by believing jinn and by believing human beings is self-evident. Disbelieving humans and jinn obviously do not say it. The difficulty is with the things in this universe we regard as insensate, without reason or intelligence.

*Some ʿulamāʾ* say their tasbīḥ is circumstantial — state-articulated, the testimony of their very state of being. The condition of everything other than Allah tells us that it is neither permanent in its existence nor self-sustaining in its survival; the whole ongoing arrangement has been set in motion under the power and control of some supreme power. That testimony is its tasbīḥ.

*Other investigative scholars* say that volitional, chosen tasbīḥ is particular to angels, believing jinn and human beings — but that Allah has cast every particle of this universe into the mould of a chanter of His glory. On this view, even those who deny Allah outright — Maʿārif names materialists, atheists and modern-day communists — are, in their very existence, compulsively busy glorifying Allah, just as trees and rocks and dust and a zillion other things are busy recounting His glory. Their tasbīḥ is compulsively ingrained, responding to the call of the creational imperative. Common people simply do not hear it.

Maʿārif then gives the argument that settles it, as mentioned by al-Qurṭubī: the ayah itself says *you do not understand their glorification*. A circumstantial, state-articulated tasbīḥ is something any intelligent person can readily identify — so if the Qurʾān tells us this glorification is beyond common understanding, it must be more than that. It is real, though beyond our comprehension.

Al-Qurṭubī supports this with further proofs. Allah says of Sayyidnā Dāwūd (peace be upon him) in Sūrah Ṣād that He subjugated the mountains with him, and they used to glorify Allah evening and morning. Al-Qurṭubī's argument is: if this glorification were merely state-articulated, why was it singled out as something particular to Dāwūd, when a state-articulated tasbīḥ is something every discerning human being can sense from everything? That it was singled out makes it obvious that this tasbīḥ was spoken, verbally and audibly. He also points to Sūrah al-Baqarah, where some rocks "fall down in fear of Allah" (2:74) — which proves that rocks have consciousness, sense and the fear of Allah — and to Sūrah Maryam, where the mountains fall down crumbling because a son is attributed to the Most Merciful (19:90–91). Once that is granted, their saying tasbīḥ should not be considered improbable.

### What the Sunnah reports

- **Sahih Al-Bukhari**, from Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him): "We used to hear the tasbīḥ of the food as it was being eaten." A variant related by Maʿārif has it: "when we ate with the Holy Prophet ﷺ, we used to hear the sound of tasbīḥ said by the food."
- **Sahih Muslim**, from Sayyidnā Jābir ibn Samurah (may Allah be pleased with him): the Prophet ﷺ said, "I know the rock of Makkah al-Mukarramah that used to say salām to me before the call of prophethood — and I know it even now." Some say the reference is to al-Ḥajar al-Aswad; Allah knows best.
- **Muʾatta Imam Malik and Sunan Ibn Majah**, on the authority of Sayyidnā Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī (may Allah be pleased with him): the Prophet ﷺ said that there is no jinn, man, tree, rock or common clod of earth that hears the call of the muʾadhdhin without bearing witness to his faith and righteousness on the Day of Qiyāmah.

Al-Qurṭubī observes that reports on such matters abound. Maʿārif relates two further well-known accounts without naming a collection: the pebbles that said tasbīḥ in the blessed hand of the Prophet ﷺ, clearly heard by the noble Ṣaḥābah; and the *Ustuwānah Ḥannānah*, the dried tree trunk that had served as his support when he gave the khuṭbah, from which the Ṣaḥābah heard the sound of wailing when he bypassed it to deliver the khuṭbah from a stepped minbar. On the pebbles, Shaykh Jalāl al-Dīn as-Suyūṭī, explaining this in *al-Khaṣāʾiṣ al-Kubrā*, said that the pebbles saying tasbīḥ was not itself the miracle — pebbles say tasbīḥ wherever they are; the miracle was that once they were in his blessed hand, that tasbīḥ became audible. Al-Qurṭubī declared this refinement the weightier view.

Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) reached the same conclusion from the other direction. He said one mountain says to another, "Say, O brother, has a man ever gone across you, someone who was good at remembering Allah?" — and if the answer is yes, that mountain is pleased with him. As proof he recited "And they say, the Most Merciful has taken a son" (19:88), then said: this verse proves that mountains are affected by hearing words of kufr and are seized by fear. That being so, do you think they listen to what is false and do not listen to what is true, do not hear Allah being remembered and are not affected by it? (Qurṭubī, with reference to the *Raqāʾiq* of Ibn Mubārak.) Ibrāhīm (may Allah have mercy on him) said this tasbīḥ is universal, including the animate and the inanimate both — so much so that not even the least sound made by the panels of doors is devoid of it.

## Living it

Two hadiths cited by Ibn Kathir here turn all of this into behaviour.

**Imam Ahmad** recorded that [Muʿādh bin Anas said that] the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came upon some people sitting on their mounts and talking to one another, and said to them: "Ride them safely then leave them safely. Do not use them as chairs for you to have conversations in the streets and marketplaces, because the one that is ridden may be better than the one who rides it, and may remember Allah more than he does." **An-Nasa'i** recorded in his Sunan that ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade us from killing frogs."

Read them alongside ayah 44 and the logic is plain. A creature that is glorifying Allah is not simply raw material for our convenience or our idle cruelty. And the animal beneath a man may be better than him and may remember Allah more than he does — which should quieten any sense of rank we carry, and shame us into more remembrance of Allah.

The other practical demand is the one in ayah 42: no intermediary. Worship Him alone, just as those you call upon besides Him worship Him.

## The closing words: *Ḥalīm, Ghafūr*

The passage ends not with a thunderbolt but with: "Truly, He is Ever Forbearing, Oft-Forgiving."

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah does not hasten to punish those who disobey Him; rather He gives them time and waits. But if they persist in their stubborn kufr, He seizes them with a punishment of the All-Mighty, the All-Capable. He cites what was recorded in **the Two Sahihs**: "Allah will let the wrongdoer carry on until, when He does seize him, He will never let him go" — after which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited, "Such is the punishment of your Lord when He seizes the (population of) towns while they are doing wrong" (11:102). Ibn Kathir adds the ayat about the many townships destroyed while they were given to wrongdoing (22:45) and the many townships given respite while given to wrongdoing (22:48).

So forbearance is not indifference, and delay is not approval. It is room — and room given for a reason. Ibn Kathir closes on exactly that: whoever gives up his disbelief and disobedience and turns back to Allah in repentance, Allah will accept his repentance, as He says, "And whoever does evil or wrongs himself but afterwards seeks Allah's forgiveness…" (4:110). He notes that the same pair of names, *Ḥalīm, Ghafūr*, closes the passage at the end of Sūrah Fāṭir, where Allah says that He grasps the heavens and the earth lest they should move away from their places, and that if they were to move away, there is not one that could grasp them after Him (35:41–45).

That is the whole passage in miniature. The heavens and the earth are held in place by Him; there is not a thing in them that does not glorify His praise; and the people who deny Him are still given time. The forbearance that lets the denier speak is the same forbearance that leaves the door of return open. Ayah 41 said the Qurʾān has been explained "that they may take heed." Ayah 44 tells us why the time to take heed still exists.

passages.title: Veiled hearts that recoil from the Quran
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These four ayat describe what happens when the Qur'an is recited to people who do not believe in the Hereafter. Allah places a veil between the reciter and the listener, coverings over their hearts and a heaviness in their ears; and when Allah is mentioned *Alone*, they turn away and flee. Ayah 47 tells the Prophet ﷺ that Allah knows exactly how they were listening and what they said in their private counsel; ayah 48 addresses the names and comparisons they coined for him.

**What holds them together.** Ayat 45–46 describe the barrier, and the ayat attribute it to Allah Himself: *"We put"*, *"We have put"*. Ayah 47 shows that these men did listen. Ayah 48 turns to the labels they invented for the one reciting. There is also a thread back to the previous ayah: *Maʿārif ul Qurʼān*, commenting there, quotes *"but you do not understand (lā tafqahūn) their extolling"* (17:44) about creation's glorification of Allah that common people cannot grasp — and here the same root returns, coverings on their hearts *"lest they should understand it" (an yafqahūhu)*.

## Ayah 45: the veil that cannot be seen

*"And when you recite the Qur'an, We put between you and those who believe not in the Hereafter, an invisible veil."*

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is addressing His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ directly: when you recite Qur'an to these idolaters, We put an invisible veil between you and them. Qatādah and Ibn Zayd said this veil is "coverings over their hearts."

The Arabic phrase is **ḥijāban mastūrā**. A *ḥijāb* is a screen or curtain — something placed between two parties; *mastūr* is the passive form, *covered* or *hidden*. Ibn Kathir gives the sense as "something which covers, or that cannot be seen, so there is a barrier between them and guidance," and he notes that this is the interpretation Ibn Jarīr (may Allah have mercy on him) thought was correct.

**A parallel from elsewhere in the Qur'an.** Ibn Kathir places beside this ayah the words the deniers say of themselves: *"Our hearts are under coverings from that to which you invite us; and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a screen"* (41:5) — which, as Ibn Kathir explains, means there is something stopping and preventing your words from reaching us. The vocabulary is the same as ayah 46: coverings, deafness, a screen. The difference in Sūrah al-Isrāʾ is who is said to place it — here the ayah says *We put*.

## Ayah 46: the covering and the heaviness

*"And We have put coverings over their hearts, lest they should understand it, and in their ears deafness."*

Ibn Kathir opens the two key words. **Akinnah** ("coverings") is the plural of *kinān*, which covers the heart. **Waqr** is a heaviness in the ears — Ibn Kathir explains it as "something that will stop them from hearing the Qur'an in such a way that they will understand it and be guided by it."

That last phrase repays attention. Ibn Kathir does not say they are stopped from hearing; he specifies the kind of hearing that is stopped — hearing that ends in understanding and guidance. And *"lest they should understand it"*, he says, means lest they should understand the Qur'an. The word for that understanding is *fiqh*, from the same root as the *lā tafqahūn* of the previous ayah. Ayah 47 will confirm that these men did listen.

**And the phrase that empties the room.** *"And when you make mention of your Lord Alone in the Qur'an, they turn on their backs, fleeing in extreme dislike."* Ibn Kathir explains "your Lord *Alone*" (*waḥdahu*) as meaning: when you declare Allah to be One in your recitation, and say *Lā ilāha illā Allāh*. On the rest of the ayah he says *wallaw* means they turn away, and *ʿalā adbārihim nufūrā* — on their backs, fleeing in extreme dislike.

So Ibn Kathir identifies precisely what triggers the flight: the declaration that Allah is One — *tawḥīd*, affirming Allah alone as the only true object of worship, with no partner. He cites the parallel: *"And when Allah Alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who believe not in the Hereafter are filled with disgust"* (39:45).

**Qatādah's comment** on this ayah, reported by Ibn Kathir, turns the picture around. When the Muslims said *Lā ilāha illā Allāh*, the idolaters disliked it and found it intolerable; Iblīs and his troops hated it — but Allah insisted on supporting it so that it would prevail over those who opposed it. Whoever uses it against his opponent will prevail, and whoever fights for it will be victorious. Qatādah adds that, out of all mankind, only the Muslims of the Arabian Peninsula — which a rider can traverse in a few nights — knew this word and accepted it.

## Ayah 47: three men, three nights

*"We know best of what they listen to, when they listen to you. And when they take secret counsel, then the wrongdoers say: 'You follow none but a bewitched man.'"*

Ibn Kathir tells us that Allah is informing His Prophet ﷺ about what the leaders of Quraysh discussed when they came and listened to him reciting Qur'an **in secret, without their people knowing about it**. Under this ayah he cites a report from Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq in *as-Sīrah*, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim ibn Shihāb az-Zuhrī:

Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb, Abū Jahl ibn Hishām and al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq — the ally of Banū Zahrah — went out one night to listen to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he prayed at night in his house. Each took up his own position for listening, and none of them knew the others were there. They stayed listening all night until dawn. Leaving, they met up on the road and blamed one another: "Do not come back again, lest you give the wrong impression" — that is, that you like what you hear. The second night, each man returned to his place and listened until dawn; again they met on the road, and again they blamed each other in the same words. The third night, each came back once more and listened until dawn — and this time, meeting on the road, they said: "Let us not leave until we promise not to come back." They made the promise and went their separate ways.

In the morning, al-Akhnas took his stick and went to Abū Sufyān's house. "Tell me, O Abū Ḥanẓalah — what do you think of what you have heard from Muḥammad?" Abū Sufyān answered, "O Abū Thaʿlabah, by Allah, I have heard something I understand and I know what is meant by it, and I have heard things I do not understand and do not know what is meant by it." "Me too," said al-Akhnas, "by the One by Whom you swore."

Then he left and went to Abū Jahl and asked him the same question. Abū Jahl's answer, as the report gives it: "We and Banū ʿAbd Manāf competed for honour and position: they fed people so we fed people, they engaged in battle so we engaged in battle, they gave so we gave, until we were neck and neck, like race horses. Then they said, we have a Prophet among us who receives revelation from heaven. How could we compete with that? By Allah, we will never believe in him." Then al-Akhnas got up and left him.

**Read the ayah again after that report.** *"We know best of what they listen to, when they listen to you"* — and Ibn Kathir places this account of three nights of secret listening, and of the conversations that followed in private houses, directly beneath those words.

**"A bewitched man" (*masḥūr*).** Ibn Kathir notes that according to the better-known view this means someone affected by magic (*siḥr*); it may also mean a man who has a lung — that is, a mere human being, as if to say that in following Muḥammad you would only be following a human being. Ibn Kathir says this second suggestion does not sound correct, because what they meant here was that he was under the influence of magic which made him see dreams in which he learned these words that he recited. Some of them, he adds, said he was a poet, or a soothsayer, or crazy, or a sorcerer.

**Can magic affect a Prophet?** *Maʿārif ul Qurʼān* takes up the question, since it stands proved from Hadith that there was an occasion when the Prophet ﷺ was affected by magic. Its answer: a prophet being affected by magic is as possible as his being affected by sickness. Prophets are not detached from human characteristics — they could be wounded, run a temperature, feel pain — and magic too is triggered by the influence of physical causes. Citing *Bayān al-Qurʼān*, it explains that when the disbelievers called him *masḥūr* in ayah 47 they really meant to call him insane, and that is what the Qur'an refutes; so the Hadith of magic is not contradictory. Muhammad Taqi Usmani adds in the footnote that magic can affect a prophet only to cause a physical illness, and can never have an adverse effect on his performance of his functions as a prophet — the sense in which the disbelievers used the word was the impossible one, while the Hadith refers to physical illness.

## Ayah 48: names instead of a way

*"See what examples they have put forward for you. So they have gone astray, and never can they find a way."*

The *amthāl* are the examples and comparisons they put forward for him — the labels Ibn Kathir has just listed: poet, soothsayer, crazy, sorcerer, bewitched. The ayah's opening word is a command to *look*: **unẓur**.

Then the ayah moves straight from those names to the outcome: *faḍallū fa-lā yastaṭīʿūna sabīlā*. Ibn Kathir's gloss is unsparing — "they will never be guided to the truth and will never find a way to reach it."

## The veil as concealment: the Prophet ﷺ hidden from his enemies

Both commentaries attach to ayah 45 an incident in which the veil worked as literal concealment.

Ibn Kathir records that al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Yaʿlā al-Mawṣilī reported from Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr (may Allah be pleased with her) that when *"Perish the two hands of Abū Lahab"* (111:1) was revealed, Umm Jamīl — Abū Lahab's wife — came with a stone pestle in her hand, screaming: we shun his religion and disobey whatever he commands. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sitting with Abū Bakr by his side. Abū Bakr said, "This woman has come and I am afraid she will see you." The Prophet ﷺ said, **"Certainly she will not see me,"** and he recited Qur'an through which he was protected from her — the very ayah under discussion: *"And when you recite the Qur'an, We put between you and those who believe not in the Hereafter, an invisible veil."* She came and found Abū Bakr, but she did not see the Prophet ﷺ. She said, "O Abū Bakr, I have heard that your companion is lampooning me." Abū Bakr said, "No, by the Lord of this House — he is not lampooning you." Then she went away, saying, "The Quraysh know that I am the daughter of their master."

*Maʿārif ul Qurʼān* reports the same event from al-Qurṭubī on the authority of Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, with added detail. Noticing her well before she arrived, Abū Bakr said to the Prophet ﷺ, "If you move away from here, it will be better. This woman has a sharp tongue. She will say things which may cause you pain." He said, "No, Allah Taʿālā will put a curtain between me and her." She arrived, could not see him anywhere, turned to Abū Bakr and complained that his companion had satirised them in poetry; Abū Bakr replied, "By Allah, he is no composer of poetry, much less that of the kind in which people are satirised." After she left, Abū Bakr asked, "Didn't she see you?" He said, "As long as she was here, an angel kept obstructing the view between me and her."

**A Qur'anic formula for remaining unseen.** *Maʿārif ul Qurʼān* then transmits from Kaʿb (may Allah be pleased with him): on occasions when the Prophet ﷺ wished to remain hidden from the sight of the idolaters, he would recite three ayat, and such was their effect that the disbelievers were unable to see him — al-Kahf 18:57 ("Surely, We have put covers on their hearts, so that they do not understand it, and deafness in their ears"), an-Naḥl 16:108 (those on whose hearts and hearing and vision Allah has put a seal), and al-Jāthiyah 45:23 (the one who takes his own desire as god, with a seal on his hearing and his heart and a veil over his vision).

Kaʿb says he related this to a Syrian who had to travel into adjoining Byzantium on business; the local disbelievers there harassed him, and when he escaped they pursued him. He remembered the account and recited the three ayat — and it was as if a screen had been placed over their eyes, so that they could not see him though he was walking on the same pathway they were passing along. Imām Thaʿlabī says he related Kaʿb's account to a resident of the town of Rayy, who was later held prisoner by the disbelievers of Daylam; escaping, he was pursued, recited the three ayat, and Allah screened their eyes so that they could not see him — though they were walking side by side, their clothes touching his.

Imām al-Qurṭubī says the ayat from Sūrah Yā Sīn may be added to those three: the opening ayat (36:1–9), ending *"And We have placed before them an obstruction and behind them an obstruction and covered them, so they do not see"*, which the Prophet ﷺ recited at the time of the Hijrah, when the idolaters of Makkah had besieged his house. He recited them and went right through them, throwing dust on their heads, and none of them knew anything about it.

And al-Qurṭubī reports an incident he went through himself, in the Manthūr Castle of al-Qarṭubah in his own country of al-Andalus. He ran in front of the enemy and sat in a corner; two horsemen were sent after him. He was on open ground, with nothing to obstruct the view between them — but he was reciting those ayat of Sūrah Yā Sīn. Both horsemen passed by him, then turned back the way they had come, saying, "This person must be some devil," because they could not see him. Allah Taʿālā, he says, had turned them blind as far as he was concerned.

## Living with these ayat

**Do not measure the Qur'an by its effect on a heart that is covered.** Ayah 45 tells the Prophet ﷺ that the veil between him and those who do not believe in the Hereafter is something Allah has put there; Ibn Kathir's report shows what that looked like in practice — three nights of listening to his recitation, ending in a mutual promise never to come back. The one who conveys the Qur'an is not carrying the outcome.

**Guard against being a listener who does not hear.** These men were not careless listeners; they crept out at night to hear, and Abū Sufyān could even sort what he understood from what he did not. Yet Ibn Kathir's gloss on *waqr* describes exactly what was withheld: hearing the Qur'an "in such a way that they will understand it and be guided by it." That is the question to put to ourselves after recitation — not only whether we followed the words, but whether they reached us as guidance.

**Watch your heart at *Lā ilāha illā Allāh*.** Ibn Kathir makes this the trigger in ayah 46: when Allah is declared One, they turn on their backs and flee. Qatādah's words are the encouragement on the other side: this is the word Allah insisted on supporting so that it would prevail over those who opposed it — whoever uses it against his opponent will prevail, and whoever fights for it will be victorious.

**Notice the reason Abū Jahl gave.** In the report Ibn Kathir cites, what he offered when asked about the recitation was his clan's rivalry with Banū ʿAbd Manāf: they had matched them in feeding people, in battle, in giving, "until we were neck and neck, like race horses" — and then came a Prophet among their rivals. "How could we compete with that? By Allah, we will never believe in him." It is worth asking, of any position we hold firmly, what we would stand to lose by letting go of it — and looking for that first in ourselves.

passages.title: Mocking resurrection and the answer to it
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** Four ayat that record a sneer and answer it. The disbelievers cannot imagine that crumbled bones will ever live again, so they say it out loud in a tone of denial — and Allah teaches His Prophet ﷺ exactly what to say back. Ibn Kathir heads this section simply: *Refutation of Those Who do not believe in Life after Death.*

**What holds the four together.** They read as a live exchange, not an essay. They object (ayah 49); the Prophet ﷺ is told *Say* — and given a challenge (ayat 50–51); they object again, twice (ayah 51); he answers both times, each answer again opening with *Say*; and then in ayah 52 the argument simply stops, because Allah lifts the curtain and shows them the Day itself. And notice the tense running through the middle: *fa-sayaqūlūn*, "then they **will** say" — the objection is named in advance, and the answer to it is given before it is even raised.

## The objection: "bones and dust" (ayah 49)

Their words are *a-idhā kunnā ʿiẓāman wa rufātan* — rendered by Ibn Kathir as "When we are bones and fragments (destroyed)." The early scholars glossed that second word directly: Mujahid took *rufāt* to mean *earth*; ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that it means *dust*. So the picture they are painting is deliberately bleak: not a corpse, but soil. Ibn Kathir explains what they meant by the rest of it — resurrection "after we have disintegrated and become nothing, and have been forgotten."

Their assumption is not merely that the body has scattered, but that the person has been *forgotten* — dropped out of the record of reality. Ibn Kathir points to how the Qur'an quotes the same mood elsewhere: "Shall we indeed be returned to our former state of life? Even after we are crumbled bones? … It would in that case be a return with loss!" (79:10–12). And he cites the verse that names their fundamental mistake: "And he puts forth for Us a parable, and forgets his own creation" (36:78–79).

## The answer: "Be stones, or iron" (ayat 50–51)

The reply does not soften their objection — it raises the stakes past what they proposed. *Qul kūnū ḥijāratan aw ḥadīdan*: "Say: Be you stones or iron." Ibn Kathir notes precisely why these two are named: they "are more difficult to restore than bones and fragments." Go further down that road than your own imagination went, and it changes nothing.

Then a third term, deliberately left open: *aw khalqan mimmā yakburu fī ṣudūrikum* — "or some created thing that is yet greater (or harder) in your breasts." Not "greater in the world" but *in your breasts*: whatever your own hearts rate as greater or harder still. The challenge is handed to the objector to fill in himself.

**How the early scholars read that third term.** Here the commentary preserves a genuine difference:

- **Death itself.** Ibn Ishaq narrated from Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid: "I asked Ibn ʿAbbas about that, and he said: 'This is death.'" ʿAtiyah reported that Ibn ʿUmar explained the ayah as: "If you were dead I would still resurrect you." Ibn Kathir notes this was also the view of Saʿid bin Jubayr, Abu Salih, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak and others. On this reading, the sense is: suppose you became death — which is the opposite of living — Allah will resurrect you when He wills, "for nothing can stop Him when He wills a thing."
- **The heavens, the earth and the mountains.** Mujahid himself is also reported to have said: "This means the heavens, earth and mountains."
- **Anything at all.** Another report gives the sense plainly: "Whatever you want to be, go ahead, Allah will still resurrect you after you die."

The three readings converge on one point rather than competing: the objection was never really about *how far gone* the material is.

## "Then who will bring us back?" (ayah 51)

Cornered on the material, they shift the question to the agent: *fa-sayaqūlūna man yuʿīdunā* — Ibn Kathir paraphrases their meaning: "who will resurrect us if we are stones or iron or some other strong created thing?"

The answer is one clause: *Qul alladhī faṭarakum awwala marrah* — "Say: He Who created you first." Ibn Kathir unfolds it: "He Who created you when you were nothing, then you became human beings, walking about. He is able to create you anew, no matter what you have become." The proof is not somewhere out in the sky; it is the objector's own body, standing there asking the question. Ibn Kathir joins to it: "And He it is Who originates the creation, then He will repeat it; and this is easier for Him" (30:27).

## The head-shake — a word worth feeling (ayah 51)

Having no reply, they answer with their bodies: *fa-sayunghiḍūna ilayka ru'ūsahum*, "then they will shake their heads at you." Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah said, "They will move their heads in a gesture of mockery." Ibn Kathir adds that this is what the Arabs understood from the language, and then opens the word up: *fa-sayunghiḍūn* indicates an up-and-down movement, *nughaḍ*. From the same root, *naghḍ* is used for the young of the ostrich, because when it walks, it walks quickly and moves its head. The same word is used to describe a tooth when it becomes loose and is detached from its place.

The word's cousins are a fast, head-bobbing bird and a tooth that will not stay put. It captures a specific human posture: the twitch of the head that says *listen to yourself* — the gesture people make when they have no argument but plenty of contempt. It is a body language of dismissal, and the Qur'an preserved it in a word.

**"When will that be?"** Their spoken taunt, *matā huwa*, is a demand for a date, not a request for information. Ibn Kathir says it "shows that they thought it very unlikely that it would happen," and puts alongside it: "And they say: 'When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?'" (36:48), and "Those who believe not therein seek to hasten it" (42:18). It is a permanent human type — treating the thing you fear least as the thing that is furthest away.

**The reply refuses the game.** *Qul ʿasā an yakūna qarīban* — "Say: Perhaps it is near!" No date is given. Ibn Kathir renders its force: "beware of it, for it is at hand and will no doubt come to you, and what will be will be." *ʿasā* ("perhaps") leaves the timing entirely with Allah while removing every excuse from the listener, because a thing that may be near must be prepared for now.

## The Day He calls (ayah 52)

*Yawma yadʿūkum* — "On the Day when He will call you." Ibn Kathir identifies the caller: the Lord, may He be blessed and exalted.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the word: *yadʿūkum* comes from *duʿāʾ*, to call out for someone by announcing it vocally. Citing al-Qurtubi, it explains that this calling to the plains of Resurrection will be through the angel Israfil: when he sounds the second trumpet the dead will come alive and assemble there; and it is also possible that, once alive, a call then goes out to all of them to assemble.

Ibn Kathir stacks up what the summons is like: "When He will call you by a single call, behold, you will come out from the earth" (30:25) — meaning, he says, when He commands you to come out from the earth, "for nothing can oppose Him or prevent His command from being fulfilled." Then: "And Our commandment is but one as the twinkling of an eye" (54:50); "Verily, Our Word unto a thing when We intend it, is only that We say unto it: 'Be!' — and it is" (16:40); "But it will be only a single *Zajrah*. When behold, they find themselves on the surface of the earth alive" (79:13–14). It is one definitive command — and then, as Ibn Kathir puts it, the people will have come out from the inside of the earth to its surface.

Set that against ayah 49. They wanted to know the *mechanism* — how do scattered particles reassemble? The passage never supplies one. It answers at a different level: the One whose word to a thing is "Be" — and it is.

**A teaching on names.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing al-Qurtubi, records that in a hadith the Prophet ﷺ said that on the Day of Qiyamah you will be called out with your name and the name of your father — therefore give good names, avoiding absurd ones. (The source names al-Qurtubi as its authority and does not name a hadith collection.) The summons of ayah 52 is not a crowd being herded; it is people called by name.

## "You will answer with His praise" — and the question it raises

*Fa-tastajībūna bi-ḥamdih.* Ibn Kathir: "you will all rise up in response to His command and in obedience to His will." Maʿārif adds the grammar, and the grammar carries the meaning: *istijābah* means to respond when called and to be present before the one calling; and *bi-ḥamdihi* ("praising Him") describes the state of those responding — they come *as praisers*, *ḥāmidīn*. So the outcome, Maʿārif says, is that all of them will present themselves praising Allah while coming to those fateful plains.

Which raises the obvious question — the disbelievers too? Here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out a real difference among the commentators:

- **Yes, everyone — and the disbelievers are the ones actually being addressed.** Outwardly the verse does seem to indicate that this will be the state of all, believers or disbelievers. And Maʿārif adds that the real addressees here are the disbelievers: it is about them that this is being said. Among the authorities of tafsir, Saʿid ibn Jubayr said that the disbelievers too will rise from their graves saying *Subḥānaka wa bi-ḥamdika* — "Pure are You, and to You belong all praises" — but that their act of praising at that hour will be of no use to them. Maʿārif explains why: when these people see life after death, the words of praise will escape their mouths involuntarily. This will be no deed deserving recompense.
- **No, this describes the believers.** Some commentators said this state has been particularised to the believers, arguing that what the Qur'an reports of the disbelievers at that moment is rather: "Woe be to us! Who made us rise from our resting-place?" (36:52), and "O my remorse over what I have neglected on the side of obedience to Allah!" (39:56).

**How Maʿārif reconciles them.** There is no likelihood of a contradiction. It may be that in the beginning all rise praising; then later, when the disbelievers are separated from the believers — "But today, O criminals, you stand out distinctly apart" (36:59) — they will also say what those other verses report. And, Maʿārif notes, it stands proved from many explications of the Qur'an and from the Sunnah that the stations of Resurrection will be different, with a corresponding difference in the states and conditions of people at each. Imam al-Qurtubi put it beautifully: the rising in Resurrection will *begin* with the praise of Allah, everyone doing it as they rise, and on that praise all matters will *end* — as Allah says: "And matters between them have been settled in accordance with the truth, and it was said: All praise belongs to Allah, the Lord of the Worlds" (39:75).

The mouth that shook its head and said "When will that be?" opens on that Day with *al-ḥamdu lillāh*.

## "You will think you stayed only a little while"

The last clause, *wa taẓunnūna in labithtum illā qalīlā*. Ibn Kathir explains: on the Day when you rise up from your graves, you will think that your stay in this earthly abode was only a little while. He gathers the parallels:

- "The Day they see it, it will be as if they had not tarried except an afternoon or a morning" (79:46).
- They will speak in a very low voice to each other, "You stayed not longer than ten"; and the best among them in knowledge and wisdom will say, "You stayed no longer than a day!" (20:102–104).
- "And on the Day that the Hour will be established, they will swear that they stayed not but an hour — thus were they ever deluded" (30:55).
- "He will say: 'What number of years did you stay on earth?' They will say: 'We stayed a day or part of a day. Ask of those who keep account.' He will say: 'You stayed not but a little, if you had only known!'" (23:112–114).

Ten days, one day, part of a day, an hour. A whole lifetime — the one that felt long enough to postpone everything in — will read, from the other side, as an afternoon.

## Living it

**Do not measure Allah's power against your imagination.** The objection in ayah 49 is really a statement about the objector's mental limits, not about reality. When something in the promise of Allah strains what you can picture — the gathering, the reckoning, a body remade from dust — remember the answer of ayah 51: He created you when you were nothing.

**Watch the head-shake in yourself.** Mockery is what people reach for when they have run out of arguments. The Qur'an did not dignify it with a debate; it named the gesture and moved on. When someone dismisses faith with a smirk rather than a reason, recognise it for what it is — and when you feel the smirk rising in your own chest toward something you have not understood, recognise it there too.

**Live as though "perhaps it is near."** That single word *ʿasā* is the practical heart of the passage. Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is a whole way of life in one line: beware of it, for it is at hand and will no doubt come to you.

**Start the praise now.** If even those who denied Him will rise with words of praise escaping their mouths involuntarily — praise that, as Saʿid ibn Jubayr said, will be of no use to them — then the difference between them and the believer is not the words. It is whether those words were a lifetime's habit or a last, useless reflex. Everything ends in the praise of Allah. The only question worth asking is when yours began.

passages.title: Gracious speech and the Lord who knows best
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Ayah 53 gives one instruction about how believers are to speak. Read together with it, ayat 54 and 55 place guidance, mercy, punishment and rank where they belong — with Allah. Your tongue is your responsibility; another person's guidance, punishment, and rank before Allah are not. Allah alone knows who deserves what, and even His Messenger ﷺ was not sent as a guardian over anyone. Once that is settled, the urge to crush someone with words loses its footing.

## "Tell My servants to say that which is best"

The command in ayah 53 reaches the believers through the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir reads it exactly so: "Allah commands His servant Muhammad ﷺ to tell the believing servants of Allah that they should address one another in their conversations and discussions with the best and politest of words."

Notice whom the speech is owed to. Allah calls them **ʿibādī** — *My servants*. The people you are being told to speak beautifully to are described by their relationship to Allah, not by their relationship to you. Whatever else a fellow believer is to you in an argument — wrong, irritating, on the other side — he is first of all one of Allah's servants.

Notice, too, where the bar is set. The Arabic word in the ayah is **aḥsan**, which the translation renders *what is best*: "Tell My believing servants to say only what is best." Ibn Kathir's phrase for it is "the best and politest of words" — not merely words that are inoffensive, and not merely words that are true. And notice the setting he names for this: "their conversations and discussions." The standard is aimed at exactly the moments when we are least inclined to meet it.

## The occasion behind it: an insult, a hot reply, and the danger of war

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits from Imam al-Qurtubi an incident that puts this ayah in a very concrete setting. Someone used foul language against Sayyidnā ʿUmar ؓ. ʿUmar retaliated harshly and wanted to kill him. This posed the danger of a war breaking out between their two tribes. Thereupon, al-Qurtubi says, this verse was revealed.

Sit with that for a moment. The chain runs: an insult, a hot answer, a drawn intention, two tribes at each other's throats. Each step is a small, reasonable-feeling escalation from the one before it. The ayah cuts the chain at its first link — the reply.

## What Shaytan is actually doing

The second half of the ayah names the danger: Shaytan "sows a state of conflict and disagreement among them. Surely, Shaytan is to man a plain enemy."

Ibn Kathir traces the mechanism precisely: if people do not speak to one another with the best and politest of words, "Shaytan will sow discord among them, and words will lead to actions, so that evil and conflicts and fights will arise among them." That phrase — **words will lead to actions** — is the whole warning in five words. Speech is not a sealed compartment. It is the antechamber of deeds.

And this enmity is not a new development. Ibn Kathir reminds us that Shaytan "is the enemy of Adam and his descendants, and has been since he refused to prostrate to Adam. His enmity is obvious and manifest." He is not a neutral bystander who occasionally stirs. He is a declared adversary, and coarse speech between believers is one of the doors he works through. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, again following al-Qurtubi, says believers "should not speak harshly at the time of mutual difference, for this is a trap door through which the Shaitan pushes them into mutual infighting and disorder."

## From the Sunnah: don't even *point*

Ibn Kathir draws out a legal consequence of this same principle: "For this reason it is forbidden for a man to point at his Muslim brother with an iron instrument, for Shaytan may cause him to strike him with it."

Imam Ahmad recorded that Abu Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "No one of you should point at his brother with a weapon, for he does not know whether Shaytan will cause him to strike him with it and thus be thrown into a pit of Fire."

Ibn Kathir notes that al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded this hadith with the chain of narration from ʿAbdur-Razzaq.

The logic is the same as the ayah's. Nobody who jokingly raises a blade at a friend intends murder — and that is exactly the point of the warning: *he does not know* what Shaytan will do with the gesture once it has been made. The door is closed well before the harm, at the harmless-looking motion. A harsh word is the tongue's version of that raised blade.

## Even against disbelievers, foul language is not the tool

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayah 53 as reaching further still: it "prohibits Muslims from talking harshly to disbelievers." Its own wording on where the limits lie should be reported exactly as it stands: "It means that a hard line should not be taken unnecessarily, and should there be the need, even killing would be in order." Its reasoning is stated plainly — "Since it is possible to suppress the aggressive might of disbelievers and their hostility to Islam through fighting and killing (as an inevitable measure of defense), therefore, it is allowed. However, by using foul language and harsh words, neither a castle stands conquered nor anyone guided right, therefore, it has been prohibited."

To carry the point, Maʿārif quotes two lines of Persian poetry: *whereas, without an injunction of the Sharīʿah, to drink water is a sin; in another case, to shed blood under a fatwa is permissible.* The couplet turns on where permission comes from. Not from the scale of the act, and not from how strongly we feel about it, but from the injunction of the Sharīʿah. The incident with Sayyidnā ʿUmar ؓ, reported a few lines later in the same passage, shows a decision being reached the other way — in the heat of an insult.

And the practical judgement in Maʿārif's own terms is worth carrying around: abuse conquers no castle and guides no one right. It wins no battle and it reaches no soul. It only feeds the enemy the ayah has just named.

## "Your Lord knows you best" — the ground beneath the command

Ayah 54 opens by widening the address: **Rabbukum aʿlam bikum** — *Your Lord knows you best*. Ibn Kathir marks this as addressed to mankind, and explains its meaning: "He knows best who among you deserves to be guided and who does not deserve to be guided."

Place that beside ayah 53 and the passage locks together. Much of our harshness rests on a quiet verdict we have already passed — *this person is hopeless, this one is beyond reach, this one deserves it.* Ayah 54 tells us who actually holds that knowledge. **Your Lord knows you best** — better than the man opposite you knows you, and better than you know him.

Then the two possibilities: **"if He wills, He will have mercy on you, or if He wills, He will punish you."** Both are placed under His will. Ibn Kathir's gloss on the mercy is beautifully concrete: it means "by helping you to obey Him and turn to Him." So obedience, and the turning back that precedes it, are placed on the side of Allah's mercy rather than on the side of our achievement — which leaves nothing to hold over anyone else's head.

## "We have not sent you as a guardian over them"

The ayah continues: **"And We have not sent you"** — O Muhammad — **"as a guardian over them"** (*wakīlan*). Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: "We have sent you as a warner, so whoever obeys you, will enter Paradise and whoever disobeys you, will enter Hell."

This is the passage's most humbling line. If the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was not made a *wakīl* over them — if his commission was to warn, with the outcome resting between them and Allah — then no student of the Qur'an, no caller to Allah, no parent, no friend in a heated exchange has been handed a larger role than that. Your job is to convey, and to convey in the best words.

Delivered gently, this is enormously freeing. A great deal of the pressure that turns discussion into combat comes from imagining that the other person's guidance depends on winning this exchange.

## Ayah 55: the Lord who knows everyone

Ayah 55 lifts the same theme to its widest horizon: **"And your Lord knows best all who are in the heavens and the earth."** Ibn Kathir explains what is known of them: "their status or level of obedience or disobedience."

So the standing of every creature — in the heavens and on the earth alike — is already established in the knowledge of Allah. What we do when we rank each other in an argument is guess loudly about a matter already known to Him.

## Allah ranks even the Prophets — so leave ranking to Him

The ayah then does something remarkable: it exercises that ranking at the highest level. **"And indeed, We have preferred some of the Prophets above others."** Ibn Kathir cites the parallel: *"Those Messengers! We preferred some of them to others; to some of them Allah spoke directly; others He raised to degrees of honour"* (2:253).

But this raises an apparent problem, which Ibn Kathir addresses directly. The Two Sahihs report that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, **"Don't give superiority to any Prophet among Allah's Prophets."** How does that sit with a verse that plainly does prefer some above others?

Ibn Kathir's answer: "What is meant in this Hadith is giving a superiority based on whims and fanaticism or sectarian feelings, not on the basis of evidence. If there is solid evidence, we have to follow it." The prohibition is on partisanship — preferring out of whim or sectarian feeling. Where there is solid evidence, we follow it, because it is evidence and not preference.

On what the evidence establishes, Ibn Kathir gives this: there is no dispute that the Messengers are better than the rest of the Prophets, and that the mighty Messengers of Great Resolve (the group commonly referred to by the Arabic term *Ulū al-ʿAzm*, "those of firm resolve" — the label is supplied here only as a familiar aid) are the best of all. They are the five mentioned in two ayat: *"and from you and from Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and ʿIsa son of Maryam"* (33:7), and *"He has ordained for you the same religion which He ordained for Nuh, and that which We have revealed to you, and that which We ordained for Ibrahim, Musa and ʿIsa"* (42:13).

Then his own sentence, which should be quoted as he wrote it: "There is no dispute that Muhammad ﷺ is the best of them, then Ibrahim, then Musa, then ʿIsa (peace be upon them all), according to the best-known view." He adds that he has discussed the evidence in detail elsewhere. He marks the ordering as the best-known view, and it is honest to leave it exactly as he left it.

## "And to Dawud We gave the Zabur"

The ayah closes with what looks at first like an unrelated detail. Ibn Kathir reads it as deliberate: mentioning the Zabur "is an indication of his virtue and honour" — a concrete instance of the preference the ayah has just announced.

Al-Bukhari recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said that the revealed Scripture of the Zabur was made easy for Dawud, "so he would call for his mounts to be saddled, and he would finish reciting it before the job was done." A whole Book of Allah recited in the time it takes to saddle a mount — a rank given by Allah, exactly as the ayah says.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds two further notes. First, on *why the Zabur in particular* is named here: perhaps, it says, because the Zabur reports that the Holy Prophet ﷺ would be a ruler along with being a messenger and prophet — as the Qur'an says, *"And We have already written in the Zabur, after the mention, that the land is inherited by My righteous servants"* (21:105).

Second, on what the Zabur contains, Maʿārif cites Imam al-Baghawi's Tafsir: it is a book of Allah revealed to Sayyidnā Dawud (peace be upon him), of one hundred and fifty surahs, all of them restricted to the praises of Allah and prayers to Him; the areas of lawful and unlawful, obligations and limits are not taken up there.

## Living it

- **Aim at the best wording, not merely a defensible one.** Ibn Kathir's standard is "the best and politest of words," and he locates it in "conversations and discussions" — the very place we usually excuse ourselves from it.
- **Read your own harshness as the enemy's opening, not as strength.** The ayah names Shaytan in the same breath as it forbids the harsh word, and Maʿārif calls harsh speech at the time of mutual difference a trap door. Feeling righteous while walking through it is part of how it works.
- **Watch the first link, not the last.** ʿUmar ؓ was insulted before he answered. And the Sunnah closes the door at a pointed weapon, long before any wound.
- **Abuse conquers no castle and guides no one.** That is Maʿārif's own verdict on foul language — and it holds whether the person opposite you shares your faith or rejects it entirely.
- **Stop carrying a load that was never yours.** The Prophet ﷺ himself was not sent as a guardian over them; he was sent as a warner. You are asked to convey, and to convey beautifully.
- **Never rank people to win an argument.** Allah reserved even the ranking of His Prophets to Himself, and the hadith in the Two Sahihs forbids preferring between them out of whim or sectarian feeling. Our own league tables of who is more guided are guesses about a matter already known to the One who "knows best all who are in the heavens and the earth."

passages.title: The powerlessness of the gods they invoke
passages.tafsir:
**These two ayat take the case of the idolaters apart from the inside.** The Prophet ﷺ is told to issue a challenge — go ahead, call on the beings you claim are divine — and then Allah tells us what those beings are actually doing: they are themselves seeking a way of drawing near to Allah, hoping for His mercy and fearing His punishment. What holds ayah 56 and 57 together is a single movement: first the "gods" are stripped of power, then they are shown to be fellow worshippers. The one being begged is himself begging.

## Where we are in the sūrah

The passage just before this (ayah 55) closes by mentioning that Allah gave Dāwūd the Zabūr. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān suggests the Zabūr may be singled out there because it reports that the Holy Prophet ﷺ would be a ruler as well as a messenger and prophet — pointing to the verse "And We have already written in the Zabūr, after the mention, that the land is inherited by My righteous servants" (al-Anbiyāʼ 21:105). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also cites Imām al-Baghawī, who says the Zabūr is a book of Allah revealed to Sayyidnā Dāwūd (peace be upon him), containing one hundred and fifty chapters, all of them restricted to praises of Allah and prayers to Him; the areas of lawful and unlawful, obligations and limits are not taken up there.

A book given over wholly to praising Allah and calling upon Him: that is a fitting doorway into two ayat about who deserves to be called upon at all.

## Ayah 56: "Say — go ahead and call them"

Ibn Kathir opens his comment plainly: Allah says **"Say"** — meaning, "O Muhammad, say to these idolaters who worship things other than Allah."

Notice the shape of the command. The Prophet ﷺ is not told to argue in the abstract; he is told to invite them to *try it*. **"Call upon those — besides Him — whom you pretend."** Ibn Kathir explains that this means "such as idols and rivals of Allah," and then adds the crucial concession: *even if you turn to them* — go on, do it — the result will be nothing.

## The two-stage collapse: no removing, no shifting

The denial in ayah 56 comes in two steps, and the order matters.

**فَلَا يَمْلِكُونَ كَشْفَ الضُّرِّ عَنكُمْ — "They have neither the power to remove the adversity from you."** Ibn Kathir's comment leaves no margin at all: "they have no such power at all."

**وَلَا تَحْوِيلًا — "nor even to shift it."** Ibn Kathir explains this second phrase as the power "to lift the distress from you and give it to someone else." This is the sharper of the two, because shifting a burden is far less than ending it. A porter who cannot lift a weight off you might at least drag it to one side; these beings cannot even do that. The denial is a staircase down to zero: they cannot solve your problem, and they cannot so much as move it.

Then Ibn Kathir names the alternative:

> The meaning is that the only one Who is able to do that is Allah Alone, with no partner or associate, Who is the One Who creates and issues commands.

Note how he grounds the exclusivity. It is not left as a bare rule; Ibn Kathir ties it to who Allah is — "the One Who creates and issues commands."

## Who exactly were they calling on?

Here the sources open the picture out, and it is more interesting than rows of idols.

Ibn Kathir reports that al-ʿAwfī related from Ibn ʿAbbās: "The people of Shirk used to say, 'we worship the angels and the Messiah and ʿUzayr,' while these (the angels and the Messiah and ʿUzayr) themselves call upon Allah."

So the objects of this worship were not only idols. Among them were beings whom the report itself describes as calling upon Allah. That is precisely why ayah 57 has the force it does. The ayah does not need to insult them. It simply reports what they are doing.

Ibn Kathir then cites a second explanation. **Al-Bukhari recorded** — from Sulaymān bin Mahrān al-Aʿmash, from Ibrāhīm, from Abū Maʿmar, from ʿAbdullāh — on the words "Those whom they call upon, desire a means of access to their Lord": **"Some of the Jinn used to be worshipped, then they became Muslims."** According to another report: "Some humans used to worship some of the Jinn, then those Jinn became Muslim, but those humans adhered to their religion (of worshipping the Jinn)."

Read that slowly. The ones being worshipped submitted to Allah — and the worship carried on without them. A religion outliving the thing it was built on.

## Ayah 57: the "gods" are themselves worshippers

Ibn Kathir titles this whole passage: *the gods of the idolaters can neither benefit nor harm; rather they themselves seek to draw close to Allah*.

Of those invoked, the ayah in Ibn Kathir's rendering says they **"desire a means of access to their Lord, as to which of them should be the nearest."** The translation given for ayah 57 puts the same clause a little differently: **"˹Even˺ the closest ˹to Allah˺ of those invoked would be seeking"** that means. Either way, the point lands in the same place. Whether you read it as a competition among them for who comes nearest, or as saying that even the very nearest of them is still seeking, nobody in that group has arrived. Every one of them is still on the road, still reaching.

## What "wasīlah" actually means

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains **al-wasīlah** in "they seek the means of closeness to their Lord" as conveying "the sense of that which is used as a means of reaching someone." And it is specific about what that means when the One to be reached is Allah:

> As for reaching Allah, the wasilah or means is to always keep the pleasure of Allah in sight when learning or doing anything while adhering to the injunctions of the Sharīʿah strictly.

So, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, "all of them are seeking the closeness of Allah Taʿālā through their righteous deeds."

This is worth pausing on. The ayah is describing beings people were calling upon as though they held power — and it tells us that their own method of drawing near to Allah is *righteous deeds*: intention aimed at His pleasure, action bound to His law. That is the same road open to anyone. A person hunting for some other channel of access is looking for a door that the very ones in this ayah never used.

## Hope and fear, held together

The ayah continues: **"and they hope for His mercy and fear His torment."** Both. At once. About the same Lord.

Ibn Kathir draws the principle straight out:

> Worship cannot be complete or perfect unless it is accompanied by both fear and hope. Fear stops one from doing things that are forbidden, and hope makes one do more good deeds.

That is a clean division of labour. Fear is the brake — it holds you back from the forbidden. Hope is the engine — it drives you toward good.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a saying of **Sahl ibn ʿAbdullāh**, transmitted through Qurṭubī, that sharpens it further:

> Hope and Fear, that is, hoping for mercy from Allah as well as fearing Him are two different states one is in. When they stay at par, one keeps on course, correct and stable. And if any one of the two overcomes the other, one finds the equilibrium of his spiritual state subjected to disorder to the measure of that imbalance.

Note the precision of that last clause: *to the measure of that imbalance*. This is not a warning that one wrong feeling ruins you. It is a description of proportion — the further one outweighs the other, the further off course a person drifts, and by exactly that much. Which also means the repair is proportional: whichever side is thin, that is the side to feed.

And the ayah closes: **إِنَّ عَذَابَ رَبِّكَ كَانَ مَحْذُورًا — "Verily, the torment of your Lord is (something) to be afraid of."** Ibn Kathir glosses this as meaning "one should beware of it and be afraid lest it happen" — and then does something a commentator rarely does mid-sentence. He stops explaining and prays: **"We seek refuge with Allah from that."** The words are not being analysed at that point; they are being felt.

Notice also who is doing the fearing in the ayah just before. Those whom people were calling upon — the ones described as nearest — hope for His mercy and fear His torment. If *they* fear it, fear is not a beginner's stage to be outgrown. It stays.

## Living it

**Ask what you actually turn to when the pressure comes.** Ayah 56 is framed as a challenge to idolaters, but its logic tests everyone: when harm lands on you, where does your heart go first for the *lifting* of it? Ibn Kathir's line is the measuring stick — the only One able to remove the adversity, or even to shift it, is Allah alone, with no partner or associate, the One who creates and issues commands.

**Nearness is sought the way this ayah describes it being sought.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's definition of *wasīlah* is a practical instruction, not a theory: keep Allah's pleasure in view in whatever you are learning or doing, and hold to the injunctions of the Sharīʿah strictly. That is how, in its words, "all of them are seeking the closeness of Allah Taʿālā through their righteous deeds."

**Audit your balance.** Following Ibn Kathir and Sahl ibn ʿAbdullāh: if you find yourself sinning easily, your fear is thin; if you find yourself doing little good, your hope is thin. Feed the lighter side until the two sit level, because that balance is what keeps a person "on course, correct and stable."

**And do not let a devotion outlive its object.** In the report al-Bukhari recorded, the jinn who had been worshipped became Muslim, and their worshippers "adhered to their religion." Habits of the heart can carry on long after the reason for them has gone. Every so often it is worth asking whether what you are still turning toward is where you actually meant to be facing.

passages.title: Doomed towns and the withheld miracles
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These three ayat answer a demand the Makkans were pressing hard: if Muhammad ﷺ is truly a messenger, why does he not produce a miracle we can watch with our own eyes? The answer moves backwards through history — no town escapes destruction or severe torment before the Day of Resurrection (ayah 58) — and then gives the reason the demanded sign was withheld: earlier peoples were sent such signs and denied them (ayah 59). It ends with the one overwhelming sign that *was* given, the Night Journey, which divided its hearers rather than settling the matter (ayah 60).

What binds the three together is a single principle: **a sign, once sent and then denied, is fatal.** Withholding the miracle was not weakness or evasion. It was mercy — and, as you will see, mercy the Prophet ﷺ himself chose on their behalf.

## Ayah 58: no town outlives its reckoning

"And there is not a town (population) but We shall destroy it before the Day of Resurrection, or punish it with a severe torment. That is written in the Book (of Our decrees)."

The Arabic word here is *qaryah*. English "town" makes us picture buildings, but in the Qur'an the word carries the **people** as much as the place — Ibn Kathir reads it as "town (population)". The threat is not to masonry; it is to a community and its collective choices.

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is telling us here of something already **decreed and written in al-Lawh al-Mahfuz** — the Preserved Tablet, which Ibn Kathir describes as being with Allah. The ayah's closing words, "that is written in the Book," are not decoration; they are the point. Nothing about the fall of nations is improvised.

Ibn Kathir also notes that the ayah names **two** outcomes, not one:

- **destruction** — "by wiping out all its people";
- **a severe torment** — "either by killing them or sending calamities upon them as He wills."

So a community may be erased outright, or it may be left standing and struck. Which of the two, and when, is left to Allah's will.

**And it is never arbitrary.** Ibn Kathir is careful to say the cause is *their sins*, and he brings the Qur'an's own commentary on earlier nations to prove it: "We wronged them not, but they wronged themselves" (11:101); "So it tasted the evil result of its affair, and the consequence of its affair was loss" (65:9); "And many a town revolted against the command of its Lord and His Messengers" (65:8). Read together, these place the responsibility squarely on the town: it *revolted*, it *tasted the result of its own affair*, it *wronged itself*.

Notice too how wide the ayah casts. Ibn Kathir titles this section the destruction or torment of *all* disbelieving towns before the Hour begins. This is not a story about a few unlucky nations in the distant past; it is a pattern stated without exceptions, and every settlement stands somewhere inside it.

## Ayah 59: the miracle they asked for, and why it never came

This is where the passage opens up, because Ibn Kathir gives us the moment behind it. In each of the reports below, the Quraysh's demand fixes on **as-Safa** — the Makkan landmark they named as the thing they wanted turned to gold.

**Sa'id bin Jubayr's account.** The idolaters said: "O Muhammad, you claim that before you there were Prophets, among whom was one to whom the wind was subjugated, and another who could bring the dead back to life. If you want us to believe in you, ask your Lord to turn as-Safa into gold for us." Allah then conveyed to His Prophet ﷺ by inspiration (*wahy* — revelation given to a prophet): "I have heard what they have said. If you wish, I will do what they say, but if they do not believe after that, the punishment will come down upon them, **because after the sign has been sent, there is no room for speculation.** Or if you wish, I will be patient with your people and give them more time." He ﷺ said: "O Lord, give them more time." Ibn Kathir adds that this was also narrated by Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj and others.

**The report of Imam Ahmad, from Ibn 'Abbas.** The people of Makkah asked the Prophet ﷺ to turn as-Safa into gold for them, and to remove the mountains from around Makkah so that they could cultivate the land. It was said to him by Allah: "If you wish, I will be patient and give them more time, or if you wish, I will do what they are asking, but if they then disbelieve, they will be destroyed as the nations before them were destroyed." He ﷺ said: "No, be patient and give them more time." Then Allah revealed this ayah. Ibn Kathir notes that an-Nasa'i also reported this from the hadith of Jarir.

**A second report of Imam Ahmad, from Ibn 'Abbas.** The Quraysh said, "Ask your Lord to turn as-Safa into gold and we will believe in you." He ﷺ asked them, "Will you really do that?" They said, "Yes." So he asked his Lord, and Jibril came to him and said: "Your Lord conveys His Salam to you and says: 'If you wish, I will turn as-Safa into gold for them, then whoever of them disbelieves after that will be punished with a torment the like of which has never been seen in creation; or if you wish, I will open the gates of repentance and mercy for them.'" He ﷺ said: **"Rather the gates of repentance and mercy."**

Sit with that. The very people mocking him were offered, on his word, either a mountain of gold followed by a torment unlike anything seen in creation, or an open door. He chose the open door — for them. This is the man they were calling a liar.

**Now the ayah reads differently.** "And nothing stops Us from sending the Ayat but that the people of old denied them." The reason no cosmic sign was produced is not that Allah could not, and not that His Messenger ﷺ lacked standing. It is that **the file on such demands was already closed by history.** The wahy in Sa'id bin Jubayr's report states the principle in one line: "after the sign has been sent, there is no room for speculation." And the reports spell out what follows from it — the punishment comes down; they would be destroyed as the nations before them were destroyed.

**Thamud and the she-camel.** The ayah then supplies the case file: "And We sent the she-camel to Thamud as a clear sign, but they did her wrong." A sign delivered, clear and unambiguous — and they wronged it. The ayah sets that precedent directly against the Quraysh's demand.

**What signs are actually for.** "And We sent not the signs except *takhwifan*" — except to make them afraid. That single Arabic word tells you a sign's function: to shake a heart awake, not to win an argument. Qatadah put it beautifully in Ibn Kathir's citation: "Allah makes people afraid with whatever signs He wills, so that they may learn a lesson and remember and return to Him."

Two illustrations follow. Qatadah continues that he was told Kufah was shaken in the time of **Ibn Mas'ud**, who said to the people: "O people, your Lord is rebuking you, so pay heed!" And it is reported that Madinah was struck by several earthquakes in the time of **'Umar bin al-Khattab**, who said: "You have changed, by Allah, and if such a quake were to strike again, I will subject you to such and such." Neither man treated the tremor as a mere curiosity: Ibn Mas'ud named it a rebuke to be heeded, and 'Umar tied it to a change in the people themselves.

**And from the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites, as a hadith whose authenticity he describes as agreed upon, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The sun and the moon are two of the signs of Allah, and they are not eclipsed for the death or life of anyone. Allah uses them to make His servants afraid, so if you see them, hasten to remember Him, call on Him and seek His forgiveness." Then he said: "O Ummah of Muhammad, by Allah, no one has a greater sense of jealousy than Allah if He sees His servant, or female servant, committing zina (unlawful sexual intercourse). O Ummah of Muhammad, if you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much."

That hadith is the ayah in practice. An eclipse is a *sign*, and the prescribed response is not analysis but **remembrance, supplication, and seeking forgiveness** — exactly the fear the ayah says signs are sent to produce.

## Ayah 60: encompassed by your Lord, and a vision that tested them

"And (remember) when We told you: 'Verily, your Lord has encompassed mankind.' And We made not the vision which We showed you but a trial for mankind, and (likewise) the accursed tree in the Qur'an. We warn and make them afraid, but it only increases them in naught save great disbelief, oppression and disobedience to Allah."

**"Your Lord has encompassed mankind."** Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah encouraging His Messenger ﷺ to go on delivering the message, telling him that He is protecting him from the people, that He is able to deal with them, and that they are in His grasp, under His domination and control. Mujahid, 'Urwah bin az-Zubayr, al-Hasan, Qatadah and others said the meaning is: **"He protected you from them."** For the Prophet ﷺ, standing against a hostile city, the practical sense was immediate: the men threatening you are already inside the grasp of the One who sent you.

**The vision.** Al-Bukhari recorded that Ibn 'Abbas said of "the vision which We showed you": "This is the vision which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw with his own eyes on the night when he was taken on the Night Journey (al-Isra')." Ibn Kathir notes this was also recorded by Ahmad, 'Abdur-Razzaq and others, and reported by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas; and that it was likewise explained as the Night of the Isra' by Mujahid, Sa'id bin Jubayr, al-Hasan, Masruq, Ibrahim, Qatadah, 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd and several others.

The Arabic word is *ru'ya*, which in ordinary usage can mean a dream. **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses this point:** what is being recounted here is no dream. Had it been a dream, there would have been no reason for anyone to apostatise over it — dreams are dreams, and anyone may see them. The word is used here precisely to indicate a marvel **witnessed while awake**. Maʿārif adds that although some commentators applied the ayah to other events as well, these do not apply here as a whole, and the majority of commentators declared the event of Mi'raj alone to be the relevant subject of the verse (as described in detail by al-Qurtubi).

**"But a trial" — what *fitnah* means here.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *fitnah* carries several senses in Arabic: falling into error and going astray; a trial or test; or some disorder and upheaval. All are possible here. Early tafsir authorities — Sayyidah 'A'ishah, Sayyidna Mu'awiyah, Hasan, Mujahid and others — took the last sense: the upheaval in question was the **apostasy (irtidad)** that followed when the Prophet ﷺ told people about the Mi'raj — how he journeyed by night to Baitul-Maqdis, from there to the heavens, and returned to Makkah before dawn.
