Many new Muslims who had yet to become staunch in their faith fell into the error of belying his statement and turned apostates (Qurtubi). Ibn Kathir says the same thing from the other side: some gave up their Islam after having followed the truth, because their hearts and minds could not comprehend it, and they denied what their knowledge could not grasp — **while Allah caused the very same report to increase and strengthen the faith of others.** Ibn Kathir glosses *fitnah* simply as "a test."

This is the second half of the passage's logic. Ayah 59 said a demanded sign would have brought destruction. Ayah 60 shows a genuine, staggering sign actually being given — and its effect was to divide people: some grew stronger, some fell away. The sign does not force the heart; it reveals it.

**The accursed tree.** Ibn Kathir, citing the same report of Ibn 'Abbas recorded by al-Bukhari, identifies "the accursed tree in the Qur'an" as the **Tree of Zaqqum**. When the Messenger ﷺ told them that he had seen Paradise and Hell, and had seen the Tree of Zaqqum, they did not believe it, and Abu Jahl even said, "Bring us some dates and butter," then began eating them and saying, "Let us have some Zaqqum; we don't know any other Zaqqum but this." This was narrated by Ibn 'Abbas, Masruq, Abu Malik, al-Hasan al-Basri and others. Ibn Kathir points out that everyone who explained the ayah as referring to the Night of the Isra' also explained it as referring to the Tree of Zaqqum.

Note the shape of the mockery: he takes the most terrifying warning in revelation and turns it into a snack. That is what a hardened heart does with a sign.

**"We make them afraid."** Ibn Kathir explains this as Allah making the disbelievers afraid with His warnings, punishments and torment — the same making-afraid as in ayah 59. And the outcome? "It only increases them in naught save great disbelief, oppression and disobedience to Allah." Ibn Kathir says it only pushes them further into their disbelief and misguidance, "and this is because Allah has forsaken them." Warning is a mercy; but a heart left to its own choices converts even that mercy into more defiance.

## Living it

**Read events as address, not accident.** When Kufah shook, Ibn Mas'ud did not treat it as a topic of conversation — he told his people, "your Lord is rebuking you, so pay heed!" When Madinah shook, 'Umar read it as a sign that the people had changed. The hadith on the eclipse gives the exact response: remembrance, supplication, seeking forgiveness. Whatever shakes your life — turn towards Him with those three.

**Stop demanding proof and start walking through the door.** The Quraysh wanted as-Safa turned to gold. What their Prophet ﷺ asked for on their behalf was the gates of repentance and mercy. Delay, in this passage, is not divine indifference — it is more time, deliberately requested.

**Do not expect certainty to come from spectacle.** The Isra' was as clear a sign as any people have been given, and it still split its audience: some hearts could not grasp it and turned away, while the same report increased others in faith. If your faith is waiting for one undeniable event, ayah 60 says: some people had exactly that, and walked away.

**Keep hope and fear in balance.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, commenting a little earlier in the surah on "they hope for His Mercy and fear His punishment" (17:57), quotes Sahl ibn 'Abdullah: hope and fear are two different states, and when they stay at par a person "keeps on course, correct and stable"; if either overcomes the other, the equilibrium of his spiritual state is disturbed to the measure of that imbalance (Qurtubi). Ayah 58 supplies the fear — no town outlasts its account. Ayah 59 supplies the hope — the gates of repentance and mercy, deliberately chosen for us.

passages.title: Iblis's refusal and his war on Adam's children
passages.tafsir:
**The oldest grudge in existence.** In ayat 61–65 Allah takes us back behind all of human history to the moment the angels were told to prostrate to Adam and one creature refused. The passage is a single conversation in two halves. Iblis speaks twice — a sneer and a boast (ayat 61–62) — and Allah answers him (ayat 63–65) with permission, a warning, and a limit. That shape is the point: a challenge and its reply. Between them the ayat tell you why the human being is opposed at all, how the opposition works, and where it stops.

## The challenge: Iblis speaks

### "Shall I prostrate to one whom You created from clay?"

Ibn Kathir's opening comment sets the tone. Allah is mentioning "the enmity of Iblis, may the curse of Allah be upon him and his progeny," and this is "an ancient hatred, dating from the time that Allah created Adam." The angels were commanded to prostrate; all of them did; Iblis alone "was too arrogant and he haughtily refused."

Notice how the refusal is phrased. He does not say "I will not." He says, in Ibn Kathir's reading, in a tone of contempt: **أَأَسْجُدُ لِمَنْ خَلَقْتَ طِينًا** — *"Shall I prostrate myself to one whom You created from clay?"* The insult is aimed at the material. Elsewhere he spells the logic out: *"I am better than he. You created me from fire, and You created him from clay"* (7:12).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes this argument apart. It was not really a question about mud and fire. It was an effort to find out the wisdom of the order given to him *before* he complied with it — and, Maʿārif says, the one who is commanded has no right to ask that. The comparison it draws is homely and exact: even among ourselves, no master would grant his servant the right to answer an instruction by demanding first to be told the reasoning behind it. So the question "was considered unworthy of an answer and no answer was given." And in any case, Maʿārif adds, the answer is already obvious: giving precedence to one thing over another is the prerogative of the Being who created and nurtured them all. Whatever He declares superior becomes exactly so.

That is the root of everything that follows in this passage. On Maʿārif's reading, the refusal was at bottom a demand to be shown the wisdom of a command before obeying it — a demand the one commanded has no right to make.

### "I will seize and mislead his offspring"

**أَرَأَيْتَكَ هَٰذَا الَّذِي كَرَّمْتَ عَلَيَّ** — *"See this one whom You have honoured above me..."* Ibn Kathir describes this plainly: he is "speaking to the Lord with disbelief and insolence, but the Lord bore it patiently." Pause on that phrase. The creature is arguing to the face of his Creator, and the Creator — in Ibn Kathir's words — bore it patiently, and then replied.

The key verb is **لَأَحْتَنِكَنَّ** — from *ihtināk*. Maʿārif, citing Qurtubi, gives its sense as to exterminate or uproot something, or to subdue and overpower it completely. The early commentators render Iblis's threat in three ways, and Ibn Kathir gathers them:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās** (reported by ʿAlī bin Abī Talhah): *"I am going to dominate his offspring, all but a few."*
- **Mujāhid**: *"I am going to surround them."*
- **Ibn Zayd**: *"I am going to lead them astray."*

Ibn Kathir notes that "all of them are close in meaning," and gives the sense of the ayah as: *"Do You see this one whom You have honoured and made greater than me? If You give me time, I will lead his descendants astray, all but a few of them."* Domination, encirclement, misguidance — the picture is of a field being stripped bare.

**How could he claim to know he would succeed?** Maʿārif raises the question honestly and offers two possibilities without deciding between them: perhaps, by looking at the ingredients that went into the making of man, he gathered that man would be desire-prone and would not be difficult to entice; or perhaps his very claim was nothing but a bland lie. Either way, notice that even in his boast he had to concede an exception — *all but a few*. The last ayah of the passage will name those few.

## The reply: Allah answers

Maʿārif reads ayat 63–65 as Allah's direct answer to the second of the two things Iblis had said. The Shaytan will have no control over Allah's sincere servants even if he rallies his entire forces against them; and as for those who fall into his trap, they will meet the same fate as his, all consigned to Hell. Watch that answer unfold in three moves.

### "Go"

Allah's reply begins with one word: **اذْهَبْ** — *"Go."* Ibn Kathir explains its force here as the granting of the respite Iblis had asked for: *"Go, I will give you respite,"* as another ayah states, *"Verily, you are of those allowed respite till the Day of the time appointed"* (38:80–81).

Then comes the warning, and Ibn Kathir notes it is aimed at Iblis *and* at those who follow him among the progeny of Adam: *"whosoever of them follows you, surely Hell will be the recompense of you (all)."* Ibn Kathir glosses that recompense as being "for your deeds" — the follower is not swept along helplessly; he is paid for what he did. On **جَزَاءً مَوْفُورًا** (*an ample recompense*), Mujāhid said "sufficient recompense," and Qatādah said, "It will be abundant for you and will not be decreased for you." Nothing is skimmed off; nothing is short-changed.

### The four instruments

Ayah 64 is the anatomy of the attack, listed as four commands. Ibn Kathir marks them as "a command (related to the divine decree)" — that is, a decree that this will happen, not an endorsement of it — and he makes the point at the second of the four, comparing it to *"See you not that We have sent the Shayāṭīn against the disbelievers to push them to do evil"* (19:83), meaning to provoke them and drive them towards evil.

**1. The voice — وَاسْتَفْزِزْ ... بِصَوْتِكَ.** Maʿārif explains *istifzāz* as, at root, to cut off or tear away from — and here, to tear a person away from the path of truth. Not a shove; a peeling-off. As for what "his voice" is, the sources give two lines:

- It refers to song and idle amusement. Ibn Kathir reports that it was said to refer to singing, and that Mujāhid said, "With idle entertainment and singing," meaning: influence them with that. Maʿārif, citing Qurtubi, reports Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās as saying that the voices of songs, musical instruments and the hullabaloo of fun and games are the voices of Shaytan that he employs to tear people away from the path of truth — and from this, Qurtubi says, we learn that music and musical instruments are prohibited.
- It is broader than that: **Ibn ʿAbbās** said it means "every caller who calls people to disobey Allah." Ibn Kathir notes this was also Qatādah's view, "and was also the opinion favoured by Ibn Jarīr."

Take the second reading seriously alongside the first. Any voice that makes disobedience sound attractive — from a stage, a screen, a friend's mouth — is on the list.

**2. The cavalry and infantry — وَأَجْلِبْ عَلَيْهِم بِخَيْلِكَ وَرَجِلِكَ.** Ibn Kathir: send whatever forces you have at your disposal against them. Who are these troops? **Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid**: "Everyone who rides or walks to go and commit sin and disobey Allah." **Qatādah**: "He has infantry and cavalry among the Jinn and among humans. They are the ones who obey him." Ibn Kathir also opens the word itself: the Arabs use the verb *ajlaba* when describing somebody shouting at another person — hence, he notes, it is forbidden in races to shout at one another and push one another. From the same root comes *jalabah*, which means raising voices. The image is of a mob riding down on a man with noise.

Maʿārif adds a balanced note: the mention of horsemen and footmen does not necessarily mean the Shaytan actually has combat support in that formation; it is a manner of referring to his full force and power — though if he does have them literally, that cannot be denied either. And Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās said: those who come out in support of disbelief and sin, horsemen or footmen, are nothing but the army of the Shaytan.

**3. A share in wealth and children — وَشَارِكْهُمْ فِي الْأَمْوَالِ وَالْأَوْلَادِ.** On wealth, **Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid** said this means what he commands them to do of spending money in disobedience to Allah. Maʿārif adds, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that wealth and property acquired by false, impermissible and unlawful means, or spent on what is haram, is where the Shaytan's share lies.

On children, the reports differ and each opens a door:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās** (as reported by al-ʿAwfī), **Mujāhid** and **aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk**: the children of *zinā* — illegitimate children.
- **Ibn ʿAbbās** (through ʿAlī bin Abī Talhah): the children whom they used to kill out of folly, without knowledge.
- **Al-Hasan al-Basrī**, reported by Qatādah, who said the same: Allah caused the Shaytan to take a share of wealth and children by making them Magians, Jews and Christians, and making them follow any religion other than Islam, and by making them give a part of their wealth to the Shaytan.
- Maʿārif, citing Qurtubi, lists further forms: illegitimacy, or naming children like disbelievers and polytheists, or indulging in polytheistic customs to ensure their security, or taking to unlawful sources of income to bring them up.

Then Ibn Kathir widens it beyond the two categories named: the mention of wealth and children "does not mean that it is limited only to those things. Everything in which a person disobeys Allah or obeys the Shaytan means that he is sharing with him." The partnership is measured in obedience, not in assets.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites two reports here. It was reported in **Sahih Muslim** from ʿIyad bin Himar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah, the Mighty and Exalted, says: *"I have created My servants as Hunafāʾ [monotheists], then the Shayāṭīn come to them and lead them astray from their religion and (tell that) what I have permitted for them is forbidden to them."* Read that against ayah 64: the human being is not born the Shaytan's; he is born upright, and the whole campaign is a work of prying loose — exactly the *istifzāz*, the tearing away, of the ayah.

And according to **the Two Sahihs**, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"When one of you wants to have intercourse with his wife, let him say, 'In the Name of Allah. O Allah, keep us away from Shaytan and keep Shaytan away from what You bestow on us (children).' Then if a child is decreed for them from that, the Shaytan will never harm him."* A claimed share in the children, answered by a sentence said before the child exists.

**4. Promises — وَعِدْهُمْ.** And here the ayah itself supplies the verdict on all four: *"But Shaytan promises them nothing but deceit."* Ibn Kathir points forward to the Day when the matter is decided, when Iblis will say it himself: *"Verily, Allah promised you a promise of truth. And I too promised you, but I betrayed you"* (14:22). Every promise he ever made comes due, and he pays none of it.

### Where the campaign stops

**إِنَّ عِبَادِي لَيْسَ لَكَ عَلَيْهِمْ سُلْطَانٌ** — *"Verily, My servants, you have no authority over them."* This is the answer to the boast. Iblis said *all but a few*; Allah names the few by relationship — **My servants** — and He does not say they are stronger than him. He says the enemy has no *sulṭān*, no authority, over them. Ibn Kathir: "Here Allah tells us that He supports His believing servants, and guards and protects them against the accursed Shaytan."

Then: **وَكَفَىٰ بِرَبِّكَ وَكِيلًا** — *"And All-Sufficient is your Lord as a Guardian"* — which Ibn Kathir explains as "a Protector, Supporter and Helper." The passage began with a creature listing his weapons and ends with the believer being told that his protection is not a matter of his own strength at all. It is *sufficient*, says the ayah, that your Lord is the Guardian.

Set the two sides beside each other and the mismatch is the point: on one side, voice, cavalry, infantry, money, offspring, promises; on the other, one word — *sufficient*.

## Living it

- **The demand to be shown the wisdom first.** Maʿārif's reading of the refusal is the practical heart of the passage: withholding compliance until the wisdom of a command has been explained to you is exactly the move that was made here — and Maʿārif's point is that the one commanded has no right to make that demand.
- **Audit what you listen to, and who you listen to.** The sources give two readings of "his voice." Qurtubi, as Maʿārif reports him, draws from Ibn ʿAbbās's words a prohibition of music and musical instruments; Ibn ʿAbbās's broader reading, favoured by Ibn Jarīr, catches everyone regardless — any caller who calls you to disobey Allah is *his* voice, however pleasant it sounds.
- **Watch the two places he claims a share.** Money in and money out — how it is earned, where it is spent. And children — how they are conceived, what they are named, what customs are used to protect them, what income raises them. Every one of those is on the commentators' list.
- **Do not negotiate with promises.** Every offer he makes is a promise he will himself disown on the Day the matter is decided (14:22).
- **Take the title seriously.** He has no authority over *ʿibādī* — Allah's servants. And the comfort the ayah offers is not that you are too clever for him. It is, in Ibn Kathir's words, that Allah supports His believing servants and protects them — that your Lord is All-Sufficient as a Guardian.

passages.title: Rescue at sea and the honour given to humanity
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** These five ayat put you out on open water, bring you safely back to dry land, and then ask what kind of creature you actually are. Allah shows His mercy in the ships that carry you (66), shows what happens inside your heart when the sea turns against you (67), asks twice whether you really imagine you have escaped Him once you are ashore (68–69) — and then announces the extraordinary dignity He has given to the children of Adam (70).

**What holds them together.** Sea and land. Allah drives the ships out over the water (66); the storm strips a man down to sincerity, and the safe harbour lets him forget it (67); then two questions ask whether dry land is really a refuge (68) and whether the sea could not simply be reopened for him (69). Ibn Kathir makes the link explicit when he paraphrases the opening of ayah 69 as addressed to "you who turn away from Us after acknowledging Our Oneness at sea once you are back upon dry land." And then ayah 70 names both places again — "We have carried them on land and sea" — only this time they are not the scene of a test but the evidence of a gift. So the passage moves from a favour, to ingratitude for the favour, to a warning about that ingratitude, and finally to a reminder of just how much has been lavished on the one who is being ungrateful. Read that way, ayah 70 is not a change of subject. It is the closing argument.

## Ayah 66 — The ships are a sign of mercy

Ibn Kathir heads this ayah simply: *Ships are a Sign of the Mercy of Allah.* The point is not that ships happen to float. As Ibn Kathir puts it, Allah "tells us of His kindness towards His servants by subjugating for them ships on the sea," making it easy for them to use those ships to serve their interests, "seeking His bounty through trade between one region and another."

Notice how the ayah is framed. It does not say the ships sail; it says **your Lord drives them** — the sense Ibn Kathir gives to *yuzjī*, the verb in the Arabic. Wind, current, hull, the sailor's skill and nerve: the ayah gathers all of it behind one subject, *your Lord*. And the purpose clause is refreshingly worldly — *li-tabtaghū*, "that you may seek of His bounty." Earning a living by sea trade is not presented as a distraction from religion. It is presented as something Allah Himself arranged on your behalf.

Then the seal of the ayah: **"Truly, He is ever Most Merciful towards you."** Ibn Kathir's comment is short and worth sitting with — "He does this for you out of His grace and mercy towards you." Nobody negotiated the sea's cooperation. It was given.

## Ayah 67 — What a storm exposes

Then the wind gets up. And Allah tells us, as Ibn Kathir says, what happens when harm befalls people: "they call on Him, turning to Him and sincerely beseeching Him."

The Arabic is striking. *Ḍalla man tadʿūna illā iyyāh* — "those that you call upon **vanish** from you except Him." Ibn Kathir explains the loss precisely: "everything they worship besides Allah disappears from their hearts and minds." The false gods do not sail away; they go missing from the mind of the man who worships them. He cannot even remember why he ever thought they mattered. This is why one common rendering is *you totally forget* whatever you used to call on. A storm does not argue anyone out of shirk — the setting up of partners alongside Allah in worship. It simply empties the heart of everything except the One who can actually do something.

### The man who worked this out in a boat

Ibn Kathir tells the story of ʿIkrimah bin Abi Jahl. After the conquest of Makkah he fled from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, heading for Ethiopia. He set out across the sea — and a stormy wind arose. The people began saying to one another: *"None can save you except Allah Alone."*

ʿIkrimah heard it, and something turned over in him. He said to himself: "By Allah, if none can benefit on the sea except Allah, then no doubt none can benefit on land except Allah." And then he made his promise: *"O Allah! I promise You that if You bring me safely out of this, I will go and put my hand in the hand of Muhammad ﷺ, and surely I will find him full of pity, kindness and mercy."*

They came out of it safely and were delivered from the sea. And ʿIkrimah went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, declared his Islam, and became a good Muslim, may Allah be pleased with him.

Sit with what he actually did, because it is the whole passage in one man. Everyone on that boat had the same realisation — *only Allah*. ʿIkrimah was the one who refused to let it stay a sea-realisation. If it is true out here, it is true on shore. That single sentence is the difference between this ayah's rebuke and this ayah's rescue. And note the last thing he expected to find on dry land: not a score to settle, but "pity, kindness and mercy." The son of Abu Jahl, of all people, was right about that.

### "But when He brings you safe to land, you turn away"

Ibn Kathir: this means "you forget what you remembered of Divine Oneness (Tawhid) when you were on the sea, and you turn away from calling on Him Alone with no partner or associate." The tragedy is not that the man never knew the truth. He knew it perfectly, in the dark, with water coming over the side. He knew it, and then the harbour came into view and he mislaid it.

**"And man is ever ungrateful."** *Kafūrā.* Ibn Kathir explains: "by nature he forgets and denies His blessings, **except for those whom Allah protects.**" Do not skip that exception. The verse is diagnosing a default setting, not passing a life sentence. Ingratitude is what a human being drifts into when left to himself; it is not what he is stuck as. Someone is protected from it, and that protection is itself something to ask for.

## Ayat 68–69 — "Do you feel secure?"

Now come two questions, and they are aimed at exactly the man described above: the one who acknowledged Allah's Oneness at sea and dropped it on the beach.

**Ayah 68 closes off the land.** Ibn Kathir paraphrases the challenge: do you think that by emerging onto dry land you will be safe from His vengeance and punishment — that a side of the land will not swallow you up, or that He will not send against you a *ḥāṣib*? Mujahid and others explained *ḥāṣib* as **a kind of rain that carries stones**. Ibn Kathir supports this from the Qur'an itself, citing "Verily, We sent against them, except the family of Lut, them We saved in the last hour of the night, as a favour from Us" (54:34–35), and, elsewhere, "and We rained on them stones of Sijjil, in a well-arranged manner one after another."

He also brings the parallel from Surah al-Mulk, where the same two questions are put in almost the same words: *"Do you feel secure that He, Who is over the heaven (Allah), will not cause the earth to sink with you, and then it should quake? Or do you feel secure that He, Who is over the heaven (Allah), will not send against you a Ḥāṣib? Then you shall know how terrible has been My warning"* (67:16–17).

The verdict of ayah 68: **"Then you shall find no guardian."** Ibn Kathir — "no helper to turn the punishment away from you and save you."

**Ayah 69 closes off the sea.** Or do you feel secure that He will not send you back out there a second time — and this time send a *qāṣif* against you? Ibn Kathir: it "will destroy your masts and sink your vessels." Ibn ʿAbbas and others said: "Al-Qāṣif is the wind of the sea which destroys vessels and sinks them." And "drown you **because of your disbelief**" means, says Ibn Kathir, "because of your rejection and turning away from Allah" — the very turning away described one ayah earlier. The punishment is shaped like the crime: you were pulled out of the water when you called on Him, and you walked off; so back to the water.

**"Then you will not find any avenger therein against Us."** The word is *tabīʿ*, and the early authorities read it in complementary ways. Ibn ʿAbbas said it means **a helper**. Mujahid said, "A helper who will avenge you" — someone to take revenge on your behalf. Qatadah put it from the other direction: "We are not afraid that anyone will pursue Us with anything of that nature." Put the three together and the picture is complete: no rescuer while it happens, no avenger afterwards, no one to take up your case against the One who decreed it.

**Feel the design of these two ayat.** Land and sea are the only two places a human being can be, and the Qur'an takes them both away in the space of two verses. The man who thought he had got away with it had not escaped to anywhere. There is no third location.

## Ayah 70 — And still, He honours you

After all that, you might brace for a verdict. Instead comes one of the most generous statements about the human being anywhere in the Qur'an: **"And indeed We have honoured the Children of Adam."**

Ibn Kathir titles the section *The Honor and noble Nature of Man*. Allah honoured the sons of Adam and made them noble "by creating them in the best and most perfect of forms" — "Verily, We created man in the best stature" (95:4). Concretely: he walks upright on his two feet and eats with his hand, while other living creatures walk on four feet and eat with their mouths; and he has been given hearing, sight and a heart "with which to understand all of that, to benefit from it, and distinguish between things to know which are good for him and which are harmful, in both worldly and religious terms."

**"And We have carried them on land and sea."** Ibn Kathir: on land, on animals such as cattle, horses and mules; and on the sea "in ships and boats, great and small." Ships appear here for the second time in five ayat. At ayah 66 they were a sign of mercy; here they stand among the marks of honour Allah has placed on the children of Adam. The plain business of getting from one place to another — which is all travel is, most days — is being described to you as something conferred.

**"And have provided them with aṭ-Ṭayyibāt"** — the good and wholesome things. Ibn Kathir refuses to keep this abstract: agricultural produce, fruits, meat and milk, "with all kinds of delicious and desirable flavors and colors and beautiful appearance," and fine clothes of all kinds of shapes, colours and sizes, "which they make for themselves or are brought to them by others from other regions and areas." That last phrase is worth pausing on next to his comment at ayah 66, where the bounty being sought was "trade between one region and another." The same long-distance traffic that the ships were driven for turns up here as the contents of your table and your wardrobe.

**"And have preferred them above many of those whom We have created with a marked preferment."** Ibn Kathir: this means over all living beings and other kinds of creation; and he adds that this ayah indicates human beings are also preferred over the angels.

### Why the children of Adam were honoured

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the reasons at length, and they are worth having in front of you, because most of them are things we never think to be grateful for:

- **Form and proportion** — beauty of form and features, balance of body, of temperament, and of height and build, in a measure not found in other living forms.
- **Reason and intelligence** — distinct reason and intelligence "through which they get things done up and down in the universe of their experience."
- **Making and compounding** — the built-in capability to take what Allah created and compound and manufacture from it the things that serve them in living, moving, eating and wearing, "in all sorts of ways."
- **Language** — communication, speech, comprehension, understanding and explanation, which "remains unmatched by other living forms": using signs and symbols to convey what lies in one's heart, telling others what one thinks and feels through letters and writing.
- **Even how we eat** — some scholars, Maʿārif notes, said that eating with the fingers of the hand is a particular human attribute. Animals eat things "single and simple" — raw meat, grass, some fruit. Man alone compounds solids, liquids, spices and herbs to make food delicious and beneficial, "which has, in our day, assumed the status of the highly publicized art of cuisine."
- **And above all** — the reason and intelligence by which human beings are meant to recognise their Creator and Master, find out what He likes and dislikes, and then do the one and avoid the other.

Then Maʿārif gives the framework that makes sense of the whole thing. In terms of reason and intelligence, the created are of three kinds. **Common animals** have desires but no reason and intelligence as we understand it. **The angels** have reason and intelligence but no desires. **Human beings have both.** And this, Maʿārif says, is the reason why, when a person suppresses his desires through reason and intelligence and succeeds in saving himself from indulging in things disliked by Allah, "he reaches a station which is even higher than that of many angels." The angel's obedience costs him no struggle. Yours does. That is where the honour is earned rather than merely received.

### "Above *many*" — the question of man and the angels

The ayah says "above **many** of those whom We have created," not "above all," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes that wording as a question worth answering carefully.

That the children of Adam are superior to all created forms in this world, higher and lower, and to all animals, "cannot be disputed by anyone." The jinn are like human beings in terms of reason and intelligence, and that human beings are superior to them as well "is accepted by all." What remains is the case of the angels — *who is superior, man or angel?* — and here Maʿārif (citing Tafsir Mazhari) gives a carefully graded answer rather than a slogan: common righteous believers among human beings, such as the men of Allah, are superior to angels in general; but **special angels, such as Jibra'il and Mika'il and others, are superior to the common righteous believers**; while **special believers, such as the blessed prophets, peace be upon them, are superior even to the special angels.** And it closes, as such discussions should, with *Allah knows best.*

So take the two commentaries as they stand rather than flattening them together: Ibn Kathir states the preference over the angels in general terms; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets it out in tiers and expressly leaves the matter with Allah.

As for disbelievers and the sinful among mankind, Maʿārif says they "just cannot be compared with angels" — in terms of the real purpose of life, that of seeking success through righteousness, they are "not even superior to animals," and the Qur'an has already given its verdict on them: *"They are like cattle. Rather, they are much more misled"* (7:179).

That is the sting in the tail of ayah 70, and it is aimed straight back at ayat 67–69. The honour is real, but it is a rank you can fall out of.

## Living it

**Bring the sea back to shore.** The whole passage turns on one hinge: what you knew in the storm is still true in the sunshine. ʿIkrimah's reasoning is the model — *if only Allah can benefit out here, then only Allah can benefit back there.* Whatever you promised Allah in your worst week is still owed in your best one.

**Treat the ordinary as evidence.** Ayah 66 and ayah 70 both put physical, nameable mercies in front of you: the vessel that carries you, the food with its flavours and colours, the clothes brought from other regions. Ibn Kathir's refusal to abstract these is a lesson in itself. Naming a blessing specifically is how you stop being *kafūr* — the one who, by nature, "forgets and denies His blessings."

**Do not confuse safety with security.** Ayat 68–69 dismantle the illusion that arriving somewhere means getting away with something. There is no location outside His reach, and — as Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Qatadah all note in their different ways — no helper, no avenger, no one to take up your case.

**Use what you were honoured with.** You were given hearing, sight and a heart in order to tell what is good for you from what harms you, "in both worldly and religious terms." You were given reason alongside desire so that reason could govern desire. That is the honour of ayah 70 turned into a daily job — and, in Maʿārif's words, the very thing by which a human being reaches a station "even higher than that of many angels."

And when the ingratitude in ayah 67 sounds a little too much like you, remember exactly where Ibn Kathir leaves the door open: **"except for those whom Allah protects."** Ask Him for that.

passages.title: Summoned with their leaders, blind then as now
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These two ayat lift the eye from this world to the great summoning. Ayah 71 shows the whole of humanity called forward, group by group, each with its *imām*, and then the record handed to a person's right hand — read with delight, and given with the promise that no one will be dealt with unjustly in the least. Ayah 72 turns back to this life and names a blindness here that carries over there.

What holds the two ayat together is a single line of sight. Ayah 71 is about being **seen** — every deed recorded, nothing overlooked. Ayah 72 is about **seeing** — and about the person who was blind to the signs and proofs of Allah.

## "The Day We summon every people with their imām"

Ayah 71 opens: *yawma nadʿū kulla unāsin bi-imāmihim* — "the Day We shall call together all human beings with their (respective) *imām*."

The word *imām* is the crux, and the classical commentators genuinely differed over it. Ibn Kathir lays the views out:

- **Their prophet.** Mujahid and Qatadah said that each nation would be called to account by its Prophet. Ibn Kathir notes that some of the Salaf — the earliest generations of Muslims — said this is the greatest honour for the people of Hadith (*ahl al-hadith*, those who devote themselves to the Prophet's ﷺ reported words and deeds), because their leader is the Prophet ﷺ.
- **Their revealed Book and law.** Ibn Zayd said they would be called to account by the Book revealed to their Prophet with its laws — the view Ibn Jarir also favoured. Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid simply: "With their Books."
- **Their own record of deeds.** Al-ʿAwfi narrated this from Ibn ʿAbbas, and it was also the view of Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Hasan and ad-Dahhak.

**Ibn Kathir judges the third view the most correct**, and his reason is that Allah Himself uses *imām* in that sense and describes the Day in those terms. He cites:

- *"And all things We have recorded with numbers (as a record) in a Clear Book"* — *fī imāmin mubīn* (36:12). Here *imām* means a written record.
- *"And the Book (one's record) will be placed, and you will see the criminals, fearful of that which is recorded therein"* (18:49).
- *"And you will see each nation humbled to their knees, each nation will be called to its record. This Day you shall be recompensed for what you used to do. This Our record speaks about you with truth. Verily, We were recording what you used to do"* (45:28–29).

That last passage sits especially close to the wording of our ayah: there, the nations are called **to their record** — the same scene in different words.

**Why call a book an "imām" at all?** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān, quoting Qurtubi, gives a beautiful reason. A *kitāb* (book) is called an *imām* because, in the event of some error or difference, one turns back to the book — very much like turning to a religious leader who is followed.

**A hadith supporting this reading.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān cites a hadith of Tirmidhi narrated by Sayyidna Abu Hurairah — Tirmidhi calls it *Hasan Gharib*, one of his grading terms — in which the Prophet ﷺ, explaining this very ayah, said: *"One of them will be called and his book of deeds will be given in his right hand."* (Maʿārif notes this comes from a lengthy hadith.) Maʿārif takes this as establishing that *imām* here means *kitāb*, and that *kitāb* signifies the book of deeds. Maulana Ashraf Thanavi accordingly rendered *imām* in his translation as "the book of deeds."

## And yet the leaders are not absent

Ibn Kathir is careful not to let one meaning cancel the other. Reading *imām* as the record of deeds, he says, **does not contradict** the fact that the Prophet ﷺ will be brought forward when Allah judges between his Ummah (his community) — for he will inevitably be a witness against his Ummah over their deeds. Both things are true; but what is meant here by *imām*, in Ibn Kathir's judgement, is the Book of deeds.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān preserves the other reading with its own weight. It reports from some commentators — including Sayyidna ʿAli al-Murtada and Mujahid — that *imām* means religious leader: everyone is to be called as the follower of a certain leader, and all those so called will be assembled at one place. So there will be the followers of Sayyidna Ibrahim, the followers of Sayyidna Musa and Sayyidna ʿIsa (peace be upon them), and the followers of Sayyidna Muhammad al-Mustafa ﷺ. And possibly, Maʿārif adds, the names will also be called out of those who were people's direct instructors or leaders — the ʿulamāʾ (scholars) and religious guides.

But the same commentary, again citing Qurtubi, states the sobering half of it: the leaders followed may be the blessed prophets or their deputies, the shaykhs and the ʿulamāʾ — **or leaders who have been inviting people to error and sin**.

There is a quiet question in this for anyone reading: *whose name will be called with mine?*

## The record in the right hand

Ayah 71 continues: *"So whosoever is given his record in his right hand, such will read their records."*

Ibn Kathir catches the emotional register of that: they will read it **because of their happiness and joy at what is recorded therein of good deeds — they will read it and they will want to read it.** He anchors it in Surah al-Haqqah: *"Then as for him who will be given his record in his right hand will say: 'Here! read my record!'"* — running on to *"But as for him who will be given his record in his left hand…"* (69:19–29).

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān presses on a detail worth pausing over: **who exactly receives it in the right hand?** Its argument is that, as it appears from several ayat, only disbelievers will be given the book of deeds in the left hand. In al-Haqqah, of that man it is said, *"Indeed, he was not used to believing in Allah, the Great"* (69:33) — faith is explicitly negated. In al-Inshiqaq, of the same figure: *"Indeed, he surmised that he would never return"* (84:14) — a denial of the Hereafter, which too is disbelief after all.

Reading these together, Maʿārif concludes that those who get their book of deeds in the right hand will be **the people of faith, pious or sinner.** The believer will read his book of deeds in delight; in fact, the happy believer will have others read it too. And the source is precise about the reason for that joy: it is because of having one's *īmān* (faith) intact and because of deliverance from eternal punishment — **though punishment may also come for some deeds.** The right hand is not a certificate of a spotless file.

## How the records arrive

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān is honest about the limits of what we know: *how* the book of deeds will be given in the right or the left hand is something not mentioned in the Holy Qur'an. What the sources add comes from narration:

- The expression *taṭāyur al-kutub*, "causing the books to fly," has appeared in some ahadith — reported by Ahmad on the authority of Sayyidah ʿA'ishah, ascending to the Holy Prophet ﷺ.
- And in some narrations of hadith it appears that all books of deeds will be at one place under the ʿArsh (the Throne). Then a wind will blow and cause these to fly and reach the hands of people, so that some will get it in the right hand and some in the left. (Reported by al-ʿUqaili on the authority of Sayyidna Anas, ascending to the Holy Prophet ﷺ; Maʿārif cites this via Bayan al-Qur'an from Ruh al-Maʿani.)

We affirm the ʿArsh as Allah has told us of it, without likening it to anything of creation and without explaining it away — and we leave the manner of these events to Allah's knowledge, exactly as the sources leave it.

## "Not wronged by a thread"

The ayah closes with *wa lā yuẓlamūna fatīlā* — "and they will not be dealt with unjustly in the least."

*Fatīl* is not an abstraction. Ibn Kathir reminds us of its concrete sense: **the long thread in the groove of a date-pit.** The Qur'an picks that tiny thing and says: not even that much of injustice will touch them. The accounting is exact down to a filament.

## What that moment will look like

Ibn Kathir records that al-Hafiz Abu Bakr al-Bazzar reported a hadith from Abu Hurayrah in which the Prophet ﷺ said, concerning this ayah:

> "One of you will be called and will be given his Book in his right hand. He will be in a good physical state, with a white face, and there will be placed on his head a crown of shining pearls. He will go to his companions and they will see him from afar, and will say, 'O Allah, let him come to us and bless us with this.' Then he will come to them and will say to them, 'Rejoice, for every man among you will be like this.'
>
> As for the disbeliever, his face will be black and his body will be enlarged. His companions will see him from afar and will say, 'We seek refuge in Allah from this, or from the evil of this — O Allah, do not let him come to us.' Then he will come to them and they will say, 'O Allah, humiliate him!' He will say, 'May Allah cast you away — every man among you will be like this.'"

Ibn Kathir then passes on al-Bazzar's own remark on it: **"This was only reported through this chain"** — a note that the report reached him by a single route of transmission.

Notice what the hadith adds to the ayah. Both men are recognised **from afar**, before a word is spoken. And both are met by their own **companions** — the people they belonged to. The believer's arrival is something his companions beg Allah to grant them; the disbeliever's arrival is something his companions beg Allah to spare them. And both men close with the same sentence — *every man among you will be like this* — which is glad tidings in one mouth and ruin in the other.

## Ayah 72: blind here, blind there

*"And whoever is blind in this, then he will be blind in the Hereafter, and most astray from the path."*

Ibn Kathir's comment is short, and each phrase about the Hereafter is explained by the same phrase about this world:

- **"in this"** — Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: this means in this worldly life.
- **"blind"** — it means **blind to the signs and proofs of Allah**.
- **"then he will be blind in the Hereafter"** — *as he was blind in this world.*
- **"and most astray from the path"** — *most astray as he was in this world.*

Ibn Kathir ends his comment on the ayah not with an argument but with a duʿāʾ (a supplication): **"We seek refuge with Allah from that."** That is the right response to it — flight to Allah.

## Living it

Put the two ayat side by side and the practical weight of the passage stands out.

**Your file is being written, and it is exact.** *"Verily, We were recording what you used to do"* (45:29). The measure of the precision is the *fatīl* — the long thread in the groove of a date-pit — and the ayah's promise is that not even that much of injustice will touch anyone.

**The joy of that Day is the joy of a reader.** Ibn Kathir says they will read it *and want to read it*; Maʿārif says the happy believer will have others read it too. Whatever makes you want that page read aloud is worth doing today.

**The right hand is about faith first.** Maʿārif's reading is a mercy and a warning at once: it is the believer, pious or sinful, who receives it in the right hand — so guard *īmān* above everything; and yet punishment may also come for some deeds, so do not treat faith as a licence.

**Ask who you are following.** On the reading reported from Sayyidna ʿAli and Mujahid, everyone is called as the follower of a certain leader — and Qurtubi's list runs from the prophets and their deputies and the scholars all the way to leaders who have been inviting people to error and sin. Choose your teachers, your guides and your influences as someone who will one day be called along with them.

**Ask Allah for sight.** Ayah 72 names the blindness that matters: blindness to the signs and proofs of Allah — and it says that the one who was blind here will be blind in the Hereafter, as he was blind in this world. Ibn Kathir's own response to that is a prayer, and it is the best thing to carry away from these two ayat: *We seek refuge with Allah from that.*

passages.title: Pressure to compromise, and Allah's steadying grace
passages.tafsir:
**Two attempts to bend the Prophet ﷺ — and Allah's hand holding him steady.** In ayat 73–75 the pressure comes from inside the conversation: an offer designed to make him adjust the message. In ayat 76–77 it turns outward: a plan to push him off his land altogether. What binds the five ayat into one unit is not just the two threats but the identical way each is introduced — *wa in kādū*, "and they were indeed about to…" — and the fact that neither attempt lands. What defeats them is named plainly in ayah 74: *lawlā an thabbatnāka*, "had We not made you stand firm."

Ibn Kathir reads the passage as one sustained statement about divine protection. Allah, he says, is telling us how He supported His Prophet ﷺ, protected him, and kept him safe from the evil plots of the wicked transgressors — that Allah is the One who took care of him and helped him, and would not leave him to any of His creation; He is his Helper, his Supporter and his Protector, the One who would make his religion prevail over those who resist him, oppose him and fight him, in the east and in the west.

## The offer: "remove these people, and we will be your friends"

To pin down what ayat 73–75 are responding to, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān turns to Tafsir Mazhari, which carries several relevant reports. The one Maʿārif considers closer and more supportive in terms of the indicators set in the Qur'an is what Ibn Abi Hatim reported, based on a narrative of Sayyidna Jubayr ibn Nufayr.

According to that report, some chiefs of the Quraysh of Makkah came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: *if you have really been sent to us, you should remove these poor and broken-down people from around you, for sitting with such people is a matter of insult for us. If you do that, we too will become your companions and friends.*

What was being asked for was a seating arrangement: move the poor and broken-down believers out of the circle, and the men of standing will come in. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that when they said this, the Prophet ﷺ leaned somewhat towards the idea that he might do something like that — and it states the motive plainly: *in the hope that they may, perhaps, become Muslims.* It was thereupon that this ayah was revealed.

That detail matters for the whole passage. What the Prophet ﷺ inclined towards for a moment came dressed as a small adjustment, urged by influential men, and was entertained only out of the hope that those men might enter Islam.

## Why the Qur'an calls it *fitnah*

The verb the ayah uses for what they were about to do is *yaftinūnaka* — from *fitnah*, which Maʿārif glosses as a trial or test, or a ruse to tempt him into creating discord in his ranks. And Maʿārif makes both halves of the offer fall under that one word: through this ayah the Prophet ﷺ was told that **their suggestion was a fitnah, and the friendship they were talking about was also a fitnah.** Therefore he should not accept it.

The ayah then names the two ends of the road they wanted him on. First, *li-taftariya* — that he would fabricate against Allah something other than what had been revealed to him. The Qur'an places their demand under that heading: to go along with it would have meant putting forward, in Allah's name, something other than what Allah had sent down. Second, "and then they would certainly have taken you as an intimate friend" — the very friendship they were dangling, which Maʿārif names as a fitnah in its own right.

## "Had We not made you stand firm" (ayah 74)

The sources handle ayah 74 with great care, and its wording rewards the same care: *"And had We not made you stand firm, you would nearly have inclined to them a little."*

Read the qualifiers. Not "you would have inclined" — you would have **come near** to inclining. And not even wholly near: *shay'an*, "a little", a slight measure. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān paraphrases the sense this way: had your Lord not been particular about your grooming and fortitude, it was not too far out that you could have come somewhat closer to tilting towards their proposal.

Then, following Tafsir Mazhari, Maʿārif draws the conclusion out explicitly. From this ayah it is clearly understood that **there was just no probability of the Prophet ﷺ ever tilting towards such absurd demands from the Quraysh disbelievers.** What was probable was only *coming close* to tilting, and that too within a very insignificant limit — and by making him *maʿṣūm* (protected, infallible), Allah saved him from drifting even to that limit.

Maʿārif then presses the point further, and it is worth following. If we were to think about it, says Tafsir Mazhari, this ayah provides a great proof of the highest moral disposition with which all the prophets, peace be upon them, were blessed. Had there been even no shield of prophetic infallibility, such was the natural disposition of the Prophet of Islam ﷺ that tilting towards the absurd proposal of the disbelievers would never have been possible for him. What did exist was the probability of his coming somewhat closer, in an insignificant measure, towards the act of tilting — and that was terminated by the prophetic infallibility.

So the ayah is doing two things at once that a careless reading collapses into one. It is honouring the Prophet ﷺ — his own disposition would never have crossed that line — while insisting that the credit for his standing firm belongs to Allah: *thabbatnāka*, "**We** made you stand firm." If even he is shown here leaning on Allah's steadying, no believer has any business trusting his own firmness.

## Why the threatened penalty is doubled (ayah 75)

Ayah 75 states the consequence of a road not taken: *"In that case We would have made you taste a double portion in this life and a double portion after death, and then you would have found none to help you against Us."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān prefixes its comment with the necessary reminder — **"supposing the impossible"** — and then explains the doubling: had he come closer to tilting towards their wrong move, the punishment would have been double in life and double after death, that is, in the grave or the Hereafter. And the reason is a principle worth carrying: *even an insignificant error made by those close to Allah is considered to be very grave.* Nearness raises the stakes rather than lowering them.

Maʿārif notes that what is said here is almost the same as what was said about the blessed wives of the Prophet ﷺ in Surah al-Ahzab: *"O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you should commit a clear act of immodesty, the punishment for her will be multiplied doubly"* (33:30). Proximity to revelation is a weight, not a licence.

And then the sentence closes: *"you would have found none to help you against Us."* The same passage that credits his firmness to Allah's steadying also states that no one else could have shielded him from Allah. Protection and accountability come from the same hand.

## Ayah 76: they were about to tear him loose from the land

The second pressure is physical. *Wa in kādū la-yastafizzūnaka min al-arḍ li-yukhrijūka minhā* — the same opening as ayah 73, but a different verb, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens it up for us. *Istifzāz* literally means **to cut off, or tear away from, or to provoke into moving from a place.** At this place, says Maʿārif, the sense is to expel the Prophet ﷺ from his station at Makkah or Madinah. And the ayah's meaning is that had they done it, their own punishment would have been that they themselves could not have lived there much longer after him.

The commentators record two reports about the occasion.

**The first relates to Madinah al-Tayyibah.** The Jews of the city came to the Prophet ﷺ and told him: *O Abu al-Qasim, if you are true in your claim to be a prophet, you should go and live in Syria, because the land of Syria is the land of al-Mahshar — the Resurrection — and the land of prophets too.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that the Prophet ﷺ was somewhat impressed by what they said, and that when he travelled to Syria at the time of the battle of Tabuk the idea of taking up residence there was still on his mind, until the revelation of this ayah stopped him from doing so. Maʿārif then adds, honestly, that after presenting this report **Ibn Kathir declared it to be unsatisfactory.**

**The second transpired in Makkah al-Mukarramah**, and this is the one Ibn Kathir considers the weightier choice as the point of reference — partly because this surah is Makki, which provides a strong coherence for that reading. As the event goes, the Quraysh disbelievers once intended to expel the Prophet ﷺ from Makkah. Ibn Kathir states it directly: this was revealed concerning the disbelievers among the Quraysh when they wanted to expel the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from among themselves, and Allah issued them a warning in this ayah — **if they expelled him, they would not stay in Makkah for very long after that.**

That the sources preserve two reports here, and that Maʿārif passes on Ibn Kathir's rejection of the one it mentions first, is itself instructive. Where the evidence is a matter of transmitted reports, the scholars weigh and differ, and honest tafsir shows the weighing rather than hiding it.

## The warning, and how it came true

The threat in ayah 76 is unusual: not "if you expel him, We will punish you at some unnamed hour," but "they would not have stayed after you, except for a little while." A short clock.

Ibn Kathir traces what happened. This is what came about after the Prophet ﷺ migrated from them, when their persecution became so intense: only **a year and a half** after that, Allah brought him and them together on the battlefield of Badr, without any pre-arranged appointment, and caused him to prevail over them and defeat them, so their leaders were killed and their families taken as captives.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān follows the same arc further. The disbelievers of Makkah saw this warning come true with their own eyes: after the migration they were unable to sit there in peace even for a day; within a period of a year and six months Allah made them assemble on the plains of Badr, where seventy of their chiefs were killed and their initial aggressive power was broken; then came the final outcome of the battle of Uhud, which made them more awe-stricken; and the last confrontation of the battle of al-Ahzab virtually broke their back. It was in the eighth year of the Hijrah that the Prophet ﷺ conquered the whole of Makkah al-Mukarramah.

## Ayah 77: an unchanging way

The passage does not end on Makkah's defeat but lifts it into a law: *"Such has been Our way with the messengers We sent before you, and you will not find any alteration in Our way."* The word rendered "way" here is *sunnah* — a settled, customary practice; in Ibn Kathir's and Maʿārif's usage, Allah's own established manner of dealing with people.

Ibn Kathir glosses *sunnata man qad arsalnā* as: this is what We usually do to those who reject Our Messengers and persecute them by driving the Messenger out from among themselves — the punishment comes to them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the same rule in general form: according to the customary way and law of Allah, when a people expel their prophet from his homeland, or compel him to leave by scaring and harassing him, those people too are not left to continue living there; they are visited by the punishment of Allah.

Two things follow from this. First, the Quraysh were not being singled out for special cruelty; they were walking into something old. Second — and the closing phrase, "you will not find any alteration in Our way," is emphatic about this — this is Allah's settled way, and it does not shift.

Ibn Kathir adds a mercy to the reckoning. If it were not for the fact that the Prophet ﷺ was the Messenger of Mercy, vengeance would have come upon them such as had never been seen before in this world. He cites Allah's word: *"And Allah would not punish them while you are among them"* (8:33). Even the punishment that fell was restrained by the presence of the man they were trying to expel.

## Living it

**A dangerous offer can arrive as a reasonable adjustment.** What the Prophet ﷺ leaned towards for a moment was a change in who sat around him, urged by men of standing, entertained in the hope that they might become Muslims. The Qur'an's answer is not that his hope was bad — Maʿārif records that hope plainly — but that the suggestion itself was a fitnah, and the friendship offered alongside it was a fitnah too. The road it led to is named in the ayah: fabricating, against Allah, something other than what had been revealed.

**Do not clear the poor out of the room.** The concession demanded in ayah 73 was social: remove the poor and broken-down believers from the circle so that the men of standing would not feel insulted. The ayah told the Prophet ﷺ that this was a fitnah and that he should not accept it.

**Firmness is a gift, not a possession.** Ayah 74 credits the Prophet's ﷺ standing firm to Allah — *thabbatnāka*. The believer who assumes he could never be moved has already missed what this ayah teaches; the right response is to ask Allah for that same steadying.

**Nearness raises the stakes.** Ayah 75, and its parallel in 33:30, teach that even an insignificant error made by those close to Allah is considered very grave. Knowledge and standing are not insulation; they are exposure.

**And the outcome is not in the hands of those applying the pressure.** They could harass, threaten and finally drive him out — and every bit of it ran inside a settled way of Allah that they did not know they were subject to, one in which you will find no alteration.

passages.title: The five prayers, night vigil, and truth's arrival
passages.tafsir:
The verses just before these set out the hostility of the enemies of Islam and their plans to harass the Prophet ﷺ, with the assurance that those plans would never succeed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays the passage out in a line: mentioned first were the pains inflicted on him ﷺ and the conspiracies against him; against these he was given the real plan — establish the five prayers, and the Tahajjud; then the promise of the Praised Station, to be fulfilled in the Hereafter; then, within this world, the first relief, his migration to Madinah (80); and then the good news of the conquest of Makkah (81). Persecution is answered with worship, and worship opens onto both worlds.

By giving the Prophet ﷺ the command to establish Salah, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, it is being suggested that this is the best remedy against the mischief and pain caused by enemies. It compares the more explicit verse of Surah al-Hijr — Allah knows his heart feels distressed at what they say, so let him proclaim the purity and glory of his Lord and be among those who prostrate (Qurtubi). Since staying safe depends on the help of Allah, the best means of acquiring that help is Salah: "Seek help through patience and prayer" (2:153).

## The five prayers, fixed by the sun and the dark (78)

The ayah names no prayer. It fixes them by the sun and the coming of the dark, and the majority of leading Tafsir authorities, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, have declared this verse a comprehensive injunction for all five daily prayers.

The word **دُلُوك (duluk)** is essentially used in the sense of "decline". Ibn Kathir carries the gloss of Ibn 'Abbas — "midday means when the sun is at its zenith" — reported also from Ibn 'Umar by Nafi', and by Malik in his Tafsir from Az-Zuhri from Ibn 'Umar; it was likewise the opinion of Abu Barzah Al-Aslami, Mujahid, Al-Hasan, Ad-Dahhak, Abu Ja'far Al-Baqir and Qatadah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supplies the nuance: the decline begins at the meridian, and the majority of the Companions and the Followers took *duluk* to mean the post-meridian decline — the time of Zuhr begins from exactly that moment (al-Qurtubi, al-Mazhari, Ibn Kathir).

The far end of the arc is **غَسَق (ghasaq)**. Ibn Kathir glosses it as darkness, noting it was also said to mean sunset. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is more precise: *ghasaq al-layl* is the darkness of the night when it is complete, and Imam Malik reported this interpretation from Ibn 'Abbas. So one sweep of words covers four prayers: Zuhr, 'Asr, Maghrib and 'Isha'.

Because that phrase also marks where 'Isha' begins, a disagreement follows, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records both sides. Close to sunset a red glow appears; after the redness, a whiteness spreads; then that too disappears. Since the darkness is complete only once the whiteness has gone, Imam Abu Hanifah ruled that 'Isha' begins after the white glow has disappeared. Other Imams ruled that it begins once the red glow has gone.

The fifth prayer is named separately, and named by its recitation: **وَقُرْآنَ الْفَجْرِ**, "and the recital at dawn." Ibn Kathir says it means Salat Al-Fajr. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why the word "Qur'an" can denote the prayer here — recitation of the Qur'an is an integral part of Salah — and notes that most Tafsir authorities, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, Mazhari and others, have adopted this meaning. It is from the word and deed of the Prophet ﷺ that we know the recitation in Fajr should be long to the measure of one's strength, less than that in Zuhr and Jumu'ah, average in 'Asr and 'Isha', and very brief in Maghrib.

Ibn Kathir observes that the details of the timings were reported in the *Mutawatir* Sunnah, from the words and deeds of the Prophet ﷺ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses harder: the injunction of five prayers appeared in this verse briefly, and was explained fully by the Prophet ﷺ through his word and deed — unless one acts in accordance with that explanation, no one can perform Salah at all. Its author says he does not know how those who claim to understand the Qur'an without Hadith go about making their Salah.

Then the ayah says of that dawn recitation that it is *mashhūdā*. The word, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, derives from *shahādah*, "to be present" — hence "well-attended". Imam Ahmad recorded from Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said concerning this ayah, "It is witnessed by the angels of the night and the angels of the day"; this was recorded also by At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah, and At-Tirmidhi said, "It is Hasan Sahih." The fullest version, in the Two Sahihs from Abu Hurayrah:

> "The angels of the night and the angels of the day come amongst you in successive groups (in shifts). They meet at the Morning prayer (Fajr) and at the Mid-afternoon prayer ('Asr). Those who stayed among you ascend, and their Lord asks them, although He knows best about you, 'How did you leave My servants?' They say, 'We came to them when they were praying and we left them when they were praying.'"

## The night that is added to the five, and where it leads (79)

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 79 as a command to the Prophet ﷺ to offer further prayers at night *after* the prescribed prayers. It was reported in Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurayrah that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked which prayer is best after the prescribed prayers, he said, "The Night prayer."

The word **تَهَجَّد (tahajjud)** comes from *hujūd*, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Mazhari, notes that this root is used for two opposite meanings, sleeping and waking both. Here it means being awake, and awake *with the Qur'an*: the pronoun in *bihi*, "with it", reverts to the Qur'an mentioned just before — the making of Salah with full compliance of what it requires, which is what the Shari'ah calls Tahajjud.

Must one sleep first? Ibn Kathir reports that the term refers to prayer offered after sleeping — the view of 'Alqamah, Al-Aswad, Ibrahim An-Nakha'i and others — and carries Al-Hasan Al-Basri's definition: "This is what comes after 'Isha', or it could mean what comes after sleeping." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers: according to Tafsir Mazhari the sense is no more than sacrificing sleep to pray during some part of the night, and the condition of sleeping first is not found in the words the Qur'an uses — so postponing sleep and praying also fulfils it. But since it was the constant practice of the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions to pray Tahajjud after waking in the later part of the night, that is the better way.

**نَافِلَةً لَّكَ — "an additional prayer for you."** The words *nafl* and *nāfilah* literally mean "additional". Why "for you" in particular? Ibn Kathir gives Mujahid's answer — the Night prayer was made an extra prayer specifically for the Prophet ﷺ because all his previous and future sins had been forgiven, whereas for others of his Ummah, optional prayers may expiate for whatever sins they may commit (also reported in Al-Musnad from Abu Umamah Al-Bahili). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it from the other side: the voluntary worship of the Ummah expiates their sins; but the Prophet ﷺ is above any shortcoming in the etiquette of Salah, so his voluntary worship makes amends for nothing — it is simply a source of increased nearness to Allah (Qurtubi, Mazhari).

When Surah al-Muzzammil was revealed, the five prayers had not yet been made obligatory; what everyone was obligated with was the night prayer. Then, on the night of the Mi'raj, the five were made *fard*, and that the obligation of Tahajjud was thereby abrogated for the community at large is agreed by consensus. What some early commentators disputed was whether it remained an obligation upon the Prophet ﷺ — in which case *nāfilatan laka* would mean "an additional obligation upon you". According to Tafsir al-Qurtubi this is not correct: there is no justification for taking *nafl* as *fard*, and in authentic Ahadith only the five fixed prayers have been mentioned as obligatory; and at the end of another Hadith it is said that the fifty prayers made obligatory in the Mi'raj were reduced and set at five, while the reward promised remained that of fifty — "The word will not be changed with Me" (50:29). The outcome, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, is that no Salah other than the five is obligatory, neither upon the Ummah nor upon the Prophet ﷺ himself. Tafsir Mazhari declares the same position correct and sound.

A second difference follows. Muslim jurists have a standing rule that whatever the Prophet ﷺ did constantly, never leaving it unless under compulsion, is *Sunnah al-Mu'akkadah* — unless it is proved that the act was special to him. Since his constancy in this prayer stands proved and there is no proof of its being restricted to him, Tafsir Mazhari rates it weightier that Tahajjud is an emphasised Sunnah for the Ummah as well; in proof it points to the Hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ said of a man who used to pray Tahajjud and then left it, "the Shaitan has soiled his ear". And Allah knows best.

As for how much: in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim, 'A'ishah reported that the Prophet ﷺ would never pray more than eleven rak'ahs, in Ramadan or other months — of which, according to the Hanafiyyah, three were Witr and the remaining eight Tahajjud. And in al-Bukhari, when Masruq asked her, she said there used to be seven, nine and eleven, besides the Sunnah of Fajr (Mazhari).

Then comes the promise: *"It may be that your Lord will raise you to Maqam Mahmud"* — the Praised Station. Ibn Kathir reads the sequence as cause and effect: do that which you are commanded to do, and We will raise you to a station of praise and glory on the Day of Resurrection, where all of creation will praise you, as will their Creator. Ibn Jarir said that most commentators explained it as the position to which Muhammad ﷺ will be raised on that Day to intercede for the people. Ibn 'Abbas said, "The position of praise and honour is the position of intercession". Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this station is particular to the Prophet ﷺ out of all the prophets, and that it is the station of the Grand Intercession (*al-shaf'ah al-kubra*).

The longest account is the Hadith of Abu Hurayrah, recorded by Imam Ahmad and also reported in the Two Sahihs. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "I will be the leader of mankind on the Day of Resurrection. Do you know why it will be so?" He described Allah gathering the first and the last in one place, so that people say to one another: why do you not find someone to intercede for you with your Lord? They go to Adam, and he recalls the Tree he was forbidden, and says, "Myself, myself, myself. Go to someone else. Go to Nuh." They go to Nuh; he recalls a prayer he prayed against his people, and sends them on. They go to Ibrahim, the close Friend of Allah; he mentions some untruths he had told, and sends them on. They go to Musa, whom Allah chose by speaking to him directly; he recalls a soul he killed whom he had not been commanded to kill, and sends them on. They go to 'Isa, His Word which He bestowed upon Maryam — and he will not mention any sin, and still says, "Myself, myself, myself" — sending them on, at the last, to Muhammad ﷺ, whose past and future sins Allah has forgiven.

Then, in his own words:

> "I will stand up and come before the Throne, and will fall prostrating to my Lord, may He be glorified and exalted. Then Allah will inspire me to speak and I will speak beautiful words of praise such as no one has ever been inspired with before. It will be said, 'O Muhammad, raise your head and ask, it will be granted to you. Intercede, and your intercession will be heard.' So I will raise my head and say, 'My Ummah, O Lord, my Ummah, O Lord, my Ummah, O Lord.'"

He comes forward with no claim, and the words he raises his head to say are about us.

Ibn Kathir lists honours of that Day in which no one else will have a share: he is the first for whom the earth will be opened; he is the first Prophet whose Ummah will be judged, the first to take them across the Bridge over the Fire, and the first to intercede in Paradise, as was reported in Sahih Muslim; and he is the one who will reach Al-Wasilah, the highest position in Paradise.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Khawarij and the Mu'tazilah deny the intercession of the prophets, holding that no major sin will be forgiven through anyone's intercession; but Ahadith coming in uninterrupted succession prove that intercession for sinners will be accepted from the Prophets.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes Mujaddid Alf Thani on the order within this verse: the Prophet ﷺ was first given the command to pray Tahajjud, and then promised the Praised Station — which tells us that Tahajjud serves as a special means of acquiring the Station of Intercession.

## The exit, the entrance, and the sentence at the Ka'bah (80–81)

Imam Ahmad recorded that Ibn 'Abbas said the Prophet ﷺ was in Makkah, then was commanded to emigrate, and Allah revealed this ayah; At-Tirmidhi said, "This is Hasan Sahih." Al-Hasan Al-Basri supplies the circumstances: when the disbelievers of Makkah conspired to kill the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, or expel him, or imprison him, Allah commanded him to go to Al-Madinah. In Ibn Kathir's text, "my entry" is his entry to Al-Madinah and "my exit" his exit from Makkah, which was also the view of 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same explanation from Hasan al-Basri and Qatadah, and notes that Ibn Kathir calls this "the most sound statement".

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *mudkhal* and *mukhraj* are nouns of place and time, and that the attribute *sidq* releases the sense of an entry and an exit wholly true to the will and pleasure of Allah (compare *qadama sidq*, 10:2; *lisāna sidq*, 26:84; *maq'ad sidq*, 54:55). So the prayer takes this form: O Allah, may my entry into Madinah be good and smooth; and may my exit from Makkah be good and smooth, without my being entangled in love of country and home.

Why is the entrance mentioned before the exit, when he must leave before he can arrive? Perhaps, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān suggests, to indicate that the exit from Makkah had no purpose of its own, while the purpose, peace for Islam and the Muslims, was what could be hoped for through the entry into Madinah.

Then: *"And grant me from You a helping authority."* Qatadah's reading explains why such a thing would be asked for: the Prophet of Allah ﷺ knew that he could not achieve this without authority or power, so he asked for authority with which to support the Book of Allah, the Laws of Allah, and to establish the religion of Allah. And Qatadah adds a whole political theology in a line: "Authority is a mercy from Allah which He places among His servants, otherwise some of them would attack others, and the strong would consume the weak." Alongside the truth, power was needed to suppress those who resisted — hence, Ibn Kathir points out, Allah's words about sending the Messengers with clear proofs, down to "And We brought forth iron" (57:25). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records what came of the du'a: Allah shielded him at every step and finally made Madinah good and promising for him and for all Muslims — which is why some scholars have said that every Muslim should remember this prayer at the beginning of any objective he means to pursue.

Ibn Kathir reads *"Truth has come and falsehood has vanished"* as a threat and a warning to the disbelievers of the Quraysh: there has come to them from Allah the truth which they have no power to resist — what He has sent them of the Qur'an, of faith and of beneficial knowledge — while their falsehood cannot stand firm in the face of the truth. He sets beside it: "Nay, We fling the truth against the falsehood, so it destroys it, and behold, it disappears" (21:18).

Ibn Kathir records from Al-Bukhari that 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud said: the Prophet ﷺ entered Makkah at the Conquest, and around the House were three hundred and sixty idols; he started to strike them with a stick in his hand, saying, *"Truth has come and falsehood has vanished. Surely falsehood is ever bound to vanish."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says this verse was revealed after the Hijrah concerning the conquest of Makkah, cites al-Bukhari and Muslim for Ibn Mas'ud's account, and reports the explanation of some scholars for the number: the idolaters of Makkah kept a separate idol for each day of the year, worshipped on its day (Qurtubi).

Imam al-Qurtubi held that this verse proves it obligatory to erase the idols of the idolaters and all other polytheistic symbols and signs. Ibn al-Mundhir said that pictures and figures sculpted in wood or metal also come under the injunction governing idols; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān recalls that the Prophet ﷺ tore a curtain that had pictures made on it, and that according to authentic Hadith 'Isa (peace be upon him) will in the later times undo the cross and eliminate the swine.

When outside pressure is at its worst, the instruction is not to strike back but to fix the prayer — the five, mapped onto a sky anyone can look at, and then the night, when nobody is watching. The promise attached to the night vigil is the highest station any created being will be given, and the man raised to it comes forward prostrating and asks for his Ummah. And falsehood may stand around the Ka'bah for a lifetime, three hundred and sixty of it, but *falsehood is ever bound to vanish*.

passages.title: Healing for believers, arrogance in the ungrateful
passages.tafsir:
**In one sentence:** Allah names the Qur'an a cure and a mercy for the believers — for those who believe in it and accept it as true (ayah 82); He then describes the weakness inherent in man, who turns away when he is given and despairs when he is deprived (ayah 83); and He closes by telling the Prophet ﷺ to say that each person acts according to his own *shākilah*, and that the Lord knows best whose path is right (ayah 84).

The three ayat sit together naturally. Ayah 82 names the remedy. Ayah 83 shows the human weakness that stands so badly in need of it. Ayah 84 puts each person's conduct back where it comes from — his own settled way — and hands the verdict to Allah.

## Ayah 82 — a cure *and* a mercy

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah's Book, revealed to His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ — the Qur'an to which falsehood cannot come, from before it or behind it, sent down by the All-Wise, Worthy of all praise — is a cure and a mercy for the believers. He then says what each word covers.

**As a cure**, it takes away whatever is in their hearts of doubt, hypocrisy, shirk, confusion, and inclination towards falsehood. Every one of those is an illness of the heart rather than of the body, and Ibn Kathir says the Qur'an cures all of it.

**As a mercy**, it is that through which a person attains faith and wisdom and seeks goodness. So the Book does not only clear something away; it is the means by which faith and wisdom are gained.

Ibn Kathir is careful about the qualifier the ayah itself gives: this is only for those who believe in it and accept it as truthful. It is a cure and a mercy only for such people.

Qatadah, an early authority Ibn Kathir cites here, describes what that acceptance looks like in three steps: when the believer hears the Qur'an, he **benefits** from it, **memorises** it, and **understands** it. Ibn Kathir then describes the wrongdoers by the exact negatives of those three verbs — they do not benefit from it, or memorise it, or understand it. That is a searching test for anyone who recites daily: which of the two descriptions fits my relationship with what I read?

## Why the same words increase some people in loss

The second half of ayah 82 is startling: the very revelation that heals believers "increases the wrongdoers in nothing but loss." Ibn Kathir's explanation is exact — the disbeliever, who is wronging himself by his disbelief, hears the Qur'an and it only makes him further from the truth and increases him in his disbelief.
