And he states plainly where the fault lies: **the problem lies with the disbeliever himself, not with the Qur'an.**

He supports this from elsewhere in the Qur'an: *"Say: It is for those who believe, a guide and a cure. And as for those who disbelieve, there is heaviness in their ears, and it is blindness for them. They are those who are called from a place far away"* (41:44); and the passage where a newly revealed sūrah increases the believers in faith so that they rejoice, while those in whose hearts is a disease only gain doubt added to their doubt (9:124–125). Ibn Kathir notes there are many other similar ayat.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical conclusion from the ayah's final clause: recited with faith and reverence, the Qur'an is certainly a cure — that is open and proven. Conversely, any denial of the Qur'an, or irreverence towards it, could itself become a source of loss and misfortune. The same encounter, two opposite outcomes.

## Does the cure reach the body too?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distinguishes two levels of claim here, and we should keep his distinction rather than flatten it.

**The first is agreed upon by the entire Muslim ummah:** that the Holy Qur'an cures hearts and delivers people from shirk and kufr, from low morals and spiritual ailments. Maʿārif says this is no secret.

**The second is held by some of the ʿUlamāʾ:** that as the Qur'an is a cure for spiritual ailments, so it is also a cure for physical diseases — by reciting its verses and blowing the breath on the body of the sick person, or by writing its words on an amulet and putting it around the neck. Maʿārif states that hadith narratives bear testimony to this.

The report he cites is the hadith of Sayyidnā Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī (may Allah be pleased with him), which he says can be seen in all books of Ahadith. A party of the noble Companions was travelling. In a village on their way, a scorpion had bitten the chief, and the village people asked the Companions if they could suggest some treatment. They recited Sūrah al-Fātiḥah seven times, blew their breath on him, and the ailing patient stood cured. When the incident was later mentioned before the Prophet ﷺ, he declared the Companions' action to be permissible. (Our source names no collection for this report, so neither will we.)

Maʿārif adds that several other hadith reports prove the Prophet ﷺ did this himself: after reciting the last two verses of the Qur'an, he would blow his breath on the sick person. It is also proved, he says, that the Ṣaḥābah and the Tābiʿīn used to treat the sick with the recital of those verses and of other verses too; and that writing them and placing them around the neck as an amulet also stands proved. He refers the reader to al-Qurṭubī, who gives the details in his commentary on this very ayah.

Worth holding steady: the levels of certainty differ. The healing of hearts is what the entire ummah agrees on; the bodily application is what "some ʿUlamāʾ" hold, on the strength of these reports.

## Ayah 83 — turning away in ease, despairing in calamity

Ibn Kathir titles this passage exactly that, and reads the ayah as Allah telling us about **the weakness that is inherent in man** — with a crucial exception stated at the outset: **except those whom Allah protects**, and He protects them at both times, ease and calamity alike. Neither condition is safe on its own.

**When the gift comes.** Ibn Kathir fills in what the blessing covers: wealth, good health, ease, provision and help — a man getting what he wants. And then he turns away from the obedience and worship of Allah, and becomes arrogant. Mujahid glossed the phrase simply: it means he goes away from Us.

Ibn Kathir sets two other ayat beside it, and they sting: *"But when We have removed his harm from him, he passes on as if he had never invoked Us for a harm that touched him"* (10:12), and *"But when He brings you safe to land, you turn away."* The pattern is the storm-prayer forgotten on dry ground.

**When evil touches him.** "Evil" here, Ibn Kathir says, means disasters, accidents and calamities. And the man is in great despair — which Ibn Kathir unpacks precisely: it means he thinks he will never have anything good again. Not merely sad; convinced the door has shut.

Ibn Kathir treats both reactions as facets of that one inherent weakness, and quotes the passage from Sūrah Hūd that names both together — man is despairing and ungrateful when a mercy is removed from him, and exultant and boastful when good comes after evil has touched him — and then names the exception: *"Except those who show patience and do righteous good deeds: those, theirs will be forgiveness and a great reward"* (11:9–11). There is the treatment, in two words: **patience (ṣabr)** when the hardship lands, and **righteous deeds** when the ease comes. That is what it looks like to be among those Allah protects at both times.

## Ayah 84 — everyone acts according to his own *shākilah*

*"Say: Each one does according to his shākilah, and your Lord knows best of him whose path is right."*

*Shākilah* is an Arabic word with no single English equivalent, and the early authorities glossed it from slightly different angles. Ibn Kathir gathers four:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās** — according to his inclinations
- **Mujāhid** — according to his inclinations and his nature
- **Qatādah** — according to his intentions
- **Ibn Zayd** — according to his religion

Ibn Kathir's verdict on this spread is that all these suggestions are close in meaning. They are not four competing theories but four angles on one thing.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports several interpretations of *shākilah* from authorities among the early righteous elders — disposition, habit, instinct, intention, way, manner — and then adds the observation that makes the ayah land: in sum, all of these turn into **a second nature** in terms of the circumstances, habits and customs everyone lives with, so that what a person does remains subservient to it. (Maʿārif cites al-Qurṭubī for this last point.) A man does not usually choose each act freshly; he acts out of who he has become.

**The practical warning drawn from this.** Maʿārif reports that Imām al-Jaṣṣāṣ took the ayah as a warning to human beings: they must abstain from bad surroundings, bad company and bad habits, and take to the company of good people and inculcate good habits. The reasoning Maʿārif gives is direct — one's response pattern, built up under the influence of surroundings, company and custom, makes one do what it dictates.

Al-Jaṣṣāṣ also offers a second meaning of *shākilah* here: **"like"** — one's own kind. On that reading, the sense is that everyone feels comfortable with a person compatible with his own temperament: a good man finds another good man familiar, while a wicked man feels comfortable with another wicked man whose style he follows without any qualms of conscience. Maʿārif illustrates this with Allah's words *"Evil women are for evil men"* and *"Good women are for good men"* (24:26) — everyone strikes familiarity according to his own temperament. Either way, Maʿārif concludes, this is a warning against falling into bad company and bad habits, and one should really make an effort to abstain from these.

**Who is being addressed?** Ibn Kathir reads the ayah — and Allah knows best — as a threat and a warning to the idolaters, comparable to *"And say to those who do not believe: Act according to your ability and way"* (11:121).

**And then the ayah hands the verdict back to Allah.** "Your Lord knows best of him whose path is right" — Ibn Kathir explains the meaning as: whether that is us or you. Everyone will be rewarded in accordance with his deeds, for nothing whatsoever is hidden from Allah. Nothing in a person's inner make-up — the inclinations Ibn ʿAbbās mentioned, the intentions Qatādah mentioned — lies outside that knowledge.

## Living it

- **Recite as one who takes the medicine.** Qatādah's three marks are a checklist: did I benefit, retain, understand? Ibn Kathir's description of the wrongdoers is precisely the absence of those three.
- **Guard reverence.** Maʿārif's warning is that denial of the Qur'an or irreverence towards it can turn the encounter from cure into loss.
- **Use it over the sick, as the Companions did** — reciting and blowing the breath — an action the Prophet ﷺ declared permissible when it was mentioned to him, and which Maʿārif reports he did himself.
- **Audit both conditions, not one.** Ayah 83 names the danger in ease as turning away and growing arrogant, and the danger in calamity as thinking you will never have anything good again. The protected servant is guarded at both times, and the exception clause of 11:9–11 names the way: patience and righteous deeds.
- **Choose your surroundings deliberately.** On Maʿārif's reading, surroundings, company and custom build the response pattern that then dictates what you do. So choose the company you want your future self to have been shaped by.

passages.title: The spirit, revelation, and the Quran's inimitability
passages.tafsir:
Someone asks the Prophet ﷺ a question meant to trip him up — what is the *rūḥ*, the spirit? — and Allah answers in one restrained sentence that quietly redraws the map of human knowledge. Everything after grows out of that answer: if your knowledge is small and on loan, then even the revelation given to the Prophet ﷺ is a gift that could be withdrawn (86–87); and if you honestly want to test whether he ﷺ is a messenger, stop hunting for riddles and look at the Book in front of you, which no creature can match (88–89). The thread through all five ayat is knowledge — how little we hold, Who owns it, and where an honest seeker should have been looking.

## The question behind the question

Ibn Kathir relays that al-Bukhari recorded in his Tafsir of this ayah that 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: "While I was walking with the Prophet ﷺ on a farm, and he was resting on a palm-leaf stalk, some Jews passed by. Some of them said to the others, 'Ask him about the Rūḥ.' Some said, 'What urges you to ask him about that?' Others said, 'Do not ask him, lest he gives you a reply which you do not like.' But they said, 'Ask him.' So they asked him about the Rūḥ. The Prophet ﷺ kept quiet and did not give them an answer, and I knew that he was receiving revelation, so I stayed where I was." When the revelation was complete, the Prophet ﷺ recited this ayah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān tells the same incident in its own wording, citing the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhari and Muslim: in the Prophet's ﷺ blessed hand was a stick from the branch of a date palm; when the question came, the Prophet ﷺ reclined on his stick and stood silent; that silence is what gave Ibn Mas'ud the inkling that revelation was about to come.

This was never an innocent enquiry. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the preceding ayat record hostile questions from the disbelievers and the *mushriks* (those who associate partners with Allah), aimed at testing the Prophet's ﷺ claim to messengership; this question is one link in that chain.

A report of Ibn 'Abbas in the *Musnad* of Ahmad, cited by Ibn Kathir, fills in the scheme: the Quraysh of Makkah, who kept firing questions at the Prophet ﷺ, reckoned that the Jews were learned in the earlier scriptures — so why not ask *them* what to ask him? Imam al-Baghawi carries a fuller version from Ibn 'Abbas (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites *Maʿālim al-Tanzīl*). The chiefs of Quraysh met and admitted among themselves: this man ﷺ was born among us and grew up among us; no one ever doubted his trustworthiness, honesty and truthfulness, or accused him of a lie — yet we cannot understand this claim of prophethood. Their delegation went to the Jewish scholars, who set a three-part test: ask him about the people who took refuge in a cave to escape shirk; about the man who travelled through the East and West of the earth; and about the Rūḥ. With it came a criterion: **if he answers all three, he is no prophet; if he answers none, he is no prophet; but if he answers two and not the third, be certain that he is the prophet.**

The delegation put the three questions, and the Prophet ﷺ said, "I shall give you the answer tomorrow" — without saying *In shāʼ Allāh*. Revelation then stopped for days (reports vary: twelve, fifteen, forty). The Quraysh had their opening for mockery, and the Prophet ﷺ became anxious. Then Jibril came with *And never say about anything, "I will do that tomorrow," without saying "In shāʼ Allāh"* (18:23–24), and after that the Prophet ﷺ recited this ayah about the Rūḥ. The People of the Cave and Dhul-Qarnayn followed in Sūrat al-Kahf — two questions answered in detail, the third left unanswered. The very sign the Jewish scholars had named as proof of true prophethood was thereby made to appear. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports this from *Mazhari*, noting that Tirmidhi also describes the event briefly.

## Makkah or Madinah?

Ibn Mas'ud's account places the incident in Madinah, and some commentators therefore call this ayah Madani even though the greater part of Sūrah Banī Isrāʼīl is Makki. Ibn 'Abbas's report places it in Makkah, keeping the ayah Makki like the rest of the surah.

**Ibn Kathir judged the Makkan account weightier**, answering Ibn Mas'ud's report by suggesting the ayah may have been revealed a second time in Madinah — repeated revelation of verses being an accepted fact among the scholars — or that the Prophet ﷺ was divinely inspired to answer with an ayah already revealed. **Tafsir Mazhari took the opposite view**, holding Ibn Mas'ud's report stronger and the incident Madani, for two reasons: it appears in the two Ṣaḥīḥs of al-Bukhari and Muslim; and Ibn Mas'ud was part of the event, narrating what he witnessed himself, whereas Ibn 'Abbas — too young at the time — would have heard it from someone else.

## What did they mean by "the Rūḥ"?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word out. In Arabic usage and in the Qur'an, *al-rūḥ* carries several meanings. The familiar one is the soul on which life depends. But the Qur'an also uses it for the archangel Jibril — *the Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart* (26:193–194); for 'Isa (4:171); for revelation (40:15); and for the Qur'an itself — *and We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command* (42:52).

So which did they mean? Some respected early commentators, reading the context, took the question to be about revelation and the Qur'an, or about Jibril who brought it — since the Qur'an is mentioned just before in ayah 82 and again in the ayat that follow; on that reading the question was *how* revelation reached him ﷺ and *who* brought it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān judges this far-fetched: calling revelation "rūḥ" is a usage internal to the Qur'an, unlikely to be what these questioners had in mind, whereas the matter of the living rūḥ — human or animal — is the kind of thing that naturally emerges in everyone's mind. The authentic reports settle it: they were asking about the living rūḥ, wanting its reality — what is it, how does it come in and go out of the body, how does it make man and animal come alive? Accordingly **the majority of commentators — Ibn Kathir, Ibn Jarir, al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, al-Alusi — confirm that the question concerned the reality of the living spirit.**

Ibn Kathir preserves one further detail from al-'Awfi, from Ibn 'Abbas. The Jews had also asked, "Tell us about the Rūḥ and how the Rūḥ will be punished that is in the body" — a matter about which only Allah knows, and concerning which no revelation had yet come. The Prophet ﷺ did not answer them at all; then Jibril came to him with *Say: the Rūḥ is one of the things, the knowledge of which is only with my Lord…* When the Prophet ﷺ told them about it, they demanded, "Who told you this?" He ﷺ said, "Jibril brought it to me from Allah." They said, "By Allah, no one has told you that except our enemy" — meaning Jibril. And Allah revealed: *Say: Whoever is an enemy to Jibril — for indeed he has brought it down to your heart by Allah's permission, confirming what came before it* (2:97).

## "Say: the Rūḥ is of the command of my Lord"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the clearest reading as the one preferred by Qadi Thanaʼullah Panipati in Tafsir Mazhari: only what was necessary, and what ordinary people could grasp, was told. The full reality the questioners were after was not unfolded, because it lay beyond common comprehension and because nothing anyone needs — in religion or in life — depends on it.

To say the rūḥ is *min amri Rabbī*, from the **command** (*amr*) of my Lord, is to say it is not like the usual created things that come into existence through the dispersal of matter and through procreation; it is something created directly through Allah's command *kun* — "Be." That much alone, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, makes clear that the rūḥ cannot be taken on the analogy of common matter, which removes the doubts that emerge from trying to understand it through the prism of materialistic enquiry: you were never going to find it by dissection, because it was never that kind of thing. So the surplus in the question was treated as redundant and left unanswered — especially since grasping its reality is not easy even for the wisest of the wise, let alone the ordinary person.

## Rūḥ and nafs

Ibn Kathir records a discussion from as-Suhayli on whether the *rūḥ* (spirit) and the *nafs* (self, soul) are one thing or two. As-Suhayli held the rūḥ to be light and soft, like air, flowing through the body as water flows through the veins of a tree. The rūḥ the angel breathes into the unborn child is the *nafs* once it joins a body and acquires qualities from it, good or bad — becoming either *a soul in complete rest and satisfaction* (89:27) or one *inclined to evil* (12:53). His image: water is the life of the tree, but mixed into it and pressed from the grape it becomes juice or wine, no longer called water except in a metaphorical sense.

Ibn Kathir's summary is worth memorising: **the rūḥ is the origin and essence; the nafs consists of the rūḥ together with its connection to the body** — the same in one sense, not in another. He calls this a good explanation, closes with *and Allah knows best*, and notes that many books have been written on the subject, among the best being that of al-Hafiz Ibn Mandah.

## "And of knowledge you have been given only a little"

This clause stung. Ibn Jarir recorded that 'Ikrimah said the People of the Book protested: "You claim that we have only a little knowledge, but we have been given the Tawrah, which is the Ḥikmah (wisdom) — *and he, to whom Ḥikmah is granted, is indeed granted abundant good* (2:269)." Then came down: *And if all the trees on the earth were pens and the sea were ink to write with, with seven seas behind it to add to its supply…* (31:27). The reply is beautifully balanced: whatever knowledge you have been given, if Allah saves you from the Fire thereby, then it is great and good — but in comparison to the knowledge of Allah, it is very little. So "little" is not contempt for learning; it is proportion.

## A working rule for teachers

Imam Abu Bakr al-Jassas derived a practical ruling from this answer: a mufti or scholar is **not** obliged to answer every question, or every aspect of it, exactly as the questioner posed it. The answer should be given with religious advisability kept in sight. An answer above the comprehension of the one addressed, or one that risks pushing him into misunderstanding, should not be given; nor should questions that are simply unnecessary (*lā yaʿnī*). But where a person faces a situation in which he must act one way or the other and is himself no scholar, it *is* necessary for the mufti or scholar to answer in the light of his knowledge. Imam al-Bukhari devoted a chapter heading in *Kitāb al-ʿIlm* to the same point: a question whose answer is likely to cause misunderstanding should not be answered.

**Does this mean nobody can ever know?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful: the ayah neither negates nor confirms it, and it does not say the Prophet ﷺ did not know the rūḥ's reality. If a prophet came to know it through *waḥy* (revelation), or a *walī* (a person close to Allah) through *kashf* or *ilhām* (illumination and inspiration), that would not be contrary to this ayah — and even debating the matter through reason and philosophy, while certainly useless and unnecessary, cannot be called impermissible.

## Ayat 86–87: what was given can be taken

*And if We willed, We could surely take away that which We have revealed to you. Then you would find no protector for you against Us in that respect — except as a mercy from your Lord. Verily, His grace unto you is ever great.*

Ibn Kathir reads these two ayat as Allah mentioning the blessing and great bounty He bestowed upon His servant and Messenger Muhammad ﷺ by revealing to him the Noble Qur'an — a Book to which falsehood cannot come, from before it or behind it, sent down by the All-Wise, Worthy of all praise. The warning is not an accusation against the Prophet ﷺ; it magnifies the gift by showing Whose it is. Ibn Kathir records that Ibn Mas'ud said: "A red wind will come to the people" — meaning at the end of time — "from the direction of Syria, and there will be nothing left in a man's *muṣḥaf* (his copy of the Qur'an) or in his heart, not even one ayah," and then he recited this ayah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the line back to ayah 85: **the sum total of the knowledge we do have is no private property of ours.** Allah can, if He so wills, take that away too. So the fitting response is gratitude for whatever knowledge one has, and staying clear of redundant enquiry — especially when pure enquiry is not really the objective at all, but testing others or belittling them. Persist in that crookedness, and it is not out of the realm of possibility that all one holds in the name of knowledge is taken away in full.

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān catches the rhetorical move: the address in ayah 86 is to the Prophet ﷺ, but the purpose is to make his followers listen and take the message. When even the knowledge of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is not within his own exclusive power and control, not much can be said about the rest of us. Then ayah 87 lands like a hand on the shoulder. The gift stays — not because it is owed, but because He is Merciful.

## Ayah 88: the challenge

*Say: If all humans and jinn were to come together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not produce the like of it, even if they helped one another.*

Ibn Kathir puts the reasoning at its root: even if mankind and the jinn all gathered and agreed to produce something like that which was revealed to His Messenger ﷺ, they would never be able to do it, even if they cooperated and supported and helped one another; this is something impossible. **How could the words of created beings be like the Words of the Creator, Who has no equal and peer, for there is none like unto Him?** The inimitability of the Qur'an is not a claim about literary taste; it follows from the difference between the Creator and everything else.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the challenge appears in other ayat of the Qur'an as well, and it is a fair one: if you do not take the Qur'an to be the word of Allah but the word of a man, then you too are human — why not come up with its like? And it is deliberately generous: not humankind alone, you are welcome to join up with the jinn, and still all of you combined will be unable to produce one sūrah — even one ayah — like that of the Qur'an.

Why go about digging into unnecessary issues when the Qur'an is sitting in front of you? When the humans and jinn of the whole world are incapable of producing the least like of it, what doubt could there be that it is the Divine Word — and once that is so manifestly proved, hardly any doubt remains that the one who brought it ﷺ was a true prophet and messenger of Allah.

## Ayah 89: every kind of lesson

*And We have truly set forth every kind of lesson for humanity in this Qur'an, yet most people refuse anything but disbelief.*

Ibn Kathir explains *wa laqad ṣarrafnā li-n-nās* — "And indeed We have fully explained to mankind" — as: We have furnished them with evidence and definitive proof, and We have shown them the truth and explained it in detail; and yet, despite that, most of mankind insist on disbelief, denying and rejecting the truth. And the explaining comes through *every kind of mathal*: every kind of similitude, parable and illustration, laid out in detail.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes the passage there: the Qur'an stands out as a miracle so clear that it leaves no room for any question or doubt, and still people do not thank Allah for His blessings, do not even recognise the real worth of the blessing of the Qur'an, and keep wandering around in error. That final "most people" is the verdict: the obstacle was never a shortage of evidence.

## Living it

**Ask to learn, not to test.** These questioners had already conceded that this man ﷺ had never told a lie, and still went hunting for a riddle. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's warning is aimed there — enquiry whose real objective is testing or belittling someone risks costing you the knowledge you already have.

**Hold back what does not help.** The Prophet ﷺ stood silent rather than improvise, and al-Jassas built a rule of teaching on the answer that came: fit the answer to what the listener can bear and needs.

**Say In shāʼ Allāh.** In al-Baghawi's report the whole pause in revelation traced back to one omitted phrase (18:23–24).

**Be grateful for what you know — it is on loan.** Ayat 86–87 teach a believer to hold knowledge the way you hold something borrowed and precious.

**Go back to the Book.** The proof they hunted for through the rūḥ was in their hands the whole time. When faith needs steadying, ayah 88 points not to speculation but to the Qur'an itself.

passages.title: The Meccans' list of impossible demands
passages.tafsir:
In these four ayat Allah records the terms the leaders of Quraysh set for believing: not a question, but a list of miracles strung together with "or … or … or" — a spring, a garden, the sky in pieces, Allah and the angels in person, a house of gold, a ladder into heaven. What holds the passage together is that it is one speech, and that it collapses at its own end: in ayah 93 they concede that even watching the Prophet ﷺ climb into the sky would not be enough — a book would have to come down with him as well. Ayat 90–92 and the first half of 93 are their words; the last line of ayah 93 is the answer Allah taught His Messenger ﷺ to give — a single short sentence that refuses the whole premise instead of bargaining with it.

## The night behind the Ka'bah

Ibn Kathir opens his comment on this passage with a long report he takes from Ibn Jarir, from Muhammad bin Ishaq. Ibn Ishaq gives his own chain: an old man from among the people of Egypt, who came to them forty-odd years earlier, told it to him from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Kathir names no hadith collection for it, so it is passed on here exactly as he passes it on, claiming no more for it than he does. What it does is lay the passage open like nothing else.

After sunset, the chiefs of Makkah gathered behind the Ka'bah: 'Utbah and Shaybah the sons of Rabi'ah, Abu Sufyan bin Harb, a man from Bani 'Abd ad-Dar, Abu al-Bakhtari, al-Aswad bin al-Muttalib, Zam'ah bin al-Aswad, al-Walid bin al-Mughirah, Abu Jahl bin Hisham, 'Abdullah bin Abi Umayyah, Umayyah bin Khalaf, al-'As bin Wa'il, and Nabih and Munabbih the sons of al-Hajjaj. They said to one another: send for Muhammad and argue with him, "so that nobody will think we are to blame." The message reached him that the nobles of his people had gathered to speak with him.

Notice what he did. "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came quickly, thinking that maybe they were going to change their minds, for he was very keen that they should be guided, and it upset him to see their stubbornness." He hurried to that meeting on hope.

**First they offered him a price.** They accused him of slandering their forefathers, criticising their religion, insulting their reason, slandering their gods and causing division — then offered wealth until he was the wealthiest man among them, or position, or kingship; and if a jinn had possessed him, they would spend their money on the medicine to rid him of it. He answered that his case was not as they said, that he had not come seeking their wealth, honour among them, or kingship over them, but that Allah had sent him as a Messenger and revealed to him a Book and commanded him to be a bringer of good news and a warner. He had conveyed his Lord's messages and given them sincere counsel; if they accepted, it was their good fortune in this world and the Hereafter; if they rejected it, he would wait patiently for Allah's command until Allah judged between them.

**Then they asked for their city.** No people, they said, had a smaller country, less wealth or a harder life than theirs: let his Lord move away the mountains that were constricting them, widen their land, cause rivers to gush forth in it like the rivers of Syria and Iraq — and raise their dead forefathers, above all Qusayy bin Kilab, "a truthful old man", to be asked whether what he was saying was true or false. His answer was the same: "I was not sent for this purpose."

**Then they told him to ask for himself.** Let an angel come down to confirm his truthfulness and speak on his behalf; let him be given gardens and treasures and palaces of gold and silver, and be made independent, so that he need not stand in the marketplaces seeking provision as they do — then they would know the virtue of his position with his Lord. He replied that he would not do it and would not ask his Lord for it; he was sent as a bringer of good news and a warner, not for this.

**Then they told him to destroy them.** "Cause the sky to fall upon us, as you claim that if your Lord wills, He can do that." He said: "That is for Allah to decide. If He wills, He will do that to you."

At the end the talk turned bitter. Why had his Lord not told him beforehand what they would ask and taught him how to reply? They had heard that the one teaching him was a man in al-Yamamah called ar-Rahman — and by Allah, they would never believe in ar-Rahman. They warned him they would not let him do what he wanted "until you or we are destroyed." One of them said they worshipped the angels, the daughters of Allah. Another said: we will never believe in you until you bring Allah and the angels before us, face to face. At that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ got up and left them.

'Abdullah bin Abi Umayyah — son of his paternal aunt 'Atikah, the daughter of 'Abd al-Muttalib — got up and followed him out, and delivered the last word: his people had offered him what they offered and he refused; they had asked things for themselves and he did not do it; they had asked him to hasten the punishment he warned them of. "By Allah, I will never believe in you unless you take a ladder to heaven and ascend it while I am watching, then you bring with you an open book and four angels to testify that you are as you say. By Allah, even if you did that, I think that I would not believe you." Then he turned away, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went home to his family, grieving over having missed out on what he had hoped for when his people called him, because he saw that they were resisting him even more.

## How that night stands behind the passage

Ibn Kathir places this report at the head of his comment on ayat 90–93, and returns to it when he explains why the demands were refused — "In the case of this gathering where the Quraysh came together to speak with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ…" So he is treating that night as the setting of the passage. What he does not do is walk through the ayat clause by clause assigning each one to a speaker, and it is better not to force a match he did not make.

Some of it, though, is simply the same words twice. In the report one of them says, "We will never believe in you until you bring Allah and the angels before (us) face to face" — the second half of ayah 92. They say, "Then cause the sky to fall upon us, as you claim that if your Lord wills, He can do that" — the first half of ayah 92. And 'Abdullah bin Abi Umayyah's parting speech has the ladder, the ascent watched by his own eyes, and an open book brought back down; Ibn Kathir's own gloss on "or you ascend up into the sky" is "you climb up on a ladder while we are watching you."

The two texts also run in the same direction at the end. The ayah has them concede in advance — "even then we will put no faith in your ascension until you bring down for us a Book that we would read." He had said it to the Prophet's ﷺ face: "even if you did that, I think that I would not believe you."

For the spring in ayah 90, Ibn Kathir gives a gloss rather than a scene, and it is worth taking exactly as he gives it (below).

## The words themselves

**"A spring" (yanbū', ayah 90)** — Ibn Kathir explains it as a spring of flowing water: they asked him to bring forth springs of fresh water in the land of al-Hijaz, here and there. He adds the point that governs the whole passage: this is easy for Allah, may He be glorified and exalted; if He willed, He could do that, and He could have responded to all their demands — but He knew they would not be guided by it.

**"As you have claimed" (ayah 92)** — Ibn Kathir reads this as a taunt built on the Prophet's ﷺ own preaching: you promised us that on the Day of Resurrection the heavens will be split asunder, broken and torn up, with parts of it falling down — so do that in this world, and make it fall in pieces. He notes it is like the prayer recorded in the Qur'an, "O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones on us from the sky" (8:32), and like the demand the people of Shu'ayb made of him: "So cause a piece of the heaven to fall on us, if you are of the truthful!" (26:187). And, Ibn Kathir continues, Allah punished them with the punishment of the day of Shadow — a gloomy cloud — which was the torment of a Great Day (26:189). It is worth pausing there. Of everything on the Quraysh list, this is the one item Ibn Kathir shows another people actually pressing for; and what came of it was punishment.

**"A house of zukhruf" (ayah 93)** — Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah all said this means gold; Ibn Kathir notes that this is also what was said in the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, "Or you have a house of gold."

**"You ascend up into the sky"** — Ibn Kathir explains: you climb up on a ladder while we are watching you.

**"A Book that we would read"** — Mujahid said this means a book with one page for each person, on which would be the words "This is a book from Allah to so-and-so the son of so-and-so", which he would find by his head when he woke in the morning. Personal, addressed, undeniable — every man his own revelation. And note where it sits in the ayah: it comes *after* they have already granted that the ascent itself would not persuade them. The bar was never at the last sign; it was always at the next one.

## Why Allah did not simply grant it

Ibn Kathir states the principle without hedging: if Allah knew that they were making these requests in order to be guided, they would have been granted, but He knew that they were making these demands out of disbelief and stubbornness. He supports it from the Qur'an itself — "Truly, those against whom the Word of your Lord has been justified will not believe. Even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful torment" (10:96–97), and "even if We had sent down unto them angels, and the dead had spoken unto them, and We had gathered together all things before their very eyes, they would not have believed" (6:111). Earlier in this same surah Allah had already said that what stops the sending of the signs is that the peoples of old denied them — Thamud were given the she-camel as a clear sign and did her wrong — and that the signs are sent only to warn (17:59).

He also brings the parallel passage where they sneer that this Messenger eats food and walks about in the markets, and ask why no angel, no treasure, no garden was given him — and Allah answers, "Blessed be He Who, if He wills, will assign you better than that — Gardens under which rivers flow, and will assign you palaces," before naming the real disease: "Nay, they deny the Hour" (25:7–11). The demands were never the obstacle. Denial of the Hour was.

## The choice he was given, and what he chose

Ibn Kathir then reports something that should be read slowly. It was said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "If you wish, We will give them what they are asking, but if they then disbelieve, I will punish them with a punishment that I have never imposed upon anyone else in the universe; or if you wish, I will open for them the gate of repentance and mercy." He said: **"Rather, You open for them the gate of repentance and mercy."** (Ibn Kathir relays this without naming a collection, so take it as he transmits it.)

Ibn Kathir calls him "the Prophet of Repentance and Mercy, who was sent as a mercy to the worlds," and says he asked Allah to delay their punishment, in the hope that Allah would bring forth from their offspring people who would worship Allah alone, with no partner or associate. And, Ibn Kathir adds, this is what indeed did happen: among those mentioned in that gathering were some who later embraced Islam and became good and sincere Muslims — even 'Abdullah bin Abi Umayyah, the man who had followed him out of that meeting and spoken to him as he did. He became a sincere Muslim and turned to Allah in repentance.

So the unanswered demands were not a refusal of mercy. They were the form mercy took: the sign withheld is the reason the door stayed open.

## The answer: "Glorified be my Lord!"

Against all of that, the reply in ayah 93 is one sentence: **قُلْ سُبْحَانَ رَبِّي هَلْ كُنتُ إِلَّا بَشَرًا رَّسُولًا** — "Say: Glorified be my Lord! Am I anything but a man, sent as a Messenger?"

Ibn Kathir unfolds it in two halves. *Subḥāna Rabbī* — glorified, exalted and sanctified be He above the notion that anyone would come before Him concerning any matter pertaining to His authority and sovereignty. He is the One Who does what He wills: if He willed, He could have given them what they asked for; if He willed, He could have refrained. The demands were not addressed to the right party.

The second half is the Prophet's ﷺ own station: "I am only a Messenger to you, sent to convey the Messages of my Lord and advise you. I have done that, and the response to what you have asked is to be decided by Allah, may He be glorified." The sentence claims only two things about him — that he is a man (*basharan*), and that he is sent as a Messenger (*rasūlan*). Not a rival lord; not a wonder-worker for hire; a man entrusted with a message.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the doctrine out plainly: the mistaken notion behind these demands is that a person who comes as a messenger of Allah should also possess all divine powers and be able to control everything. He does not. The duty of a Messenger of Allah ﷺ is only to convey the divine message. It is a different matter that Allah also sends many miracles to prove the veracity of the mission of His messengers — but that takes place exclusively with the power and under the control of Allah. A *rasūl* (messenger) is not given divine powers; he is a human being, never outside the framework of human power, except where Allah alone manifests His great subduing power to help him.

## Living it

**Answer hostility with clarity, not with anger.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that these were conditions anyone would hear as weird mockery and a very absurd excuse for not believing — and that when a person has to answer such things, he naturally becomes angry and retorts in the same manner. Yet in the answer Allah taught His Prophet ﷺ, nothing was said about their lack of sense, no mention was made of their hostile mischief, no verbal duel was fought. Instead the truth of the matter was made clear in very simple words. Maʿārif adds that the leaders and reformers of the Muslim community would do well always to remember this, making it a regular feature of their work among people.

**Do not confuse spectacle with proof.** The evidences Ibn Kathir cites (10:96–97, 6:111) say that those set against belief are not moved even if every sign comes to them; and in ayah 93 the Quraysh proved it themselves, conceding in advance that the ascent into the sky would not satisfy them. If your own faith is waiting on one more sign, it is worth asking honestly whether a sign is really what is missing.

**Know your job and stay inside it.** Four times in that meeting he was pressed to be something other than a messenger — a rich man, a leader or king, a transformer of their city and raiser of their dead, a man of gardens and treasures and palaces. Three times he answered that this was not what he was sent for: he was sent to convey and to advise, and he would wait patiently for Allah's command until Allah judged between them. And when they demanded their own destruction, he said only, "That is for Allah to decide." It is a restful place to stand.

**Prefer the door of repentance to the satisfaction of being vindicated.** He was offered the vindication and asked instead for the gate of repentance and mercy — and some of the men in that gathering did enter Islam, 'Abdullah bin Abi Umayyah among them. When people wrong you and you are tempted to want them ruined, remember what the mercy to the worlds chose when the choice was actually put to him.
